questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the name of the fracture depicted in the image, resulting from a fall from a significant height?
questions.explanation: The X-ray shows a pelvic fracture with widening of the pubic symphysis, giving the pelvis an appearance similar to an “open book.” This occurs due to anteroposterior compression forces, commonly seen in high-impact trauma such as falls from height or road traffic accidents. In an open book fracture, the pelvic ring is disrupted anteriorly, and the two halves of the pelvis are forced apart. This leads to: 1. 1. Widened pubic symphysis 2. 2. Possible sacroiliac joint disruption 3. 3. Risk of significant internal bleeding The mechanism described in the question (fall from significant height) supports a high-energy injury consistent with this fracture pattern. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Chauffeur fracture : Fracture of radial styloid (wrist), unrelated (C) Malgaigne fracture : Vertical shear injury with displacement, not symmetric opening (D) Bucket handle fracture : Seen in children, involves pelvic ring, different pattern

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with deep vein thrombosis was started on a new drug. After 2 days, he presented with the given finding. Which of the following drugs is implicated in causing the above condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Warfarin

The clinical scenario of the development of purple toe syndrome, after starting a new drug for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis, is suggestive of the adverse effect of warfarin.

Purple toe syndrome is a rare complication of warfarin therapy. It occurs due to cholesterol microemboli released from atheromatous plaques, which cause arteriolar occlusion. Warfarin must be immediately stopped and replaced with an oral factor Xa inhibitor (e.g. apixaban).

Activation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S are done by carboxylation of their glutamate residues, with the help of the reduced form of vitamin K as a co-factor. This reduced form of vitamin K needs to be constantly recycled back from its oxidized form for the reaction to continue. This recycling is done by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is competitively inhibited by warfarin. Hence, there will be a reduction in the activation of coagulation factors.

The image below shows warfarin's mechanism of action.

The half-life of proteins C and S are 8 and 24 hours, respectively, which is relatively shorter than the half-lives of other clotting factors, particularly factor II. Therefore, the full antithrombotic effect of warfarin is not achieved for 4 to 5 days. For this reason, warfarin must be bridged with a rapidly acting parenteral anticoagulant, such as heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), or fondaparinux, in patients with thrombosis or at high risk for thrombosis.

Uses of warfarin are acute deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and preventing stroke or systemic embolization in patients with a mechanical heart valve.

Adverse effects of warfarin are bleeding, skin necrosis, purple toe syndrome, and fetal warfarin syndrome (hypoplasia of the nose, eye socket, hand bones, and growth retardation).

The therapeutic dose of warfarin is monitored by an INR range of 2-3. Warfarin toxicity can occur when the INR exceeds 4 and can lead to fatal bleeding. Treatment includes withholding warfarin, with vitamin K, and blood transfusions or fresh frozen plasma to replenish clotting factors.

Warfarin, LMWH, and UFH do not accumulate in breast milk and do not have an anticoagulant effect in the newborn. They are compatible with breastfeeding.

Warfarin is mainly metabolized by the CYP2C9 enzyme. Drugs that affect the CYP2C9 enzyme can alter the anticoagulant function of warfarin and these include the following:

Reduced efficacy:

• CYP2C9 activation by drugs: barbiturates, carbamazepine, rifampin
• Oral contraceptives: increase blood levels of clotting factors

Increased efficacy:

• Drugs causing CYP2C9 inhibition:

• Amiodarone
• Azole antifungals
• Cimetidine
• Clopidogrel
• Cotrimoxazole
• Disulfiram
• Isoniazid
• Metronidazole
• Fluoxetine
• Sulfinpyrazone
• Zafirlukast

Other options:

Option B: Heparin acts by activating antithrombin III, thereby inactivating the active form of clotting factors II, IX, X, XI, XII, and XIII. Adverse effects are bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) due to the formation of antibodies against the heparin-platelet complex.

Option C: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor. It is used for the prevention of embolism and stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation. Bleeding and dyspepsia are the most important adverse effects.

Option D: Rivaroxaban is a direct inhibitor of factor Xa. It is used for prophylaxis and treatment of deep vein thrombosis. Side effects reported are bleeding, nausea, hypotension, tachycardia, and edema.
questions.learning: Warfarin — The clinical scenario of the development of purple toe syndrome, after starting a new drug for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis, is suggestive of the adverse effect of warfarin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On administration of phenylephrine, the following change was noted as shown in the images below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nodular episcleritis

The image shows a nodule surrounded by redness. On administration of phenylephrine, blanching of superficial episcleral vessels is seen. Hence, the probable diagnosis is nodular episcleritis.

2.5% phenylephrine can be used to differentiate episcleritis and scleritis. Since the vessels of the episclera are superficial, they blanch. Whereas, in scleritis, the vessels do not blanch.

Episcleritis is benign, recurrent, inflammation of the episclera, involving the overlying Tenon's capsule but not the underlying sclera. It is more common in women than in men. It is an allergic reaction to an endogenous toxin. It is commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Episcleritis is characterized by redness, mild ocular discomfort described as a gritty, burning, or foreign body sensation

Clinically, two types of presentations may occur:

• Simple episcleritis is characterized by sectorial or diffuse inflammation of the episclera.
• Nodular episcleritis is characterized by a pink or purple flat nodule surrounded by injection, usually situated 2-3 mm away from the limbus. The nodule is firm, and tender and can be moved separately from the sclera, and the overlying conjunctiva also moves freely.

Treatment includes topical NSAIDs, corticosteroid eye drops, cold compress, and artificial tears. In recurrent cases, systemic NSAIDs are used.

Scleritis refers to an inflammation of the sclera proper. It usually occurs in elderly patients (40-70 years) involving females more than males. It is frequently associated with an underlying systemic inflammatory condition. The patient presents with moderate to severe pain, redness, lacrimation, photophobia, and diminution of vision.

Scleritis can be classified as immune-mediated non-infectious scleritis and infectious scleritis. Immune-mediated non-infectious scleritis is further classified as:

I. Anterior sclerltis (98%)

a. Non-necrotizing scleritis (85%)

• Diffuse
• Nodular

b. Necrotizing scleritis(13%)

1. With inflammation:

• Vasa-occlusive
• Granulomatous
• Surgically induced

2. Without inflammation(scleromalacia perforans).

II. Posterior scleritis (2%)

Treatment options include:

• Non-necrotizing scleritis- Topical steroids and systemic indomethacin.
• Necrotizing scleritis- Topical and oral steroids, immunosuppressive agents and surgical treatment like scleral patch graft.
• Infectious scleritis- Antimicrobial therapy, and surgical debridement.

Other options-

Option C: Tenon's cyst or conjunctival inclusion cyst is a benign condition filled with serous fluid and slimy mucous secretions of congenital or acquired origin. Acquired cysts can occur following strabismus surgery, pars plana vitrectomy, scleral buckling, and Ahmed glaucoma valve insertion. The patient presents with swelling near the limbus with no pain or redness. The consistency is cystic to firm, non-tender with no mobility suggesting that the cyst is adherent to the underlying scleral tissue.

Option D: Phlycten is a white-pinkish nodule surrounded by hyperemia on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction due to endogenous allergens like Staphylococcus aureus (most common) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Treatment includes topical steroids; atropine if the cornea is involved.
questions.learning: Nodular episcleritis — The image shows a nodule surrounded by redness. On administration of phenylephrine, blanching of superficial episcleral vessels is seen.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following equations is used to determine the pH of a buffer solution?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is used to calculate the pH of a buffer solution based on the ratio of a weak acid and its conjugate base.

This equation explains how blood pH is maintained by the balance between bicarbonate (kidneys) and CO₂ (lungs).

Other equations:

A. Nernst equation: Calculates equilibrium potential of ions across membranes.

B. Goldman equation: Determines membrane potential considering multiple ions.

C. Gibbs–Donnan equation: Describes ion distribution across membranes with impermeant charged molecules.
questions.learning: Henderson–Hasselbalch equation — The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is used to calculate the pH of a buffer solution based on the ratio of a weak acid and its conjugate base.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the condition as shown below in the X-ray radiograph of a neonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia. The above X-ray radiograph shows congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Note the presence of bowel loops in the chest and absence of bowel loops in the abdomen.

* Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a birth defect of the diaphragm.

* The most common type of CDH is a Bochdalek hernia; other types include Morgagni hernia, diaphragm eventration and central tendon defects of the diaphragm.

* Malformation of the diaphragm allows the abdominal organs to push into the chest cavity, hindering proper lung formation.

* CDH is a life-threatening pathology in infants and a major cause of death due to two complications: pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension.

Bochdalek hernia:

* The Bochdalek hernia, also known as a postero-lateral diaphragmatic hernia, is the most common manifestation of CDH, accounting for more than 95% of cases.

* In this instance the diaphragm abnormality is characterized by a hole in the postero-lateral corner of the diaphragm which allows passage of the abdominal viscera into the chest cavity.

Morgagni hernia:

* This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia.

* It accounts for approximately 2% of all CDH cases, and is characterized by herniation through the foramina of Morgagni which are located immediately adjacent and posterior to the xiphoid process of the sternum.

Diaphragm eventration:

* Diaphragmatic eventration refers to an abnormal contour of the diaphragmatic dome.

* Elevation of the affected portion of the diaphragm is usually seen as a smooth hump, while the remainder of the hemidiaphragm contour is normal.

* This rare type of CDH occurs because in the region of eventration the diaphragm is thinner, allowing the abdominal viscera to protrude upwards.

Treatment:

* The first step in management is orogastric tube placement and securing the airway (intubation).

* The baby will usually be immediately placed on a ventilator.

* Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has been used as part of the treatment strategy in some cases.
questions.learning: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia — This rare anterior defect of the diaphragm is commonly referred to as Morgagni, retrosternal, or parasternal hernia. The above X-ray radiograph shows congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The children in a school underwent a health check-up whose ages were 2,3,4,4,5,6,7,8. What is their median age?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4.5

The median age here is 4.5 years.

In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value. In a distribution that has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the middle values, i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two middle values.

Here: elements: 2,3,4,4,5,6,7,8, therefore median = (4+5)/2= 4.5
questions.learning: 4.5 The median age here is 4.5 years. In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are congenital abnormalities of the gall bladder? I. The phrygian cap II. Floating gall bladder III. Absence of gall bladder IV. Spigelian gall bladder Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

The gallbladder may have several congenital anomalies involving its shape, position, number, and development. Most are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during imaging or surgery, but some predispose to torsion, gallstone formation, or surgical complications.

The following are recognized congenital anomalies of the gallbladder:

• I. Phrygian cap: The most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder. It is a folding of the fundus over the body, resembling the cap worn by ancient Phrygians. It is usually clinically insignificant.
• II. Floating gall bladder: The gallbladder is suspended by a long mesentery, making it unusually mobile and predisposing it to gallbladder volvulus (torsion).
• III. Absence of gall bladder (Gallbladder agenesis): A rare congenital anomaly resulting from failure of gallbladder development.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Spigelian gall bladder: There is no recognized congenital anomaly known as a Spigelian gallbladder. The term Spigelian refers to a Spigelian hernia, which occurs through the Spigelian fascia of the abdominal wall.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Early-onset fetal growth restriction is diagnosed before:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 32 weeks of gestation

Early-onset fetal growth restriction (FGR) is diagnosed when FGR is identified before 32 weeks of gestation.

• Early-onset FGR → <32 weeks
• Late-onset FGR → ≥32 weeks

Early-onset FGR is more often associated with placental insufficiency, preeclampsia, abnormal Doppler findings, and adverse perinatal outcomes.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Pott’s puffy tumor is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subperiosteal abscess of frontal bone

Pott's puffy tumor is the subperiosteal abscess of frontal bone. It is a complication of frontal sinusitis.

An acute infection of the frontal sinus can cause osteomyelitis of the frontal bone. Suppurative material then breaches the frontal bone leading to subperiosteal abscess formation in the tissues of the forehead. Pus may form externally under the periosteum as a soft boggy swelling with a doughy consistency called Pott’s puffy tumor. It may spread internally causing subdural, epidural, and periorbital abscesses as well as secondary septic thrombosis of the dural sinuses. It is more often seen in adults as frontal sinus is not developed in infants and children.

CT of the brain and paranasal sinuses is the most appropriate investigation. It can show the involvement of sinuses as well as intracranial or soft tissue spread of infection.

Treatment consists of large doses of antibiotics, abscess drainage, and trephining of the frontal sinus through its floor. Sometimes, the removal of sequestra and necrotic bone may also be required.

The images below show the clinical presentation and radiographic findings of the condition: red arrow - Pott's puffy tumor; blue arrow - intracranial spread

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year old pregnant woman came for a routine antenatal check-up in her second trimester. Four years back, she delivered 2 healthy full-term twins. What would her obstetric score be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. G2P1

The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1 (gravida 2 para 1).

The term gravida refers to the number of times the woman has been pregnant, irrespective of whether it crossed the period of viability. The current pregnancy is included in this count. Since she has been pregnant once before with twins and is currently pregnant now, gravida will be 2.

The term para refers to the number of previous pregnancies reaching a period of viability (gestation of 28 weeks). It does not increase to a higher number if multiples (twins/triplets) are delivered in a given pregnancy and still count as one birth. A current pregnancy, if any, is not included in this count. Therefore, para here will be 1 since she had one birth of twins and the present pregnancy is not counted.

Both gravidity and parity refer to the pregnancies and not the fetuses.

Note: The period of viability is when the fetus is capable of independent existence. The WHO defines it to be 24 weeks while the Indian definition is 28 weeks.
questions.learning: G2P1 — The obstetric score of a pregnant woman who previously delivered twins would be G2P1 (gravida 2 para 1). The term gravida refers to the number of times the woman has been pregnant, irrespective of whether it crossed the period of viability.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The culture media that is used to differentiate lactose fermenters and non-lactose fermenters is______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mac-Conkey agar

MacConkey agar is used to distinguish lactose fermenters (pink) from non-lactose fermenters (colourless or pale). It is a selective and differential media.

It is selective because bile salts and dyes inhibit gram-positive organisms and gram-negative cocci. It is differential because the pH indicator turns pink-red when the lactose is fermented.

Contents of MacConkey agar: Mnemonic: PLANT

* Peptone

* Lactose

* Agar

* Neutral red

* Sodium Taurocholate

Lactose-fermenting organisms (Eg: E. coli) produce a pink colour, and non-lactose-fermenting organisms (Shigella sp., Salmonella sp.) do not change the colour as shown below.

Other options:

Option B: Alkaline bile salt agar (BSA) at pH 8.2 is a simple medium used for the culture of Vibrio cholerae. The colonies are similar to those on nutrient agar.

Option C: Thayer–Martin agar is used for Nesseria.

Option D: Sabouraud Dextrose agar is used for fungal culture.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following combinations of seizure types and their corresponding medications is not accurate? 1. Generalized onset tonic-clonic: Lamotrigine 2. Focal seizures: Levetiracetam 3. Typical absence seizures: Topiramate 4. Myoclonic: Valproic acid
questions.explanation: The combination of "typical absence seizures with Topiramate" is "not accurate". Typical absence seizures (formerly petit mal) are standardly treated with "Ethosuximide" (the first-line agent) or Valproate. While Topiramate is broad-spectrum, it is not a primary or indicated treatment for absence seizures and can occasionally worsen them. Combination 1 is accurate: Lamotrigine is an effective first-line agent for "generalized onset tonic-clonic" seizures. Combination 2 is accurate: Levetiracetam is a first-line treatment for "focal (partial) seizures" due to its favorable side-effect profile (Option B). Combination 4 is accurate: Valproic acid remains the most effective "broad-spectrum" anticonvulsant and is the drug of choice for "myoclonic seizures" (Option D). Understanding the correct medication for each seizure type is critical, as giving the wrong drug (e.g., Carbamazepine for absence or myoclonic seizures) can lead to paradoxical exacerbation of the patient's epilepsy
questions.learning: The combination of "typical absence seizures with Topiramate" is "not accurate". Typical absence seizures (formerly petit mal) are standardly treated with "Ethosuximide" (the first-line agent) or Valproate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient, 10 years post-mastectomy, presents with multiple confluent, hemorrhagic, necrotic, elevated purple-black papules on the right upper limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This presentation describes Stewart-Treves Syndrome, which is the development of Lymphangiosarcoma in a limb affected by chronic, long-standing lymphedema. It classically occurs in women approximately 10 years after a radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. The lesion characteristically appears as confluent, purple-black, hemorrhagic nodules that may undergo necrosis. While cutaneous metastasis (Option A) can occur after breast cancer, it usually presents as firm, flesh-colored nodules rather than the distinct vascular-necrotic appearance of an angiosarcoma. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option C) arises from the epidermis and lacks this specific hemorrhagic/vascular profile. Kaposi sarcoma (Option D) is an opportunistic malignancy associated with HHV-8 and usually presents in different clinical contexts (e.g., HIV/AIDS). Lymphangiosarcoma is highly aggressive with an extremely poor prognosis due to rapid hematogenous spread. Treatment often involves radical amputation, though survival rates remain low. The primary prevention strategy is the aggressive management of post-mastectomy lymphedema through compression garments and physical therapy to reduce the chronic stimulus for malignant transformation
questions.learning: This presentation describes Stewart-Treves Syndrome, which is the development of Lymphangiosarcoma in a limb affected by chronic, long-standing lymphedema.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which surgical procedure should a 21-year-old boxer avoid to maintain optimal visual health?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RK

Radial keratotomy (RK) should be avoided in individuals prone to ocular trauma (e.g., boxers), as it causes permanent structural weakening of the cornea.

Why RK is contraindicated:

• Involves deep radial incisions in the cornea
• These incisions never regain full strength
• High risk of corneal rupture even with minor trauma

Why other options are relatively safer:

• PRK, LASIK, SMILE:

• Do not involve full-thickness radial cuts
• Better structural integrity compared to RK
• Though trauma precautions still apply, they are safer than RK
questions.learning: RK Radial keratotomy (RK) should be avoided in individuals prone to ocular trauma (e.g., boxers), as it causes permanent structural weakening of the cornea.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the type of placenta previa shown in the image below:
questions.explanation: In the given image, the placenta is located in the lower uterine segment and is seen reaching the edge of the internal cervical os but not covering it. This is the defining feature of marginal placenta previa. In marginal placenta previa, the placenta lies adjacent to the cervical opening (internal os) but does not overlap it. This distinguishes it from more severe types like partial or complete previa. Clinically, it may cause antepartum bleeding, but vaginal delivery may still be possible depending on the situation. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) Low-lying placenta: Placenta is in lower segment but does not reach the os (C) Incomplete (partial): Placenta partially covers the os (D) Complete: Placenta completely covers the os
questions.learning: In the given image, the placenta is located in the lower uterine segment and is seen reaching the edge of the internal cervical os but not covering it.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the preferred method for inducing anesthesia through inhalation in children?
questions.explanation: In pediatric anesthesia, inhalation induction is often preferred over intravenous induction to avoid the distress of needle sticks in an awake child. Sevoflurane (Option A) is the gold standard for this purpose. It has a non-pungent odor and does not irritate the airway, which minimizes complications like breath-holding, coughing, and laryngospasm. Furthermore, its low blood-gas solubility allows for rapid induction and quick emergence. Desflurane (Option B) and Isoflurane (Option D) are highly pungent and irritating to the respiratory tract, making them unsuitable for induction in an awake child. Halothane (Option C) was the historical choice but has been largely replaced due to risks of halothane hepatitis and cardiac arrhythmias (sensitization to catecholamines). Therefore, sevoflurane's combination of airway safety and rapid pharmacokinetics makes it the most appropriate and preferred inhalational induction agent in the pediatric population
questions.learning: In pediatric anesthesia, inhalation induction is often preferred over intravenous induction to avoid the distress of needle sticks in an awake child. Sevoflurane (Option A) is the gold standard for this purpose.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is not classified as a non- depolarizing muscle relaxant?
questions.explanation: Muscle relaxants (neuromuscular blocking agents) used in anesthesia are divided into two main categories based on their mechanism of action at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. "Suxamethonium" (Succinylcholine) is the only clinically used "depolarizing" muscle relaxant. It works by mimicking acetylcholine, causing persistent depolarization of the motor endplate, which is often visible as muscle fasciculations. Pancuronium (Option A), Rocuronium (Option B), and Vecuronium (Option D) are all "non-depolarizing" muscle relaxants. These act as competitive antagonists, blocking the receptor without triggering a response. Suxamethonium is favored for rapid sequence induction due to its very fast onset and short duration, but it is associated with side effects like hyperkalemia and malignant hyperthermia. Non-depolarizing agents are used for maintaining relaxation during surgery and their effects can be reversed with agents like neostigmine or sugammadex. Identifying the category is essential for managing the timing of intubation and the reversal of anesthesia
questions.learning: Muscle relaxants (neuromuscular blocking agents) used in anesthesia are divided into two main categories based on their mechanism of action at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked as A.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Terminal bronchiole

The arrow-marked structure in the given image is the terminal bronchiole. It can be identified by the absence of cartilage, which would be present in the bronchus, and the presence of cilia and stratified columnar epithelium, which would not be seen in respiratory bronchioles and alveolar sac.

The following is a summary of the intrapulmonary passages:

Trachea → Main Bronchi → Lobar Bronchi → Segmental Bronchi → Terminal Bronchiole → Respiratory Bronchiole → Alveolar Duct → Alveolar Sac → Alveoli

Bronchi and bronchioles can be distinguished by the presence of cartilage and glands in the bronchi which are not present in the bronchioles.

Terminal bronchioles represent the most distal parts of the conducting passage. Each terminal bronchiole ends by dividing into respiratory bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles contain cilia and stratified columnar epithelium, whereas respiratory bronchioles contain few or no cilia, and simple cuboidal epithelium. Another differentiating point between the two is that terminal bronchioles would not communicate with the alveoli but respiratory bronchioles would have a communication with the alveoli.

Each respiratory bronchiole ends by dividing into a few alveolar ducts. Each alveolar duct ends in a passage, the atrium, which leads into a number of rounded alveolar sacs. Each alveolar sac is studded with a number of air sacs or alveoli.

A: Terminal Bronchiole, B: Respiratory Bronchiole, C: Alveolar Sac, D: Alveolar Duct

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presented with a history of fever, conjunctival congestion, and erythematous desquamation of the skin as shown in the images below. A 2D echo shows a coronary aneurysm. What is the first line of treatment for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IVIG

This child with a history of fever, conjunctival congestion, strawberry tongue, and erythematous desquamation of the skin is likely to have Kawasaki's disease. The first line of treatment in Kawasaki disease is IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin).

Kawasaki's disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome. It is a vasculitis condition of unknown etiology.  Clinical features include a high spiking fever that is unresponsive to antipyretics. The fever can last between 5 days to 3-4 weeks. The five principal clinical criteria for Kawasaki's disease are:

• Bilateral nonexudative conjunctival infection with limbal sparing
• Erythema of the oral and pharyngeal mucosa, strawberry tongue, and red, cracked lips
• Edema and erythema of the hands and feet
• Various forms of rash- maculopapular, erythema multiforme, scarlatiniform
• Nonsuppurative cervical lymphadenopathy

Diagnosis requires fever and at least four of the five principal criteria. Myocarditis develops frequently in acute Kawasaki disease. It presents as tachycardia and reduced ventricular systolic function. The tachycardia will be disproportionate to the fever. Patients may develop coronary artery aneurysms in the 2nd to 3rd week of illness. They are generally asymptomatic and diagnosed on echocardiography. However, if large it can lead to death. Thus, echocardiography should be performed at diagnosis and after 1-2 weeks.

Other symptoms include periungual desquamation, gastrointestinal symptoms (vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea), cough, rhinorrhea, and arthritis. Laboratory evaluation will reveal elevated leukocytes, platelets, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein levels.

Treatment involves 2g/kg of intravenous immunoglobulin as an infusion over 10-12 hours within 10 days of onset. Moderate to high-dose aspirin should be administered until the patient is afebrile.
questions.learning: IVIG — This child with a history of fever, conjunctival congestion, strawberry tongue, and erythematous desquamation of the skin is likely to have Kawasaki's disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with persistent lower back pain, and imaging studies reveal sclerotic lesions involving the vertebral bodies. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In an elderly male presenting with back pain and sclerotic (osteoblastic) lesions on spinal imaging, metastatic prostate cancer must be the primary suspicion. While most cancers (like lung, breast, and kidney) cause lytic (bone-destroying) lesions, prostate cancer is unique in its tendency to produce dense, sclerotic bone metastases. Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease, Option B) usually causes lytic destruction of the vertebral bodies and disc space narrowing, often with a paravertebral abscess. Renal cell carcinoma (Option C) and colon cancer (Option D) typically cause lytic lesions when they metastasize to the bone. Sclerotic lesions in the spine are a common cause of pathological fractures and spinal cord compression in these patients. Diagnosis is supported by an elevated serum Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) level and confirmed by prostate biopsy. Bone scans are highly sensitive for detecting these osteoblastic areas throughout the skeleton, which represent the body's attempt at disorganized bone formation in response to tumor cells
questions.learning: In an elderly male presenting with back pain and sclerotic (osteoblastic) lesions on spinal imaging, metastatic prostate cancer must be the primary suspicion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A male patient complained of visual disturbances. On examination, the light reflex is absent but the accommodation reflex is present. what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neurosyphillis

The clinical picture where his pupils accommodate but do not react to light is called Argyll Robertson pupil. It is seen in neurosyphillis.

Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP) are bilateral small pupils with the following characteristics:

* Accommodation Reflex Present (ARP): Reduce in size on a near object (i.e., they accommodate)

* Light Reflex absent: Do not constrict when exposed to bright light (i.e., they do not react to light).

* This is an example of light near dissociation.

* Seen in neurosyphilis, along with other features such as the following:

* Loss of reflexes in the legs; impaired position and vibratory sense; Romberg’s sign; and, in almost all cases, bilateral Argyll Robertson pupils, which fail to constrict to light but accommodate.

Other causes of light-near dissociation are:

In unilateral eye

* Adie pupil

* Herpes zoster ophthalmicus

* Aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve

In bilateral eyes

* Type 1 diabetes mellitus

* Myotonic dystrophy
questions.learning: Neurosyphillis — The clinical picture where his pupils accommodate but do not react to light is called Argyll Robertson pupil. Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP) are bilateral small pupils with the following characteristics: * Accommodation Reflex…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which vitamin is given to prevent neural tube defects?
questions.explanation: Folic acid (Vitamin B9) supplementation is the standard of care to significantly reduce the risk of Neural Tube Defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida and anencephaly. NTDs occur during the first few weeks of pregnancy, often before a woman knows she is pregnant. For this reason, women of childbearing age are advised to take of folic acid daily. For those with a prior history of an NTD-affected pregnancy, a higher dose of daily is recommended starting three months before conception. Vitamin B1 (Thiamine, Option A), Vitamin B3 (Niacin, Option B), and Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin, Option D) are essential for general health and fetal development but do not share the specific, evidence-based protective role of folic acid in closing the neural tube. Consequently, ensuring adequate folate levels through diet and supplementation is a critical public health strategy in prenatal care
questions.learning: Folic acid (Vitamin B9) supplementation is the standard of care to significantly reduce the risk of Neural Tube Defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida and anencephaly.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the name of the physical sign shown in the image as observed in a 30-year-old male patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical image demonstrates a significant thickening of the distal parts of the fingers and increased curvature of the nail plates, leading to the loss of the normal angle between the nail and the nail bed (Schamroth's window). This finding is known as digital clubbing. It is associated with various chronic conditions including cyanotic heart disease, lung abscesses, bronchiectasis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Spoon-shaped nails (Option A), or koilonychia, are concave and typically associated with chronic iron deficiency anemia. Raynaud's phenomenon (Option B) involves sequential color changes (white to blue to red) in the digits due to vasospasm in response to cold or stress. Pallor (Option C) refers to an abnormal paleness of the skin or mucous membranes often seen in the conjunctiva or nail beds in anemic states. The "drumstick" appearance shown is specifically characteristic of clubbing. Evaluation should focus on identifying the underlying systemic disease responsible for the periosteal changes and increased vascularity in the fingertips
questions.learning: The clinical image demonstrates a significant thickening of the distal parts of the fingers and increased curvature of the nail plates, leading to the loss of the normal angle between the nail and the nail bed (Schamroth's window).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is amplified in an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DNA

In an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus DNA is amplified.

COVID-19 virus (Coronavirus) is a single-stranded linear RNA virus. RT-PCR is used to identify the RNA of this virus by generating complementary DNA (cDNA) copies of the mRNA using the reverse transcriptase enzyme.

The steps of RT-PCR can be explained as follows:

* Isolation of RNA

* Reverse transcription- Synthesis of DNA from RNA by using an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase

* Polymerase chain reaction- Using heat-stable DNA polymerase, such as Taq polymerase, DNA is amplified

* Separation of the PCR products-  by agarose gel electrophoresis

* Visualisation of the amplified DNA (with ethidium bromide)

(Note again that it is the DNA that is amplified and not RNA even though we are trying to detect an RNA virus)
questions.learning: DNA — In an RT-PCR test for the COVID-19 virus DNA is amplified. COVID-19 virus (Coronavirus) is a single-stranded linear RNA virus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with renal insufficiency presented with very low urine output, pedal edema, headache and BP 160/90. Which anti-hypertensive can be administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chlorthalidone

The antihypertensive that can be given in this case is chlorthalidone. The patient in this case is having renal insufficiency but there is no proteinuria mentioned in the question stem. So among the given options, the thiazide diuretic chlorthalidone can be administered as antihypertensive in this patient.

Management of hypertension in chronic kidney disease(CKD):

ACE inhibitors or ARBs are considered the first-line drugs in patients with proteinuria. These agents effectively reduce blood pressure, proteinuria and prevent kidney decline. Calcium channel blockers can be added if necessary.

For patients who do not have proteinuria, there is no established first-line therapy. One or two of the following drugs can be used:

• Thiazides/thiazide-like diuretics
• ACE inhibitors or ARBs
• Calcium channel blockers

In patients presenting with fluid retention or fluid overload, thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide are recommended for management. In CKD stages 1 to 3 (GFR >=30ml/min), thiazides are recommended, while loop diuretics such as bumetanide, furosemide are used in stages 4-5 (GFR < 30ml/min).

Other options:

Option A: Aliskiren is a direct renin inhibitor. It effectively lowers blood pressure, reduces albuminuria, and limits left ventricular hypertrophy.

Option C: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. A common side effect of amlodipine is the production of peripheral edema.

Option D: Prazosin is a selective α1 antagonist. It is generally not used as an initial agent to treat hypertension, except in symptomatic prostatism or nightmares linked to posttraumatic stress disorder. Headache is one of the side effects of prazosin.
questions.learning: Chlorthalidone — The antihypertensive that can be given in this case is chlorthalidone. The patient in this case is having renal insufficiency but there is no proteinuria mentioned in the question stem.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with gradually progressive, nonspecific symptoms over several months. He reports painless swelling in the neck due to enlarged lymph nodes and a recent onset of hearing loss, which is found to be conductive on evaluation. Otoscopic examination shows a dull tympanic membrane, and further assessment reveals reduced mobility of the soft palate. Considering this constellation of findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of painless neck nodes (lymphadenopathy), unilateral conductive hearing loss (due to Eustachian tube obstruction and serous otitis media), and decreased palate mobility is the classic clinical triad for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC). The "dull tympanic membrane" reflects the middle ear effusion common in these patients. NPC often presents silently in the Rosenmüller's fossa. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (Option B) typically involves major salivary glands. Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (Option C) is a benign, highly vascular tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, not 60-year-olds. Quinsy (Option D) is an acute peritonsillar abscess causing severe pain, fever, and trismus, not chronic lymphadenopathy and hearing loss. In an older patient presenting with unilateral ear effusion and neck nodes, the nasopharynx must always be examined to rule out carcinoma. Therefore, NPC is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of painless neck nodes (lymphadenopathy), unilateral conductive hearing loss (due to Eustachian tube obstruction and serous otitis media), and decreased palate mobility is the classic clinical triad for Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A lymph node biopsy of a 30-year-old male with cervical lymphadenopathy showed the following picture. The diagnosis is_____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hodgkin disease

In the picture given above, Reed–Sternberg (RS) cells are seen, which is a pathognomonic feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL).

Reed–Sternberg cells :

* RS cells are large and either multinucleated or have a bilobed nucleus (thus resembling an "owl's eye" appearance) with prominent eosinophilic inclusion-like nucleoli.

* The RS cell is clonal in origin and arises from the germinal center B cells but typically has lost most B-cell gene expression and function.

* Reed Sternberg cells are not diagnostic for any condition since they are seen in many conditions such as:

* Hodgkin’s lymphoma

* Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (commonly in immunoblastic type)

* Infectious mononucleosis

* Sarcomas

Hodgkin's lymphoma:

* The patient commonly presents with palpable, firm, rubbery, non-tender lymphadenopathy in the cervical or supraclavicular region. Systemic symptoms that are classified as B symptoms including Hodgkin's lymphoma are persistent fever (>100.4ºF), drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss of >10% body weight over the past 6 months.

* It is characterized by a variable number of RS cells surrounded by an inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils in different proportions, depending on the HL histologic subtype.

* The interaction between the RS cell and these background inflammatory cells with their associated cytokine release is important in the development and progression of HL.

Other options:

Option A: A peripheral blood smear showing numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes is characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). There is also the presence of bilobed nuclei and multiple coarse azurophilic granules.

Option C: Histopathology of human papillomavirus lesion shows koilocytes, perinuclear halo, multinucleation, and acanthosis.

Option D: In chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) the peripheral smear contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.

Pearl PF1558: Variants of Reed Sternberg Cells

Variant Reed–Sternberg cells and the corresponding subtype of Hodgkin's Lymphoma

* Lacunar Variant: Nodular Sclerosis

* Mononuclear variant: Mixed cellularity and Lymphocyte rich

* Pleomorphic/Necrotic/Mummified Variant: Lymphocyte depleted

* L&H/Lymphohistiocytic/Popcorn Variant: Lymphocyte predominant

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32-year-old patient presents with a visible swelling just below the ear accompanied by pain in the earlobe. The patient also reports difficulty in completely closing the left eye and problems while eating. This combination of findings points toward involvement of a cranial nerve. Which nerve is most likely damaged based on this presentation?
questions.explanation: The patient’s inability to fully close the eye and difficulty eating (likely due to cheek muscle weakness) are classic signs of facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) palsy. The facial nerve passes through the parotid gland, located just beneath the ear. A swelling in this area, such as a parotid tumor or inflammation, can compress the nerve and result in paralysis of the muscles of facial expression, including the orbicularis oculi and buccinator. The greater auricular nerve (Option A) provides sensation to the earlobe and skin over the parotid but is not involved in eye closure or mastication movements. The auriculotemporal nerve (Option B) provides sensory innervation to the temple and ear but not motor control of the face. The vagus nerve (Option D) controls visceral functions and palate/throat muscles. Therefore, the combination of periauricular swelling and motor facial paralysis identifies the facial nerve as the site of injury
questions.learning: The patient’s inability to fully close the eye and difficulty eating (likely due to cheek muscle weakness) are classic signs of facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) palsy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient complains of decreased sensation in the lateral 3 ½ fingers of the palmar side of the right hand along with difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb. Associated thenar atrophy is also present. What is the associated nerve injury in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High median nerve

• Sensory loss over the lateral 3½ fingers (palmar side) with thenar muscle atrophy indicates a proximal median nerve lesion.
• Difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb reflects weakness of thenar muscles (OP, APB, FPB) supplied by median nerve.
• Ulnar and radial nerves have different sensory distributions, while anterior interosseous nerve is purely motor and spares sensation and thenar eminence.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman presents with chronic sinusitis, recurrent respiratory infections, and infertility. Examination reveals situs inversus. Which condition is most likely responsible for this combination of findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of chronic sinusitis, recurrent respiratory infections (bronchiectasis), and infertility in a patient with situs inversus is diagnostic for Kartagener syndrome, which is a classic form of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD). This autosomal recessive condition involves a structural defect in the ciliary dynein arms, rendering cilia and sperm flagella immobile. The lack of ciliary clearance leads to chronic airway infections, while the immobile flagella cause female (due to impaired fallopian tube cilia) and male infertility. Akinesia (Option B), Tardive dyskinesia (Option C), and Athetosis (Option D) are various types of motor movement disorders associated with basal ganglia dysfunction or drug side effects, entirely unrelated to ciliary or organ-positioning pathologies. Diagnosis of PCD is supported by low nasal nitric oxide and confirmed by electron microscopy of ciliary biopsies. Management centers on aggressive respiratory hygiene, prompt treatment of infections, and assisted reproductive techniques for infertility. The presence of situs inversus is the definitive clinical anchor for this diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical triad of chronic sinusitis, recurrent respiratory infections (bronchiectasis), and infertility in a patient with situs inversus is diagnostic for Kartagener syndrome, which is a classic form of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida woman at 26 weeks gestation, presented with a BP of 150/90 mm Hg. Which test should be done next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urine dipstick

Urine dipstick should be the test that should be done next.

The patient is found to have BP> 140/90mm/hg after 20 weeks of gestation. It can be either gestational hypertension or Preeclampsia.

Gestational hypertension: BP≥ 140/90 mm of hg for the first time in pregnancy after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive woman without proteinuria.

Pre-eclampsia: Gestational hypertension along with proteinuria.

Proteinuria is the presence of total protein in 24 hours of urine of 0.3 g or more OR urine protein/creatinine (P/C) ratio >0.3 OR equal to 1 + (persistent 30 mg/dL) protein in at least two random clean-catch urine samples tested 4 hours apart in the absence of urinary tract infection is considered significant.

Hence the test done next is a urine dipstick.

Other investigations in pre-eclampsia:

* Ophthalmoscopic examination

* Blood values: They are usually non-specific. Serum uric acid level and S. creatinine is done. A liver function test is also done. A coagulation profile is not necessary when platelet count and liver enzymes are normal.

* Antenatal fetal monitoring

Gestational Hypertension

Pre-Eclampsia

Chronic Hypertension in pregnancy

Rise in BP >140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks of pregnancy

Rise in BP >140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks of pregnancy

Previously known hypertensive or BP  >140/90mmHg before 20 weeks of gestation

No Proteinuria

Proteinuria present(>300 mg in 24 hrs urine or >30 mg/dl in the random urine sample or urine dipstick 1+)

No proteinuria
questions.learning: Urine dipstick Urine dipstick should be the test that should be done next. The patient is found to have BP> 140/90mm/hg after 20 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old primigravida who conceived after in-vitro fertilization therapy came for an antenatal checkup at 38 weeks of gestation. Her obstetric history revealed that she was pregnant with DCDA twins. On examination, the first twin was found to be in a breech position and the maternal blood pressure was found to be greater than 140/90 mm Hg on two occasions with grade 1+ proteinuria. What should be done next? (NEET PG 2020)
options: Monitor BP and terminate pregnancy if BP rises
Terminate pregnancy at 40 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediate Caesarean section

In twin pregnancy, the presentation of the first twin determines the mode of delivery.

Key Principles:

•

First twin breech → Cesarean section indicated

•

Twin pregnancy at term (≥37 weeks) with complications (e.g., preeclampsia) → prompt delivery recommended

•

Vaginal delivery is considered only when first twin is cephalic

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following undergoes Hofmann elimination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atracurium

Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, which is spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation.

Rocuronium, and vecuronium are dependent on the liver for excretion. Pancuronium excretion is primarily renal. A small percentage of the drug is excreted through bile (hepatic elimination).
questions.learning: Atracurium Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, which is spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation. Rocuronium, and vecuronium are dependent on the liver for excretion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with diabetes on insulin therapy plans to conceive and presents for preconception counseling. Her HbA1c is 8.5%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Conceive, increase insulin dose and then start folic acid
Increase insulin dose, reduce HbA1C levels and then conceive
Plan conception and increase the insulin dose once she conceives
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase insulin dose, reduce HbA1C levels and then conceive

Women with pre-existing diabetes should achieve optimal glycemic control before conception to reduce the risk of congenital malformations, miscarriage, and adverse maternal-fetal outcomes. Pregnancy should be deferred until HbA1c is optimized, with insulin therapy adjusted as needed.

Why not the other options?

• A. Conceive, increase insulin dose, then start folic acid: Organogenesis occurs in the first 8 weeks, so poor glycemic control at conception increases the risk of fetal anomalies. Folic acid should also be started before conception.
• C. Plan conception and increase insulin dose once she conceives: Optimizing glucose control after conception is too late to prevent many congenital malformations.
• D. Start folic acid and conceive: Although folic acid is essential, HbA1c of 8.5% indicates suboptimal glycemic control, which should be corrected before pregnancy.
questions.learning: Increase insulin dose, reduce HbA1C levels and then conceive Women with pre-existing diabetes should achieve optimal glycemic control before conception to reduce the risk of congenital malformations, miscarriage, and adverse maternal-fetal outcomes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 78-year-old woman with osteoarthritis is started on standard-dose warfarin for new-onset atrial fibrillation. She has no history of liver disease and drinks alcohol only occasionally. Five days after starting therapy, she presents to the emergency department with gingival bleeding and extensive bruising on her arms and legs. Laboratory studies show: • INR: 6.8 • Platelet count: 240,000/mm³ • AST/ALT: within normal limits Her only other medications are acetaminophen as needed and a daily multivitamin. She denies taking antibiotics or herbal supplements. Which of the following best explains this patient’s adverse response?
options: Increased drug effect due to heightened sensitivity at the drug target
Dose-dependent predictable toxicity occurring in all patients
Accumulation of an active toxic metabolite due to CYP450 induction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased drug effect due to heightened sensitivity at the drug target

This scenario represents a Type B (idiosyncratic) adverse drug reaction, where the patient develops an exaggerated pharmacologic response to a standard dose of a drug.

• Warfarin acts by inhibiting vitamin K–dependent clotting factor synthesis (II, VII, IX, X)
• Some individuals have increased sensitivity to warfarin, leading to:

• Excessive anticoagulation (↑ INR)
• Bleeding manifestations even at standard doses

This is due to heightened response at the drug target, often influenced by:

• Genetic variations (e.g., VKORC1, CYP2C9 polymorphisms)

Why not other options:

A. IgE-mediated hypersensitivity: Would present with rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis, not isolated ↑ INR

C. Dose-dependent predictable toxicity: Occurs in all patients at high doses, not at standard dosing

D. CYP450 induction: Would decrease warfarin effect (↓ INR), not increase

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with significant dyspnea and a paradoxical increase in jugular venous distension during inspiration. On examination, no cardiac murmurs are heard. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical finding of neck vein distension during inspiration is known as "Kussmaul's sign." Normally, the jugular venous pressure (JVP) decreases during inspiration due to the negative intrathoracic pressure pulling blood into the heart. Kussmaul's sign occurs when the right ventricle cannot expand to accommodate this increased venous return. This is a classic finding in Constrictive Pericarditis, where the heart is encased in a rigid, calcified pericardium. Patients also present with progressive dyspnea and signs of right-sided heart failure (ascites, edema) but usually have no significant heart murmurs. Aortic regurgitation (Option B) would cause a diastolic murmur. Tricuspid stenosis (Option C) could cause a murmur and an elevated JVP but would show a prominent 'a' wave rather than a positive Kussmaul sign. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (Option D) can cause right heart failure but is less classically associated with a positive Kussmaul's sign than constrictive pericarditis. Therefore, the combination of dyspnea, elevated JVP with inspiration, and no murmurs is highly diagnostic of pericardial constriction
questions.learning: The clinical finding of neck vein distension during inspiration is known as "Kussmaul's sign." Normally, the jugular venous pressure (JVP) decreases during inspiration due to the negative intrathoracic pressure pulling blood into the heart.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with vesicles and oral lesions. Histopathological examination reveals suprabasal split. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pemphigus vulgaris

The image given shows the row of tombstone appearance seen in Pemphigus vulgaris.

Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disease caused by the deposition of IgG antibodies against desmoglein 3, a protein that holds skin cells together. It is characterized by widespread flaccid bullae, which are large, fluid-filled blisters that rupture easily. The lesions typically start on the trunk and spread to the extremities. Oral lesions are common in pemphigus vulgaris. Histologically, pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by a suprabasal split with acantholysis (loss of cohesion between skin cells).

Acantholysis and cell apoptosis are the key pathological processes in pemphigus. Histological changes include:

• Intercellular oedema with loss of intercellular attachments in the basal layer is the earliest change
• Suprabasal epidermal cells separate from the basal cells to form clefts and blisters.
• Basal cells remain attached to the basement membrane, in a ‘row of tombstones’ on the floor of the blister.
• Blister cavities contain rounded‐up acantholytic cells, also seen in Tzank smears.

IgA disease (Linear IgA bullous dermatosis): Autoimmune blistering disease caused by the deposition of IgA antibodies at the dermal-epidermal junction. It is characterized by vesicles and bullae, which are large, fluid-filled blisters. The lesions typically start on the trunk and spread to the extremities. Oral lesions are not common in IgA disease. Histologically, IgA disease is characterized by a suprabasal split with linear IgA deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction. Anti-transglutaminase antibodies are positive in dermatitis herpetiformis. Patients present with erythematous papules and vesicles on the extensor aspect of elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. Histopathology demonstrates subepidermal blister formation with neutrophils located at the tips of the dermal papillae. Direct immunofluorescence will reveal the deposition of IgA in the papillary dermis in a granular or fibrillar pattern.

Pemphigus foliaceus

Pemphigus foliaceus is an autoimmune blistering disease caused by the deposition of IgG antibodies against desmoglein 1, a protein that holds skin cells together. It is characterized by superficial, flaccid bullae that are prone to rupture and erosion. The lesions typically start on the face and scalp and then spread to the trunk and extremities. Oral lesions are not common in pemphigus foliaceus. Histologically, pemphigus foliaceus is characterized by a subcorneal split with acantholysis and minimal inflammation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme is deficient in Von Gierke's disease?
questions.explanation: Von Gierke's disease, also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (GSD I), is the most common form of GSD . it is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase (Option D). This enzyme is critical because it catalyzes the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, converting glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose in the liver and kidneys. Without it, glucose cannot be released into the bloodstream, leading to severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (due to glycogen accumulation), hyperuricemia, and lactic acidosis. Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Option A) causes GSD Type VI (Hers disease). Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Option B) causes GSD Type V (McArdle disease). Glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency (Option C) results in GSD Type III (Cori disease). Therefore, the absence of glucose-6-phosphatase is the biochemical hallmark that distinguishes Von Gierke's from other glycogen storage disorders
questions.learning: Von Gierke's disease, also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (GSD I), is the most common form of GSD . it is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase (Option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A man presents with high VLDL and chylomicrons, with eruptive xanthomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presentation of elevated VLDL and chylomicrons signifies extremely high triglyceride levels. This profile is characteristic of Familial Hypertriglyceridemia (Type IV Hyperlipoproteinemia). The massive triglyceride elevation results in "eruptive xanthomas," which are small, yellowish skin papules appearing suddenly on the skin. This condition also carries a significant risk of acute pancreatitis. Familial hypercholesterolemia (Option D) involves isolated high LDL and total cholesterol, typically presenting with tendon xanthomas rather than eruptive ones. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Option B) involves high IDL and would show palmar xanthomas. Familial hyperlipidemia (Option A) is a general term rather than the specific biochemical entity described. Because the eruptive xanthomas and the specific elevation of triglyceride-rich VLDL and chylomicrons are described, Familial Hypertriglyceridemia is the most accurate clinical diagnosis. Management focuses on fibrates and lifestyle changes
questions.learning: The presentation of elevated VLDL and chylomicrons signifies extremely high triglyceride levels. This profile is characteristic of Familial Hypertriglyceridemia (Type IV Hyperlipoproteinemia).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss who does not benefit from conventional hearing aids, what is the most appropriate next line of management?
questions.explanation: When a child has profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) and derives insufficient benefit from conventional high-power hearing aids after a trial period, a cochlear implant is the gold standard of care. Unlike hearing aids that amplify sound, a cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells in the cochlea and directly stimulates the auditory nerve. Option A (BAHA) is used for conductive or mixed hearing loss where the inner ear is functional but sound cannot reach it. Option B (Tympanoplasty) is a surgical repair for a perforated eardrum or middle ear structures and does not treat sensorineural loss. Option C is what the patient has already failed. Early implantation (ideally before age 2) is critical for the development of normal speech and language skills due to the brain's neuroplasticity. The success of the procedure depends on an intact auditory nerve and dedicated post-operative auditory-verbal habilitation
questions.learning: When a child has profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) and derives insufficient benefit from conventional high-power hearing aids after a trial period, a cochlear implant is the gold standard of care.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with raised, erythematous nodular skin lesions, respiratory symptoms, and lymphadenopathy. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and biopsy demonstrates granulomas without central necrosis. Based on this presentation, which histopathological finding is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: The clinical constellation of skin nodules (erythema nodosum), respiratory symptoms, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is highly characteristic of Sarcoidosis. The definitive histological marker for sarcoidosis is the presence of Non-caseating granulomas. These are well-formed aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells that lack central (caseous) necrosis. Caseating granulomas (Option A) are the hallmark of tuberculosis, which presents similarly but shows central necrotic "cheesy" debris. Stellate granulomas (Option B) are seen in cat-scratch disease or lymphogranuloma venereum. Eosinophilic granulomas (Option D) are a manifestation of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Sarcoidosis granulomas may also contain inclusions like Asteroid bodies or Schaumann bodies. Diagnosis is established when these histological findings are correlated with the classic radiographic signs. While many cases resolve spontaneously, symptomatic pulmonary involvement often requires treatment with corticosteroids to suppress the granulomatous inflammation and prevent long-term fibrosis. Accurate histological identification is critical for differentiating sarcoidosis from systemic infections like TB
questions.learning: The clinical constellation of skin nodules (erythema nodosum), respiratory symptoms, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is highly characteristic of Sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 41-year-old woman presents with low mood, lack of interest in activities, poor appetite, and disturbed sleep. She had a similar episode five years ago, from which she made a full recovery. There is no history of elevated mood, rapid thoughts, or reduced need for sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Recurrent depressive disorder

The given clinical scenario of low mood, lack of interest in activities, poor appetite, and disturbed sleep, along with a similar episode 5 years ago, followed by complete recovery, is indicative of recurrent depressive disorder.

ICD-11 code 6A71 refers to Recurrent Depressive Disorder, which is defined by the presence of at least two depressive episodes, each separated by a period of several months without significant mood symptoms. However, according to the DSM-5, Major Depressive Disorder is classified as recurrent when there is a gap of at least 2 consecutive months between episodes, during which the individual does not meet the criteria for a major depressive episode.

A depressive episode is characterised by a period of depressed mood or diminished interest in activities occurring most of the day, nearly every day during a period lasting at least two weeks accompanied by other symptoms such as difficulty concentrating, feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt, hopelessness, recurrent thoughts of death or suicide, changes in appetite or sleep, psychomotor agitation or retardation, and reduced energy or fatigue. There have never been any prior manic, hypomanic, or mixed episodes, which would indicate the presence of bipolar disorder.

People with recurrent depressive disorder have more severe symptoms and have an episodic disorder, which sets them apart from people with dysthymia.

Other options:

Option B: Cyclothymia is a chronic disorder characterized by at least 2 years of fluctuating, mild hypomanic & depressive symptoms (that do not meet the full criteria for hypomanic episodes or major depressive episodes). It is a symptomatically milder form of bipolar II disorder.

Option C: Dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) is characterized by at least 2 years of depressed mood that does not satisfy the criteria for a major depressive episode and with no episodes of mania or hypomania. In children, a diagnosis of dysthymia is made if depressive symptoms are present for more than 1 year.

Option D: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a psychiatric disorder characterized by low mood, anhedonia (lack of interest in usual activities), loss of appetite, insomnia or hypersomnia, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and/or suicidal thoughts. While this episode does qualify in terms of symptoms, she has a history of a previous episode, which now qualifies her for recurrent rather than single-episode MDD.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents to the outpatient department with a congenital deformity of the external ear. What is the ideal age for performing otoplasty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5-6 years

Otoplasty (pinnaplasty) is ideally performed at 5–6 years of age, when:

• The external ear has reached approximately 85–90% of its adult size, allowing durable correction.
• The auricular cartilage is still soft and pliable, making surgical reshaping easier.
•

The procedure is completed before school age, helping reduce psychological distress, teasing, and bullying related to prominent or malformed ears.

•

Common indication: Prominent ears (bat ears), congenital auricular deformities (when adequate cartilage is present).

• Goal: Improve ear shape and symmetry while minimizing psychosocial impact.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man sustained a spinal cord injury as a result of a road traffic accident. On examination, his blood pressure is found to be 90/60 mmHg. The patient most likely suffered from which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurogenic shock

The clinical scenario of the presence of hypotension associated with the spinal cord injury is suggestive of neurogenic shock.

Neurogenic shock refers to reduced tissue perfusion due to loss of vasomotor tone to peripheral arterial beds. Neurogenic shock is usually secondary to spinal cord injuries due to vertebral body fractures of the cervical or high thoracic region that disrupts the sympathetic regulation of peripheral vascular tone. Loss of vasoconstrictor impulses results in increased vascular capacitance, decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output.

Primary injury in neurogenic shock occurs due to damage to axons and the membrane of neurons. Secondary injury occurs doe to vascular damage hours to days after the primary insult.

The clinical features are bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, hypotension and autonomic dysreflexia. The skin often appears warm and flushed and there is also presence of radiological evidence of vertebral fracture.

Treatment involves securing of airways, adequate ventilation and perfusion with fluids and blood products followed by administration of vasoconstrictors to improve vascular tone.

Other options:

Option A: Cardiogenic shock is caused due to the failure of the myocardial pump.

Option B: Septic shock is not likely in this clinical scenario, as there is no evidence of any infection.

Option D: Hypovolemic shock is caused due to a significant decrease in blood or plasma volume, caused by the loss of fluid from the vascular compartment. Haemorrhage, fluid loss from severe burns, diarrhea, excessive urine formation, perspiration, and trauma are some of the major mechanisms of fluid loss that can lead to hypovolemic shock.
questions.learning: Neurogenic shock — The clinical scenario of the presence of hypotension associated with the spinal cord injury is suggestive of neurogenic shock. Neurogenic shock refers to reduced tissue perfusion due to loss of vasomotor tone to peripheral arterial beds.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In which poisoning is cherry red hypostasis seen on postmortem examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CO Poisoning

Cherry red hypostasis seen on postmortem examination is seen in CO poisoning.

Postmortem appearance in CO poisoning:

* Bright cherry red discoloration of the skin, mucosa, blood, tissues, and internal organs.

* Congestion of the lungs with pink fluid blood.

* Pleural and pericardial hemorrhages are commonly seen.

* Bilateral symmetrical necrosis and cavitation of basal ganglia (globus pallidus and putamen) is the most characteristic feature of delayed deaths.

* Punctiform and ring form hemorrhages in the white matter of the brain.

Other options:

Option B: In hydrogen sulfide poisoning, postmortem hypostasis is bluish-green in color.

Option C: In yellow phosphorus poisoning, postmortem hypostasis is dark brown or yellow in color

Option D: In hydrogen cyanide poisoning, postmortem hypostasis is bright red in color.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action (MOA) of Rivaroxaban?
questions.explanation: Rivaroxaban belongs to a class of medications known as Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) that work by directly inhibiting Factor Xa. Factor Xa is a critical enzyme at the convergence of the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, responsible for the "thrombin burst" that converts prothrombin to thrombin. By blocking Factor Xa, Rivaroxaban effectively prevents blood clot formation. Inhibition of thrombin (Factor IIa) (Option A) is the mechanism for drugs like Dabigatran. Activation of antithrombin III (Option C) is how heparin and its derivatives function. Inhibition of platelet aggregation (Option D) describes antiplatelet drugs like aspirin or clopidogrel. Rivaroxaban is commonly used for the prevention of stroke in atrial fibrillation and for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). Its advantages over warfarin include a rapid onset, a predictable dose-response, and the lack of a need for routine blood monitoring (PT/INR)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1-year-old child presents to a village clinic with a two-day history of fever and cough and is now refusing feeds. Examination shows the child is calm, with a respiratory rate of 51/min and stridor. According to the IMNCI guidelines, how should this child be classified?
questions.explanation: According to IMNCI guidelines, the classification of respiratory illness depends on "danger signs" and breathing rate. In a 1-year-old child, a respiratory rate of 51 bpm indicates "fast breathing" (threshold is ). However, the presence of stridor in a calm child and the fact that the child is refusing feeds (an IMNCI general danger sign) automatically upgrades the classification to Severe Pneumonia or Very Severe Disease (Option C) . Pneumonia (Option A) is classified by fast breathing without danger signs. Cough and cold (Option B) is used when there is no fast breathing and no danger signs. ARDS (Option D) is a severe ICU-level clinical syndrome not typically part of the basic IMNCI classification colors. Because the child has both an audible airway obstruction (stridor) and is unable to feed, they require urgent referral to a hospital for oxygen and parenteral antibiotics. Thus, Severe Pneumonia is the definitive IMNCI category

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following correctly represent the basic criteria for identifying “at risk” infants, except:
options: Failure to gain weight during three successive months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Birth order 3 and above

The basic criteria used to identify “at-risk” infants include:

• Twins or multiple births → At risk because of increased risk of prematurity and low birth weight.
• Failure to gain weight for three successive months → Indicates possible nutritional or underlying health problems.
• Artificial feeding → Increases the risk of infections and nutritional problems compared with appropriate breastfeeding.
• Birth order ≥3 is not a standard criterion for identifying an individual infant as “at risk.”

Therefore, the exception is A. Birth order 3 and above.
