questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which one of the following is an antidote for Rivaroxaban and Apixaban, when reversal of anticoagulation is needed due to uncontrolled bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Andexanet Alfa

Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent (antidote) for Factor Xa inhibitors, including Rivaroxaban and Apixaban. It is indicated in patients with life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding requiring rapid reversal of anticoagulation.

It acts as a recombinant modified factor Xa decoy protein, which binds Factor Xa inhibitors with high affinity, thereby restoring normal coagulation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Idarucizumab: Specific antidote for Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor).
• C. Hydroxocobalamin: Antidote for cyanide poisoning.
• D. Glucarpidase: Used to treat methotrexate toxicity by rapidly degrading methotrexate.
questions.learning: Andexanet Alfa Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent (antidote) for Factor Xa inhibitors, including Rivaroxaban and Apixaban. It is indicated in patients with life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding requiring rapid reversal of anticoagulation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presents after an injury with the deformity shown in the image below. This appearance is characteristic of a specific nerve injury. Which nerve is most likely damaged in this condition?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a clinical condition known as "wrist drop," which is the hallmark sign of radial nerve injury. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers. When this nerve is damaged—often due to a mid-shaft humerus fracture or prolonged pressure in the axilla—the patient loses the ability to extend the wrist against gravity, causing the hand to hang in a flexed position. Injury to the ulnar nerve (Option A) would result in a "claw hand" deformity affecting the 4th and 5th digits. Median nerve damage (Option C) typically leads to the "ape hand" deformity or "hand of benediction" when attempting to make a fist, primarily affecting thumb opposition and finger flexion. Damage to the musculocutaneous nerve (Option D) would result in weak elbow flexion and loss of sensation over the lateral forearm. Therefore, the specific "drop" shown is diagnostic for radial nerve palsy
questions.learning: The image depicts a clinical condition known as "wrist drop," which is the hallmark sign of radial nerve injury. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A woman visits the gynaecology OPD for a scheduled ANC check-up. A 1st-trimester scan reveals that her child has anencephaly. This occurs due to the inability of neural tube closure at what weeks of intrauterine life?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4th week

Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. Neural tube defects (NTDs) result from the failure of the neural tube to close spontaneously between the 3rd and 4th week of in utero development.

Anencephaly is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation.  Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP).

The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly.

* Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, prominent orbits thereby resembling the face of a frog.

* Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.

Neural-tube defects can be prevented with pre-conceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies. 400 μg of folic acid is given starting preconceptionally and continud throughout pregnancy(In cases with no prior history).

The major NTDs include the following:

* Spina bifida occulta

* Meningocele

* Myelomeningocele

* Encephalocele

* Anencephaly

* Caudal regression syndrome

* Dermal sinus

* Syringomyelia

* Diastematomyelia (split spinal cord)

* Lipoma involving the conus medullaris or filum terminale

* Iniencephaly
questions.learning: 4th week Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. Neural tube defects (NTDs) result from the failure of the neural tube to close spontaneously between the 3rd and 4th week of in utero development.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Please rearrange the given options to correspond correctly with the cardiac auscultation areas shown in the image provided.
questions.explanation: Heart sounds are best heard at specific surface locations where the sound is transmitted through blood flow toward the chest wall. According to the markers in the image: 1. Marker : The second right intercostal space at the sternal border, which is the Aortic area. 2. Marker : The second left intercostal space at the sternal border, which is the Pulmonary area. 3. Marker : The fourth or fifth left intercostal space at the lower left sternal border, representing the Tricuspid area. 4. questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the wrong statement regarding the period of gestation calculation.
options: 1st trimester USG is the best assessment
Calculated from the last day of the last menstrual period
In an IVF pregnancy, day of embryo transfer/day of fertilization is needed to calculate POG
Crown-rump length is the best measure of period of gestation in the first trimester
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calculated from the last day of the last menstrual period

Gestational age or period of gestation (POG) refers to the duration of pregnancy calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP). It is usually expressed in weeks.

According to Naegele's rule, the estimated due date (EDD) is obtained by adding 7 days and subtracting 3 months from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP). Another method involves adding 9 months and 7 days to the LMP. Less than 5% of births follow Naegele's rule. It is based on a 28-day regular cycle.

If the cycle is shorter/longer than 28 days, corrected EDD is calculated as follows:

• For a 35-day cycle, add another 7 (35-28=7) days to the calculated EDD to get the corrected EDD.
• For a 25-day cycle, subtract 3 (28-25=3) days from the calculated EDD to get the corrected EDD.

Other options:

Option A and D: The best method of assessing the gestational age is by measuring the crown-rump length (CRL) using ultrasonography between 7 to 12 weeks of gestation. It is measured from the vertex to the coccyx. CRL (in mm) + 6.5 = gestational age in weeks.

Option C: In an IVF pregnancy, the day of embryo transfer/day of fertilization is needed to calculate POG.
questions.learning: Calculated from the last day of the last menstrual period Gestational age or period of gestation (POG) refers to the duration of pregnancy calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 30 y/o athlete reports sudden pain in the back of his left leg and an inability to push off the ground while sprinting. Examination reveals a significant weakness in plantar flexion. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the action of plantar flexion in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gastrocnemius

Plantar flexion of the ankle is mainly produced by the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, which together form the triceps surae.

Gastrocnemius:

• Origin: Medial and lateral condyles of the femur
• Insertion: Calcaneus via the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon
• Actions:

• Powerful plantar flexion of the foot
• Flexion of the knee

Clinical relevance:

• Sudden pain in the posterior leg with inability to push off while running often suggests gastrocnemius strain or Achilles tendon injury.
• This leads to weakness in plantar flexion.

Other options:

• A. Tibialis anterior: Dorsiflexion of the ankle.
• C. Tibialis posterior: Plantar flexion and inversion but not the primary powerful plantar flexor.
• D. Fibularis longus: Assists in plantar flexion and eversion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in "green"?
questions.explanation: The image shows an anatomical illustration of the larynx/throat from anterior view, with the green structure marked at the entrance of the larynx — classic position of the epiglottis, a leaf-shaped cartilaginous flap that guards the laryngeal inlet. Key Anatomical Features: 1. Leaf/spoon-shaped structure at laryngeal inlet 2. Located posterior to tongue base 3. Guards the laryngeal opening during swallowing 4. Attached to thyroid cartilage anteriorly via thyroepiglottic ligament Why other options are wrong: (B) Hyoid bone is incorrect because hyoid bone is a U-shaped bone located superior to the thyroid cartilage : it would appear higher up in the neck and has a distinctly different horseshoe shape. (C) Thyroid cartilage is incorrect because thyroid cartilage forms the anterior shield-shaped prominence of the larynx (Adam's apple) : it is a large bilateral plate structure, not the rounded leaf-shaped structure marked green here. (D) Cricoid cartilage is incorrect because cricoid cartilage is a complete ring-shaped cartilage located inferior to thyroid cartilage : it lies lower in the larynx, not at the laryngeal inlet where the green structure is marked

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of liver dysfunction presents to the outpatient department, and characteristic ocular changes are noted on examination. Considering the underlying liver pathology, which substance is most likely responsible for these ocular findings?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the clinical link between liver dysfunction and specific ocular findings, namely Wilson's disease. As discussed previously, Wilson's disease is a disorder of copper metabolism. In this condition, the liver's ability to excrete copper into bile is impaired, and its incorporation into ceruloplasmin is also defective. This leads to the systemic accumulation of copper. The liver is the first organ affected, presenting as anything from asymptomatic enzyme elevation to fulminant hepatic failure or cirrhosis. The "notable changes" in the eyes refer to Kayser-Fleischer rings (copper in Descemet's membrane) and sometimes "sunflower cataracts" (copper in the lens capsule). Zinc (Option B) is actually used as a treatment for Wilson's disease because it blocks intestinal copper absorption. Selenium (Option C) is a trace element whose deficiency is linked to Keshan disease. Iron (Option D) accumulation causes hemochromatosis, which primarily affects the liver, pancreas, and skin ("bronze diabetes") but does not typically produce the specific corneal rings seen with copper toxicity. Thus, copper is the primary pathological substance
questions.learning: This question reinforces the clinical link between liver dysfunction and specific ocular findings, namely Wilson's disease. As discussed previously, Wilson's disease is a disorder of copper metabolism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following effects of puberty are not mediated by estrogen? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hair growth

• Hair growth (Pubarche): The development of axillary and pubic hair is not mediated by estrogen. It occurs due to testosterone in both sexes.
• Estrogen effects: Estrogen plays a crucial role in various aspects of puberty, including:

• Breast development (thelarche)
• Development of internal genitalia
• Menarche
• Regulation of growth spurt
• Epiphyseal closure
• Cervical mucus plug formation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A ventouse vacuum was placed at the flexion point. What is the correct statement regarding flexion point?
options: Midpoint of anterior and posterior fontanelle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 cm from posterior fontanelle

An important step in vacuum extraction is proper cup placement over the flexion point which is a point on the sagittal suture that lies 3 cm in front of the posterior fontanelle.

Advantages of correct positioning of the cup in vacuum extraction:

• Maximum traction
• Minimum cup detachment
• Twisting of the fetal head is avoided
• The smallest head diameter is delivered through the pelvic outlet
• The success rate is improved
• Fetal scalp injury rates are lowered
• Perineal trauma is reduced because the smallest fetal head diameter distends the vulva

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Production of oxaloacetate is from which of the following amino acid?
questions.explanation: In amino acid metabolism, certain amino acids are classified as glucogenic because they can be converted into intermediates of the TCA cycle or gluconeogenesis. Aspartate is directly converted into oxaloacetate via a transamination reaction. In this reaction, catalyzed by aspartate aminotransferase (AST), the amino group of aspartate is transferred to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing oxaloacetate and glutamate. Alanine (Option A) is transaminated to produce pyruvate. Lysine (Option B) and Leucine (Option C) are strictly ketogenic amino acids; they are broken down into acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate and cannot be used for the net production of glucose or TCA cycle intermediates like oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate is a critical four-carbon intermediate that condenses with acetyl-CoA to initiate the TCA cycle and is also the starting material for gluconeogenesis in the liver. Thus, aspartate serves as a vital nitrogen and carbon source for these central metabolic pathways
questions.learning: In amino acid metabolism, certain amino acids are classified as glucogenic because they can be converted into intermediates of the TCA cycle or gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is being evaluated for endocrine disorders. It is noted that some hormones are stored in secretory granules before release, while others are synthesized on demand and not stored. Which of the following hormones is not stored before secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cortisol

• Hormones differ in their storage and release mechanisms based on their chemical nature.
• Peptide and protein hormones (e.g., insulin, growth hormone):

• Synthesized in advance
• Stored in secretory granules
• Released by exocytosis on demand

• Thyroid hormones (T3/T4):

• Unique among amines
• Stored extracellularly in the colloid (thyroglobulin) of the thyroid gland
• Released after proteolysis

• Steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol):

• NOT stored
• Synthesized on demand from cholesterol
• Rapidly diffuse out of cells after synthesis

Why not other options:

• A. Insulin: Stored in pancreatic β-cell granules
• B. Thyroxine (T4): Stored in colloid (thyroglobulin-bound form)
• C. Growth hormone: Stored in anterior pituitary granules
questions.learning: Cortisol • Hormones differ in their storage and release mechanisms based on their chemical nature. • Peptide and protein hormones (e.g., insulin, growth hormone): • Synthesized in advance • Stored in secretory granules • Released by exocytosis on demand •…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 21-year-old patient with a history of chronic alcohol abuse presents with confusion, tremors, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. What is the underlying cause responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with chronic alcoholism is diagnostic of Wernicke’s Encephalopathy. This condition is caused by a severe deficiency of Vitamin B1, also known as thiamine. Thiamine is a vital cofactor for several enzymes in glucose metabolism; its deficiency leads to neuronal damage, particularly in the mamillary bodies and periaqueductal gray matter. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option A) typically causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Vitamin B9 or folic acid deficiency (Option B) results in megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin B3 or niacin deficiency (Option D) leads to pellagra, characterized by the "3 Ds": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Immediate treatment with high-dose intravenous thiamine is mandatory to prevent progression to the irreversible Korsakoff syndrome
questions.learning: The classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with chronic alcoholism is diagnostic of Wernicke’s Encephalopathy. This condition is caused by a severe deficiency of Vitamin B1, also known as thiamine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old patient with a history of hypertriglyceridemia was prescribed statins to help stabilize his levels. Despite taking statins, the levels remained elevated at around 600 mg/dL. Which of the following drugs can be added to help lower his triglyceride levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gemfibrozil

In this case of a 50-year-old patient with a history of hypertriglyceridemia who was prescribed statins for his elevated triglyceride levels and still had elevated triglyceride levels, gemfibrozil can be given to help lower his triglyceride levels.

Gemfibrozil belongs to the fibrate group of drugs that bind to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARα), which stimulate fatty acid oxidation, reduce the expression of apo C-III (inhibitor of lipolysis), and thereby reduce triglyceride levels.

Gemfibrozil is a first-line drug for patients with markedly raised triglyceride levels. Episodes of acute pancreatitis are prevented in patients with chylomicronaemia and severe hypertriglyceridemia. It is most effective in type III hyperlipoproteinemia.

Other options:

Option A: Niacin - Decreases the production of VLDLs and decreases the catabolism of HDLs.

Option C: Cholestyramines are bile acid-binding resins and they increase the excretion of bile acids. This results in increased conversion of cholesterol mobile acids by the liver.

Option D: Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal sterol absorption, reduces LDL cholesterol, minimal increase in HDL level and also decreases the absorption of phytosterols.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents with diffuse muscle pain, generalized weakness, and marked tenderness a few days after completing treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis. He has a history of hypertension and ischemic heart disease, including a myocardial infarction treated with coronary stenting 6 months ago. His medications include metoprolol, simvastatin, aspirin, clopidogrel, lisinopril, and erythromycin prescribed for his throat infection. On examination, he is afebrile with no rash. Laboratory investigations reveal: • AST: 540 U/L • ALT: 45 U/L • Creatine kinase (CK): 10,100 U/L Which of the following best explains this patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Drug interaction

This patient has statin-induced rhabdomyolysis, evidenced by:

• Severe diffuse myalgia and muscle weakness
• Markedly elevated CK (>10,000 U/L)
• AST much higher than ALT, reflecting skeletal muscle injury rather than liver disease

The precipitating factor is the combination of simvastatin and erythromycin.

• Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, the enzyme responsible for metabolizing simvastatin.
• This markedly increases simvastatin plasma concentrations, predisposing to myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Allergic drug reaction: Usually presents with rash, eosinophilia, fever, or urticaria, not isolated severe CK elevation.
• B. Post-streptococcal autoimmune myositis: Rare and not associated with recent initiation of a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor.
• C. Viral myositis: Typically follows viral illnesses (eg, influenza), not bacterial pharyngitis treated with antibiotics.

High-yield pearl:

• Macrolides (especially erythromycin and clarithromycin), azole antifungals, protease inhibitors, and grapefruit juice inhibit CYP3A4 and significantly increase the risk of simvastatin- and lovastatin-induced rhabdomyolysis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
An alcoholic patient presented with severe abdominal pain. Pancreatitis was suspected and a CT scan revealed lesions with fluid collected near the body of the pancreas. Which of the following enzymes is most likely to be elevated in this scenario?

GGT- Gamma-glutamyltransferase

CEA- Carcinoembryonic antigen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serum lipase

In an alcoholic patient with acute pancreatitis, serum lipase is the enzyme most likely to be elevated.

Acute pancreatitis is often caused by gallstones (70%) or alcoholism (25%). The cardinal symptom is acute-onset severe pain in the upper quadrant of the abdomen. The patient usually presents in shock (hypotension and tachycardia) and tachypnoea. Some may also present with signs of bleeding into the fascial planes leading to discoloration of the sites involved:

1. Cullen’s sign: Around the umbilicus
2. Grey Turner’s sign: Flanks
3. Fox sign: Inguinal region
4. Bryant’s sign: Scrotum

The diagnosis is often clinical with a laboratory diagnosis. Though serum amylase (>3 times) is indicative of pancreatitis, serum lipase is preferred over serum amylase as it is more sensitive and specific. Contrast-enhanced tomography (CECT) of the abdomen can be used to exclude pancreatitis if in doubt.

The severity of the acute pancreatitis is assessed using the Ranson and Glasgow scoring system ( ≥3 at 48h of onset of pain ). APACHE, SOFA, SAPS, and MODS can also be used to assess the severity of pancreatitis in intensive care (ICU) settings.  Pancreatitis is managed conservatively with initial nasogastric drainage followed by intravenous fluids, analgesia, and frequent monitoring of vital signs, urine output, and blood gases.

Other options:

Option A: Serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) can also be elevated. It is a biomarker for pancreatic disease and alcohol consumption but is not sensitive and specific to acute pancreatitis.

Option B: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), a tumor marker that is elevated in the adenocarcinoma of the pancreas.

Option D: Elevated serum bilirubin is a result of (i) overproduction of bilirubin (E.g: hemolytic anemia) or (ii) impaired uptake by the liver (liver cirrhosis) or (iii) regurgitation of bilirubin (obstructive jaundice). It is not seen in acute pancreatitis.
questions.learning: Serum lipase — In an alcoholic patient with acute pancreatitis, serum lipase is the enzyme most likely to be elevated. Acute pancreatitis is often caused by gallstones (70%) or alcoholism (25%).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: After a normal delivery of a healthy baby, how soon should a primigravida initiate breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: According to WHO and national health guidelines, the initiation of breastfeeding for a healthy baby delivered via a normal vaginal delivery should occur within 1 hour of birth. This "golden hour" is critical for establishing successful long-term lactation and promoting maternal-infant bonding through skin-to-skin contact. Waiting for 1 hour or more (Option B) or several hours (Option C and D) is unnecessary and detrimental, as it delays the baby's intake of colostrum—the first milk rich in antibodies and essential nutrients. Early suckling also stimulates the release of oxytocin in the mother, which helps in uterine contraction and reduces the risk of postpartum hemorrhage. Options C and D reflect outdated practices. For a primigravida (a first-time mother), early initiation is especially important for building confidence and ensuring a proper latch under the guidance of healthcare staff. Universal adherence to the "within 1 hour" rule is a foundational component of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI)
questions.learning: According to WHO and national health guidelines, the initiation of breastfeeding for a healthy baby delivered via a normal vaginal delivery should occur within 1 hour of birth.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding ABO blood grouping?
options: Antibodies are naturally present since birth
The antigens are carbohydrate in nature
Antibodies are present only if antigens are absent
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Antibodies are naturally present since birth

Antibodies are not present since birth. At 2 to 8 months after birth, an infant begins to produce agglutinins (antibodies).

In the absence of type A agglutinogen(antigen) in an individual's RBCs, antibodies called anti-A agglutinins form in the plasma. Similarly, when type B agglutinogen is lacking in the RBCs, antibodies referred to as anti-B agglutinins develop in the plasma. Type A blood carries type A agglutinogens and anti-B agglutinins, while type B blood contains type B agglutinogens and anti-A agglutinins. Type AB blood possesses both A and B agglutinogens but no agglutinins. On the other hand, type O blood, which lacks agglutinogens, does have both anti-A and anti-B agglutinins.

The A and B antigens are complex oligosaccharides that differ in their terminal sugar. The agglutinins are gamma globulins produced by the bone marrow and lymph gland cells. Most of them are IgM and IgG immunoglobulin molecules.
questions.learning: Antibodies are naturally present since birth Antibodies are not present since birth. At 2 to 8 months after birth, an infant begins to produce agglutinins (antibodies).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child on workup is found to be suffering from a rare form of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency for which he has developed high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which of the following is the best dietary advice for the patient?
options: High protein and low carbohydrate intake
High carbohydrate and low fat intake
High fat and low carbohydrate intake
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High fat and low carbohydrate intake

Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency(PDH) can be due to a defect in any one/more of the components of the PDH enzyme complex. Patients are advised to follow a high fat and low carbohydrate intake.

In pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, there is a defect in the pyruvate dehydrogenase enzyme complex, leading to impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. This results in the accumulation of pyruvate and subsequent conversion to lactate, causing lactic acidosis and high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

To provide an alternative fuel source for the body, patients with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency are often advised to follow a high-fat and low-carbohydrate diet. By reducing the intake of carbohydrates, which are metabolized to pyruvate, and increasing the intake of fats, which can be metabolized via alternative pathways, the reliance on the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex can be minimized.

Therefore, option C (High fat and low carbohydrate intake) is the most appropriate dietary advice for a patient with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency and high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Other options:

Option A: High protein and low carbohydrate intake - This option is incorrect because a high protein intake would still involve the metabolism of amino acids, which can contribute to the production of pyruvate and further exacerbate the metabolic acidosis in pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency.

Option B: High carbohydrate and low-fat intake - This option is incorrect because pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, resulting in the accumulation of pyruvate and subsequent lactic acidosis.

Option D: Only carbohydrate intake henceforth - This option is incorrect because pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency specifically affects the metabolism of carbohydrates, leading to the accumulation of pyruvate. Relying solely on carbohydrate intake would exacerbate the metabolic acidosis by increasing pyruvate levels.
questions.learning: High fat and low carbohydrate intake Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency(PDH) can be due to a defect in any one/more of the components of the PDH enzyme complex.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought with barking cough and noisy breathing of 2 days’ duration. He has a history of running nose and some fever for the preceding 3–4 days. Examination reveals respiratory rate of 40 per min, subcostal retractions and stridor. The most important step in the management is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nebulized adrenaline

• The child has moderate-to-severe viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), suggested by the classic barking cough, inspiratory stridor, preceding upper respiratory infection, and subcostal retractions.
• Nebulized adrenaline (epinephrine) is the most important immediate treatment for moderate-to-severe croup with stridor at rest and respiratory distress. It produces rapid α₁-mediated vasoconstriction of the subglottic mucosa, reducing airway edema and improving stridor.

Why not the other options?

• B. Nebulized salbutamol: Acts primarily on bronchial smooth muscle and is useful for bronchospasm/wheezing, not upper-airway edema of croup.
• C. Subcutaneous adrenaline: Not the preferred route for croup; nebulized adrenaline acts directly on the upper airway.
• D. IV hydrocortisone: Corticosteroids are useful in croup, but dexamethasone is preferred. In significant respiratory distress, nebulized adrenaline provides the rapid improvement required.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deficiency of CD 55 and CD 59

Deficiency of CD55 and CD59 is seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).

It is due to an acquired mutation in the X-linked phosphatidylinositol class A PIG-A gene (Option A) causing a deficiency of GPI anchor proteins. GPI is a glycolipid that anchors membrane protective factors such as CD59 and CD55 to the membrane. The deficiency of CD55 and CD59 makes the RBC sensitive to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis(Option B). The anemia is usually normo-macrocytic (Option D).

Hemolysis tends to occur at night due to a slight decrease in blood pH during sleep, which triggers complement activity (nocturnal hemoglobinuria). PNH is characterized by hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis.

PNH is diagnosed using flow cytometry. The drugs of choice for treatment are Eculizumab or Ravulizumab which work against complement C5. Supportive management of PNH includes folic acid and iron supplementation. Bone marrow transplantation is another option for the treatment of this condition.
questions.learning: Deficiency of CD 55 and CD 59 Deficiency of CD55 and CD59 is seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). It is due to an acquired mutation in the X-linked phosphatidylinositol class A PIG-A gene (Option A) causing a deficiency of GPI anchor proteins.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient has cyanosis in the lower extremities, but examination reveals that the upper extremities are pink and well oxygenated. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Large Patent Ductus Arteriosus

Differential cyanosis (cyanosis of the lower extremities with pink upper extremities) is a classic finding in large Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) with Eisenmenger syndrome. Progressive pulmonary hypertension causes reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) across the PDA, allowing deoxygenated blood to enter the descending aorta distal to the origin of the subclavian arteries, thereby affecting the lower limbs while sparing the upper limbs.

• In a large PDA with Eisenmenger physiology:

• Initial shunt: Left → Right
• With pulmonary hypertension: Right → Left
• Deoxygenated blood enters the descending aorta distal to the branches supplying the upper limbs.
• Upper extremities remain pink, while the lower extremities become cyanotic (differential cyanosis).

Why not the other options?

• A. Severe peripheral vascular disease: Causes ischemia but does not produce differential cyanosis.
• C. Atrioventricular septal defect: Eisenmenger syndrome causes central cyanosis, not differential cyanosis.
• D. Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome: Causes hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with recurrent epistaxis and AVMs, not differential cyanosis.
questions.learning: Large Patent Ductus Arteriosus Differential cyanosis (cyanosis of the lower extremities with pink upper extremities) is a classic finding in large Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) with Eisenmenger syndrome.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child immediately cries after breastfeeding, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Which enzyme deficiency might be responsible?
questions.explanation: Symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, and distress immediately following the ingestion of milk (including breast milk) in an infant or young child point toward Classic Galactosemia. Breast milk contains lactose, which is broken down into glucose and galactose. A deficiency in Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) leads to the toxic accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate, causing immediate gastrointestinal distress and long-term organ damage. Aldolase B deficiency (Option A) causes Hereditary Fructose Intolerance, where symptoms start only after introducing fruits or juices, not with breastfeeding. Phenylalanine Hydroxylase deficiency (Option B) is PKU, which does not cause acute GI symptoms after feeding. Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Option D) is Gaucher's disease, which presents with hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain, not acute feeding intolerance. Because milk is the primary source of the offending sugar in this age group, GALT deficiency is the most likely enzymatic cause for these feeding-related symptoms
questions.learning: Symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, and distress immediately following the ingestion of milk (including breast milk) in an infant or young child point toward Classic Galactosemia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40 year old P2L2 presents to your office with foul smelling bloody discharge per vaginum. She has been diagnosed with Carcinoma of the cervix Stage III B as per FIGO classification. What is the primary treatment option for this case?
options: Radical Hysterectomy + Pelvic lymph node dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chemoradiation

The treatment option for Stage III B Ca Cervix ,as per FIGO 2018 guidelines is Chemoradiation.

Chemoradiation can improve survival rates. It allows for remission in certain cases or reduction in morbidity.

Pelvic exenteration may be considered in cases where a fistula is present.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the followings are seen in GDM except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malformations

Malformations are not associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Malformations occur due to the disruption of organogenesis, usually occurring in the first trimester. The abnormal glycemic status in GDM manifests only in the second trimester.

Overt diabetes (pregestational diabetes) is associated with higher rates of malformations compared to the general population. Neural tube defects (encephalocele, meningomyelocele, anencephaly), transposition of great vessels (TGA), ventricular septal defect (VSD), atrial septal defect (ASD), hypoplastic left heart, aortic stenosis and coarctation of the aorta are commonly seen.

Caudal regression syndrome is rare, but a specific anomaly seen in infants of diabetic mothers. Small left colon syndrome is a rare anomaly that develops in the second and third trimesters.

Other options:

Option B:  In GDM, increased blood glucose in the mother leads to fetal hyperglycemia. This can cause polyhydramnios due to increased fetal urine production.

Option C: Fetal hyperinsulinemia causes increased hepatic glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, accelerated lipogenesis, and augmented protein synthesis resulting in macrosomia

Option D: Fetal hyperglycemia in GDM triggers fetal hyperinsulinemia, resulting in neonatal hypoglycemia
questions.learning: Malformations Malformations are not associated with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Malformations occur due to the disruption of organogenesis, usually occurring in the first trimester.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a history of injury to the eye caused by a leaf 5 days ago, resulting in pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye for 2 days. What would be the most likely pathology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fungal corneal ulcer

The given clinical vignette of the patient presenting with pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye following trauma by a vegetative matter is suggestive of a fungal corneal ulcer.

Fungal corneal ulcer also known as mycotic keratitis is usually caused by trauma from vegetative matter such as branches of trees, leaves and animal tails. Injudicious use of topical steroids and antibiotics increases the predisposition to develop secondary fungal keratitis.

Mycotic keratitis can be caused by

• Filamentous fungi such as Aspergillus and Fusarium
• Yeasts such as Candida and cryptococcus
• Dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma and Blastomyces

Typically in fungal corneal ulcers, the signs are more prominent than the symptoms. The symptoms of fungal keratitis are similar to that of bacterial ulcers which include pain, lacrimation, photophobia, blurred vision, and redness of the eyes.

A typical fungal ulcer has the following signs:

• Greyish white looking dry corneal ulcer with rolled out margin.
• Feathery finger-like extensions into the corneal stroma under intact epithelium
• Wessley ring which is a sterile immune ring that occurs due to the deposition of immune complexes
• Multiple small satellite lesions around the ulcer
• Hypopyon: The hypopyon in fungal ulcer is immobile and unsterile unlike bacterial ulcer (sterile hypopyon)
• Perforation is rare
• Corneal vascularization is usually absent.

A diagnosis of fungal ulcer is made by a typical history of trauma with vegetative matter followed by clinical examination and KOH mount or SDA agar cultures from corneal scrappings.

The image below depicts a fungal corneal ulcer with the arrowhead indicating a satellite lesion.

Other options:

Option A: Anterior uveitis is the inflammation of the uveal tissue from the iris up to the pars plicata of the ciliary body. Infectious uveitis can be caused by the exogenous entry of the organisms following penetrating injuries, perforation of corneal ulcer, and post-intaocular operations.

Acute anterior uveitis presents with symptoms of pain, photophobia, lacrimation, blurring of vision and redness of the eye. Signs of anterior uveitis include:

• Aqueous flare -  It is the earliest sign of acute anterior uveitis, it occurs following the leakage of protein particles into the aqueous humor.
• Keratic precipitates(KP) - These are pathognomonic for anterior uveitis. They are proteinaceous cellular deposits at the back of the cornea arranged in a triangular fashion. These include mutton fat KP's as seen in granulomatous uveitis and granular KP's of non granulomatous uveitis.
• Iris nodules: typically occur in granulomatous uveitis. Koppe's nodules are at the pupillary border and Busacca's nodules are situated near the collarette.

Option C: Conjunctivitis is the inflammation of the conjunctiva of which the bacterial conjunctivitis is the most common. Acute bacterial conjunctivitis is characterized by marked conjunctival hyperemia, swelling of the conjunctiva(chemosis), edematous eyelids, sticking together of lid margins and mucopurulent discharge from the eye.

The image shows a patient with bacterial conjunctivitis.

Option D: Corneal laceration: Partial corneal laceration or lamellar corneal laceration occurs from a blunt trauma and is treated by patching and antibiotics.
questions.learning: Fungal corneal ulcer — The given clinical vignette of the patient presenting with pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye following trauma by a vegetative matter is suggestive of a fungal corneal ulcer.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which major histocompatibility complex (MHC) type is most likely associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The 26-year-old patient presents with acute unilateral anterior uveitis, characterized by blurred vision, photophobia, pain, and redness in one eye. The presence of concurrent joint pain suggests an underlying seronegative spondyloarthropathy, such as ankylosing spondylitis or reactive arthritis. This clinical constellation is strongly associated with the HLA-B27 antigen (Option A). HLA-B51 (Option B) is linked with Behçet’s disease, which typically causes bilateral uveitis and oral/genital ulcers. HLA-B47 (Option C) and HLA-B57 (Option D) have different associations (e.g., congenital adrenal hyperplasia or drug hypersensitivity) and are not classically linked with the combination of acute unilateral anterior uveitis and arthritis. Testing for HLA-B27 is a standard part of the systemic workup for recurring anterior uveitis. Therefore, given the classic inflammatory presentation in a young adult, HLA-B27 is the most likely associated major histocompatibility complex

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following metabolic changes is most commonly associated with hyperemesis gravidarum? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperthyroidism

Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe, persistent nausea and vomiting during pregnancy leading to dehydration, weight loss, electrolyte imbalance, and ketosis. It is commonly associated with transient hyperthyroidism due to:

• Markedly elevated β-hCG levels
• β-hCG weakly stimulating TSH receptors because of structural similarity to TSH

Clinical/laboratory findings may include:

• Elevated free T4
• Suppressed TSH
• Tachycardia and tremor in some patients

Typical metabolic abnormalities in hyperemesis gravidarum:

• Hypokalemia
• Hyponatremia
• Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
• Ketonuria

Conditions with very high β-hCG levels (eg, molar pregnancy, multiple gestation) increase the risk of hyperemesis gravidarum and gestational thyrotoxicosis.
questions.learning: Hyperthyroidism Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe, persistent nausea and vomiting during pregnancy leading to dehydration, weight loss, electrolyte imbalance, and ketosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following is the most life-threatening manifestation of CKD?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperkalemia

Of the given options, hyperkalemia is the most life-threatening complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD) as it can result in cardiac arrhythmias and sudden death.

CKD is staged based on declining glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and albuminuria. The various clinical manifestations occur due to loss of kidney function and accumulation of various uremic toxins (urea, creatinine, and other products of protein metabolism).

Complications of declining kidney function include:

• Volume overload
• Hyperkalemia
• Metabolic acidosis
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Mineral and bone disorders
• Hypertension
• Anemia
• Dyslipidemia
questions.learning: Hyperkalemia Of the given options, hyperkalemia is the most life-threatening complication of chronic kidney disease (CKD) as it can result in cardiac arrhythmias and sudden death.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following terms denotes the extensive sclerosis of the skin of the chest wall which restricts chest wall movement and is seen as a rare complication of systemic sclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hidebound Chest

Hidebound chest refers to extensive fibrosis and sclerosis of the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall seen in systemic sclerosis (scleroderma). The skin becomes thick, tight, and adherent, restricting chest wall expansion and leading to reduced respiratory movements and a restrictive ventilatory defect.

In addition to skin fibrosis, interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a common pulmonary manifestation of systemic sclerosis and further contributes to restrictive lung disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. Flail chest: Caused by multiple consecutive rib fractures resulting in paradoxical chest wall movement after trauma.
• C. Barrel chest: Increased anteroposterior diameter of the chest, classically seen in emphysema/COPD.
• D. Pigeon chest (Pectus carinatum): Congenital protrusion of the sternum and anterior chest wall.
questions.learning: Hidebound Chest Hidebound chest refers to extensive fibrosis and sclerosis of the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall seen in systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A hypertensive patient is taking three antihypertensive drugs including diuretics but the blood pressure is not controlled. He also has hypokalemia. Which of the following drug should be used to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spironolactone

Resistant hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic suggests aldosterone-mediated volume excess.

Associated hypokalemia further supports hyperaldosteronism.

Hypokalemia strongly suggests: Excess aldosterone

Aldosterone causes:

• Na⁺ retention → hypertension
• K⁺ loss → hypokalemia

This condition is known as:

Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)

Spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist, is the drug of choice in resistant hypertension.

It controls BP and corrects hypokalemia, unlike loop diuretics or potassium supplements alone.
questions.learning: Spironolactone Resistant hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic suggests aldosterone-mediated volume excess. Associated hypokalemia further supports hyperaldosteronism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the bleeding vessel in extradural hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: An extradural (or epidural) hemorrhage (EDH) occurs between the skull and the dura mater. The most common cause is a fracture of the temporal bone, which results in the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. This arterial bleeding causes the rapid accumulation of blood and the formation of a biconvex (lens-shaped) hematoma on CT scans. Bridging veins (Option B) are the vessels responsible for subdural hemorrhages, which typically occur in elderly or alcoholic patients following minor trauma. The Circle of Willis (Option C) and its branches, like the anterior cerebral artery (Option D), are common sites for aneurysms; their rupture results in subarachnoid hemorrhage, classically presenting with a "thunderclap" headache. Clinically, EDH is famous for the "lucid interval," where a patient initially regains consciousness after trauma before rapidly deteriorating as the hematoma expands and increases intracranial pressure. Urgent neurosurgical evacuation is required to prevent death from brain herniation
questions.learning: An extradural (or epidural) hemorrhage (EDH) occurs between the skull and the dura mater. The most common cause is a fracture of the temporal bone, which results in the rupture of the middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The following test is done to assess
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median nerve

The given image shows the pen test which is used to assess the median nerve.

It tests the abductor pollicis brevis muscle which is supplied by the median nerve. The hand must remain flat with the palm facing upwards; a pen is held above the palm and the patient is asked to touch the pen with his thumb - positive sign is unable to touch the pen.

Median nerve lesions can be high lesions or low lesions depending on the site of injury.

Low lesions - It occurs due to injuries at the distal third of the forearm such as carpal dislocation or cut wound of the wrist.  There is paralysis of the hand muscles; the patient is unable to abduct the thumb and has a loss of sensation over the radial three-and-a-half digits. The forearm muscles supplied by the median nerve are spared in these lesions. Wasting of thenar eminence is seen in long-standing cases.

High lesions - It occurs due to injuries above the elbow such as forearm fractures or elbow dislocation. There is paralysis of the forearm muscles along with all the features of low lesions.

Muscles supplied by the median nerve are given in the table:

Level
Motor supply

In the arm
No muscles

Proximal one-third of the forearm
All the flexor muscles of the proximal forearm, except the flexor carpi ulnaris and the  medial half of the flexor digitorum profundus

Distal one-third of the forearm
No muscles

In the hand

Abductor pollicis brevis

Opponens pollicis

Flexor pollicis brevis

First two lumbricals

Other tests for median nerve:

Pointing index sign or Oschner’s clasp test: The patient is asked to clasp both hands together. When this is done the index and the middle finger fail to flex due to the loss of action of long finger flexors which are supplied by the median nerve.

Benediction test: Due to loss of activity of the long finger flexors the patient is unable to flex the index and middle finger on lifting the hand. As this is the position a clergyman uses to bless the couple during the marriage, it is called the benediction test.
questions.learning: Median nerve — The given image shows the pen test which is used to assess the median nerve. It tests the abductor pollicis brevis muscle which is supplied by the median nerve.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Hangman’s fracture is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of axis vertebra (C₂)

Hangman’s fracture is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (C2 vertebra) caused by bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis (pedicles) of C2. It classically results from forceful hyperextension and axial loading of the cervical spine, as seen in road traffic accidents or judicial hanging.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of atlas vertebra (C₁): C1 fracture is known as a Jefferson fracture, caused by axial loading.
• C. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of thoracic vertebra (T₁): This is not termed a Hangman’s fracture.
• D. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of lumbar vertebra (L₁): Lumbar spondylolisthesis is unrelated to Hangman’s fracture.
questions.learning: Traumatic spondylolisthesis of axis vertebra (C₂) Hangman’s fracture is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (C2 vertebra) caused by bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis (pedicles) of C2.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with hematuria and left flank pain. Imaging studies reveal a renal mass, and a subsequent biopsy confirms the diagnosis of papillary renal cell carcinoma. Which of the following cytogenetic abnormalities is most characteristic of papillary chromophilic renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trisomy 7/17

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) subtypes are associated with characteristic cytogenetic abnormalities, which helps in diagnosis and correlates with tumor biology.

Papillary (chromophilic) RCC

This subtype commonly shows Trisomy of chromosomes 7 and 17 and often:

• loss of Y chromosome (in males)

• may be associated with activating alterations of MET proto-oncogene (esp hereditary type)

Differentiation from other RCC subtypes

• Clear cell RCC → loss of 3p, VHL gene inactivation

• Chromophobe RCC → multiple chromosomal losses (1,2,6,10,13,17)

• Xp11 translocation RCC → Xp translocations (TFE3 gene fusion), seen in children/young adults
questions.learning: Trisomy 7/17 Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) subtypes are associated with characteristic cytogenetic abnormalities, which helps in diagnosis and correlates with tumor biology.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Gold standard investigation for endometriosis?
questions.explanation: Laparoscopy is universally recognized as the gold-standard investigation for the diagnosis of endometriosis. It allows for direct visualization of the characteristic "powder-burn" or "mulberry" lesions on the peritoneal surfaces and pelvic organs. Ideally, suspicious areas are biopsied for Histopathological Examination (HPE, Option A), which provides the definitive proof of endometrial glands and stroma; however, the procedure of laparoscopy itself is the diagnostic standard. Ultrasound (Option C) and MRI (Option D) are valuable for identifying deep infiltrating endometriosis or an "endometrioma" (chocolate cyst) in the ovary, but they are not sensitive enough to rule out superficial peritoneal disease. Endometriosis classically presents with the triad of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and dyschezia, often leading to chronic pelvic pain and infertility. During laparoscopy, the stage of the disease is assigned based on the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) classification, which guides subsequent medical or surgical management
questions.learning: Laparoscopy is universally recognized as the gold-standard investigation for the diagnosis of endometriosis. It allows for direct visualization of the characteristic "powder-burn" or "mulberry" lesions on the peritoneal surfaces and pelvic organs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the hospital due to 2 days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and headache. She was recently hospitalized due to a stroke, and the hospitalization was complicated by a urinary tract infection and delirium. The patient has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and her treatment regimen includes theophylline. Temperature is 37⁰C (98.6⁰F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, and respirations are 22/min. On physical examination, the patient appears agitated and restless. There is a coarse tremor of the outstretched arms. Chest auscultation reveals mild expiratory wheezing. Serum theophylline levels are markedly elevated. Treatment with which of the following agents most likely precipitated this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ciprofloxacin

The patient has theophylline toxicity, suggested by nausea, vomiting, headache, agitation, tremor, tachycardia, and elevated serum theophylline levels. Ciprofloxacin is a strong CYP1A2 inhibitor, the primary enzyme responsible for theophylline metabolism. Inhibition of this pathway markedly reduces theophylline clearance, leading to drug accumulation and toxicity. Elderly patients are particularly susceptible to this interaction, especially during acute illness.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Amoxicillin: Does not affect theophylline metabolism.

B. Cephalexin: No significant CYP interaction with theophylline.

D. Haloperidol: May cause extrapyramidal symptoms but does not elevate theophylline levels.
questions.learning: Ciprofloxacin — The patient has theophylline toxicity, suggested by nausea, vomiting, headache, agitation, tremor, tachycardia, and elevated serum theophylline levels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries passes through the splenorenal ligament?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Splenic artery

The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament is a double layer of peritoneum that extends between the left kidney and the spleen. It contains the splenic artery and splenic vein, along with the tail of the pancreas. This anatomical relationship is of major surgical importance during splenectomy, as inadvertent injury to the tail of the pancreas may result in pancreatic fistula or pancreatitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Left gastric artery: Travels within the lesser omentum (hepatogastric ligament) along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
• C. Common hepatic artery: Runs in the superior border of the pancreas and gives rise to the proper hepatic artery, which enters the hepatoduodenal ligament, not the splenorenal ligament.
• D. Superior mesenteric artery: Arises from the abdominal aorta and passes behind the neck of the pancreas into the root of the mesentery; it is not contained within any peritoneal ligament.
questions.learning: Splenic artery — The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament is a double layer of peritoneum that extends between the left kidney and the spleen. It contains the splenic artery and splenic vein, along with the tail of the pancreas.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following syndromes are caused due to genomic imprinting? I. Rubinstein Taybi syndrome II. Prader-Willi syndrome III. Angelman syndrome IV. Edward syndrome Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II and III

Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon in which the expression of a gene depends on whether it is inherited from the mother or the father. One parental allele is silenced by DNA methylation, so only the other allele is expressed. Disorders of genomic imprinting commonly result from deletions, uniparental disomy, or imprinting defects.

Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome are the classic disorders caused by abnormalities involving chromosome 15q11-q13.

Why is B correct?

• I. Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome ✘

• Caused by mutations in CREBBP or EP300 genes.
• It is not an imprinting disorder.

• II. Prader-Willi syndrome ✔

• Caused by loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13.
• Mechanisms include paternal deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or imprinting defects.

• III. Angelman syndrome ✔

• Caused by loss of maternally expressed UBE3A gene on chromosome 15q11-q13.
• Mechanisms include maternal deletion, paternal uniparental disomy, or imprinting defects.

• IV. Edwards syndrome ✘

• Caused by Trisomy 18.
• It is a chromosomal aneuploidy, not an imprinting disorder.
questions.learning: II and III Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon in which the expression of a gene depends on whether it is inherited from the mother or the father.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with curd-like white vaginal discharge. On examination, petechiae appear when the discharge is removed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A thick, white, "curd-like" (or cottage-cheese-like) vaginal discharge is the hallmark of Vulvovaginal Candidiasis (yeast infection). The discharge is characteristically adherent to the vaginal walls; when it is forcibly removed or scraped away during examination, the underlying mucosa often appears inflamed and may show small, pinpoint hemorrhages known as petechiae. Trichomoniasis (Option B) involves a frothy, yellow-green discharge. Gardnerella vaginalis (Option C, Bacterial Vaginosis) features a thin, greyish discharge with a fishy odor. Gonorrhea (Option D) presents with a mucopurulent cervical discharge. Candidiasis is most commonly caused by Candida albicans and is triggered by factors such as antibiotic use, pregnancy, or uncontrolled diabetes. The associated pruritus is usually intense. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding budding yeast or pseudohyphae on a KOH mount. Treatment involves topical or oral antifungal agents like fluconazole or clotrimazole. The curd-like consistency and the petechiae upon removal are the key diagnostic anchors

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for postoperative pulmonary complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Well controlled asthma

Well-controlled asthma is not a risk factor for postoperative pulmonary complications.

Risk factors for postoperative pulmonary complications:

1. Age >70 years
2. COPD (uncontrolled)
3. Neck, upper abdominal, Aortic, neurologic surgical procedures
4. Prolonged procedure >2 hours
5. General anesthesia with intubation
6. BMI > 30
7. Albumin concentration < 35 g/L
8. Inability to walk two blocks on level land or one flight of stairs

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with micrognathia and low-set ears. These clinical features are commonly associated with which type of genetic abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Deletion

The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with micrognathia and low-set ears is suggestive of cri-du chat syndrome, and it is associated with the deletion of chromosome 5p.

Cri du Chat syndrome, also known as 5p- syndrome, is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deletion of a portion of the short arm of chromosome 5. The syndrome is named after the characteristic high-pitched cry of affected infants, which resembles a cat's meow due to abnormal laryngeal development. Other key clinical features include microcephaly, low birth weight, micrognathia (small jaw), low-set ears, widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), and intellectual disabilities. Affected children often experience developmental delays, speech difficulties, and behavioural challenges. The severity of symptoms varies depending on the size of the chromosomal deletion.

In addition to the physical and cognitive impairments, individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome may have congenital heart defects, scoliosis, and feeding difficulties. While there is no cure, early intervention with speech therapy, physical therapy, and educational support can improve quality of life and functional abilities. The condition is typically diagnosed through genetic testing, such as karyotyping or fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), to detect the deletion on chromosome 5. With proper medical care and supportive therapies, many individuals with Cri du Chat syndrome can achieve a degree of independence and lead fulfilling lives.

Image: 5p chromosome deletion in Cri-du-chat syndrome.
questions.learning: Deletion — The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with micrognathia and low-set ears is suggestive of cri-du chat syndrome, and it is associated with the deletion of chromosome 5p.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following veins is involved in esophageal varices?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left gastric vein

Varices of the lower end of the esophagus receive their portal venous supply mainly from the left gastric vein, which communicates with the veins of the lower esophagus. Therefore, the vein involved in esophageal varices is the left gastric vein.

It is a tributary of the portal vein. In portal hypertension,when the pressure in the portal vein increases, the submucosal veins of the proximal stomach and distal esophagus which receive portal flow from the short gastric veins and the left gastric vein can become dilated, forming varices with a high risk of hemorrhage.

Esophageal variceal bleeding is a complication of portal hypertension, most commonly due to cirrhosis. Endoscopic intervention is the mainstay of treatment for bleeding esophageal varices. The two most commonly used techniques are endoscopic band ligation (EVL), where rubber bands are applied to the base of the varix, and endoscopic sclerotherapy, which involves injecting a sclerosant into or around the varix.

Endoscopy is usually performed in a head-down position with good suction and visualization using a double-channel endoscope and power washers. Once the bleeding site is identified, treatment is focused only on the active varices. Both EVL and sclerotherapy effectively control bleeding, but EVL is preferred as it significantly reduces the risk of rebleeding, and a single session is often sufficient.

The protocol for the management of variceal bleeding involves the following:

TIPSS or Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Stent Shunt placement involves the placement of a shunt to redirect blood flow and reduce portal pressure. It is very effective but requires analgesia, sedation, and fluoroscopic guidance. It is done if medical and endoscopic measures fail to control bleeding.

Pearl PF2179: Causes of Portal Hypertension
questions.learning: Left gastric vein Varices of the lower end of the esophagus receive their portal venous supply mainly from the left gastric vein, which communicates with the veins of the lower esophagus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about CT scan?
options: CT consists of unfiltered x-ray beams
It is the investigation of choice for gallstones
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT score of water is 0

The correct statement is that the CT score of water is 0.

On CT, each image consists of a matrix of data points (pixels) that are assigned a number that represents the X-ray attenuation(μ) at that point in the body. CT number is a scaled version of μ that is normalised to the X-ray attenuation of water (μW).

CT = 1000 × (μ/μW − 1)

The resulting numbers are called ‘Hounsfield units’(HU). Due to this normalisation, water is assigned 0 HU, and air is assigned a CT number of −1000 HU.

CT numbers:

• Water = 0 HU
• Solid soft tissues are centred around 0 HU
• Lungs = -1000 HU
• Air = −1000 HU
• Dense cortical bone = +1000 HU
• Acute Blood Clot = 60-90 HU
• Fat = -100 HU

Other options:

Option B: Computed tomography (CT) imaging involves the use of a narrow beam of X-rays that are emitted from a rotating X-ray tube.CT scanners typically use a combination of X-ray beams at different energies and filters to reduce scatter and improve image quality. Therefore, the X-ray beams used in CT imaging are often filtered to enhance image contrast and reduce radiation dose to the patient.

Option C: The investigation of choice for gallstones is an Abdominal ultrasound and not a CT Abdomen. An ultrasound can assess for complications of gallstones, such as inflammation of the gallbladder (cholecystitis) or obstruction of the bile ducts. In cases where ultrasound findings are inconclusive or further characterisation is needed, other imaging modalities such as CT scan or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) may be used.

Option D: The mSv (millisievert) value for a non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) scan of the head typically ranges from around 1 to 2 mSv. This radiation dose can vary depending on factors such as the specific CT scanner used, the scanning protocol, and the individual patient characteristics. However, in general, NCCT head scans are associated with relatively low radiation doses compared to other medical imaging procedures.
questions.learning: CT score of water is 0 — The correct statement is that the CT score of water is 0. On CT, each image consists of a matrix of data points (pixels) that are assigned a number that represents the X-ray attenuation(μ) at that point in the body.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Jack knife position causes death due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Positional asphyxia

Jack-knife position leads to positional asphyxia.

It is a position where the victim's thighs and knees are driven against the chest causing indirect compression of the chest and restriction of breathing movements.
questions.learning: Positional asphyxia Jack-knife position leads to positional asphyxia. It is a position where the victim's thighs and knees are driven against the chest causing indirect compression of the chest and restriction of breathing movements.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old nulliparous woman in active labor has been pushing for the past 2 hours without progress and feels extremely fatigued. CTG is normal. On examination, the fetal head is 1 cm above the ischial spines (station −1) in the occipitoanterior position. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency cesarean section

Operative vaginal delivery (forceps/vacuum) requires the fetal head to be engaged (station ≥0). If the head is high (above ischial spines, station −1) and there is failure of descent in the second stage, the appropriate management is cesarean section.

1. Station of fetal head

• 0 station: At the level of ischial spines (engaged)
• Negative station (−1, −2, etc.): Head not engaged
• Positive station (+1, +2 etc.): Head descending toward outlet

2. Requirements for operative vaginal delivery

Before attempting forceps or vacuum, the following must be present:

• Fully dilated cervix
• Ruptured membranes
• Engaged fetal head (≥0 station)
• Known fetal position
• Adequate pelvis
• No suspicion of cephalopelvic disproportion

Why cesarean section here:

• Patient has no progress after 2 hours of pushing
• Station −1 → head not engaged
• Attempting forceps with a high head is contraindicated

Why other options are incorrect:

• Observe: Already prolonged second stage with maternal exhaustion.
• Forceps: Contraindicated when head is above ischial spines.
• Fetal blood sampling: Used for abnormal CTG, but CTG here is normal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of case-control studies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Follow up

Among the given options, follow-up is not a part of case-control studies.

Case-Control Studies are also called retrospective studies. This study proceeds from effect to cause and is done after the exposure and outcome have occurred. They focus on diseases or health problems that have already developed. They are less time-consuming and have no risk of attrition because they do not require follow-up.

There are four basic steps in conducting a case-control study:

• Selection of cases and controls
• Matching- This is done to ensure comparability between cases and controls. Controls are selected such that they are similar to cases with respect to certain pertinent selected variables that influence the disease outcome.
• Measurement of exposure - This is obtained by interviews, questionnaires, or study of the past records of cases.
• Analysis in the form of exposure rates, risk ratio, and odds ratio.

Odds Ratio (OR) calculated from a case-control study, is a measure of the strength of the association between risk factor and outcome.

Note: Follow-up is a part of cohort studies. The elements in cohort studies include selecting study subjects, obtaining data on exposure, selecting comparison groups, follow up and analysis.
questions.learning: Follow up Among the given options, follow-up is not a part of case-control studies. Case-Control Studies are also called retrospective studies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common type of renal stones are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium oxalate

The most common type of renal stone is calcium oxalate stone.

Note:

Uric acid stones are more common than calcium oxalate stones in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

Calcium carbonate stone is the most common type of stone formed in chronic pancreatitis.

Pearl PF0036: Microscopic Appearance of Various Stones

* Cystine stones: Hexagonal

* Uric acid stones: Varying shapes (rhomboids or parallelograms)

* Calcium oxalate

* Monohydrate: Dumbbell shaped

* Dihydrate: Octahedral or envelope shaped

* Struvite stones: Rectangular or coffin lid
questions.learning: Calcium oxalate — The most common type of renal stone is calcium oxalate stone. Note: Uric acid stones are more common than calcium oxalate stones in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The major thyroxine-binding protein is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyroxine-binding globulin

Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) is the major protein that binds to thyroxine and tri-iodothyronine.

Thyroid hormones bind to transthyretin and albumin to a much lesser extent than TBG.

Hormones and their Binding Proteins

* T4  and T3  bind to thyroxine-binding globulin  (TBG), albumin, and thyroxine-binding pre-albumin (TBPA)

* Cortisol binds to cortisol-binding globulin (CBG);

* Androgen and estrogen bind to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG);

* IGF-I and -II bind to multiple IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs);

* GH interacts with GH-binding protein (GHBP), a circulating fragment of the GH receptor extracellular domain;

* Activin binds to follistatin.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with nasal obstruction and merciful anosmia. Greenish-black crusts were found in the nasal cavity of a patient. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrophic rhinitis

The presence of merciful anosmia and greenish-black crusts in the nasal cavity points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis.

Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The exact etiology of this condition is not known. It is more common in females and starts around puberty.

Clinically patients present with nasal obstruction, foul odor, and merciful anosmia. Merciful anosmia is when the patient has marked anosmia and is unable to smell the foul odor coming from their nose.

On examination of the nose, greenish or greyish crusting of the nasal passage, pale nasal mucosa, atrophied nasal turbinates, and epistaxis following the removal of the crusts. The roomy nasal cavity is seen due to the resorption of bones of the turbinates.

Treatment:

* Nasal irrigation - using warm saline or an alkaline solution composed of sodium bicarbonate 1 part, sodium biborate 1 part, sodium chloride 2 parts in 280 mL of water.

* Local antibiotics - Kemicetine antiozena solution containing chloromycetin, estradiol, and vitamin D2.

* 25% glucose in glycerine, estradiol spray, systemic use of streptomycin, potassium iodide, placental extract.

* Surgical management:

* Young's operation: In this procedure, flaps are raised within the nasal vestibule and both the nostrils are completely closed and are opened after 6 months. During this time, the mucosa may revert to normal and the crusting is reduced.

* Modified Young's operation: In this procedure, the nostrils are partially closed and thereby avoiding the discomfort of complete closure of the nostrils. The results are the same compared to Young's operation.

* Narrowing of the nasal cavity can be done by submucosal injection of Teflon paste, or by insertion of fat, cartilage, or Teflon strips under the mucoperiosteum.

Other options:

Option B: Rhinitis sicca is a crust-forming disease seen in people who work in hot, dry, and dusty surroundings, e.g. bakers and iron- and goldsmiths. It usually affects the anterior third of the nose, particularly the nasal septum.  The affected areas develop crusts, which may result in bleeding, ulceration, and even septal perforation on removal.

Option C: Allergic rhinitis is associated with inferior turbinate hypertrophy and can cause chronic nasal obstruction. It is characterized by watery nasal discharge, sneezing, and itching in the nose.

Option D: Hypertrophic rhinitis is a condition characterized by the thickening of mucosa, submucosa, seromucinous glands, periosteum, and bone. It occurs as a result of recurrent nasal infections, chronic sinusitis, and chronic irritation of the nasal mucosa. Symptoms include nasal obstruction, discharge, and headache.

Pearl PF1339: Clinical Features of Atrophic Rhinitis

* More common in females

* Usually starts at puberty

* It is a bilateral condition

* Symptoms:

* Foul smell from the nose

* Nasal obstruction in spite of roomy chambers due to large crusts filling nasal cavity

* Epistaxis on removing of the crusts

* Anosmia due to degeneration of nerve elements (merciful anosmia)

* Signs:

* Greenish or greyish black dry crusts covering the turbinates and septum

* After removal of crusts, nasal cavities appear roomy with atrophy of turbinates

* Nasal mucosa appears pale

Pearl PF2102: Etiology of atrophic rhinitis

Etiology of primary atrophic rhinitis:

* Hereditary- Involves more than one member of a family

* Endocrinal- More common in females, starts at puberty and regresses after menopause

* Racial- More common in mongoloid and caucasian races

* Nutritional deficiency- Vitamin A, D, iron deficiencies

* Autoimmune- Antigens of the nasal mucosa

* Organism- Klebsiella ozaenae

Etiology of secondary atrophic rhinitis:

* Specific infections like syphilis, lupus, leprosy and, rhinoscleroma

* Long-standing purulent sinusitis

* Radiotherapy to nose

* Excessive surgical removal of turbinates

* Diphtheroids, Proteus vulgaris, Escherichia coli, staphylococci and streptococci
questions.learning: Atrophic rhinitis — The presence of merciful anosmia and greenish-black crusts in the nasal cavity points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis. Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones.
