questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Dr. Sarah made a presentation on Infectious diseases. She spoke about the prevention and treatment of Zika virus. Which of the following is true with respect to the prevention and treatment of Zika virus?
options: Sexual abstinence, using condoms, and delaying pregnancy helps control the disease
Purified, inactivated FDA-approved vaccine is found to be helpful in prevention
Immunoglobulin and plasmapheresis are used in the treatment of Zika
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sexual abstinence, using condoms, and delaying pregnancy helps control the disease

Sexual abstinence, using condoms, and delaying pregnancy help control Zika virus infections.

Zika virus can be transmitted by the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Zika virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family. It is an arbovirus that is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, primarily Aedes aegypti. The reservoir of infection is unknown and has not yet been reported in India. Zika virus can also be transmitted via sexual contact, blood transfusion, and also from mother to fetus during pregnancy.

Infection with Zika virus is usually asymptomatic. The symptoms are usually mild and include fever, skin rashes, conjunctivitis, and muscle and joint pain. These symptoms usually resolve in 2-7 days. Complications include Guillain-Barré syndrome, neuropathy, and myelitis, and are particularly seen in adults and older children.

Zika virus infection during pregnancy is associated with complications such as fetal loss, preterm birth, and stillbirth. The transmission of the infection to the baby can lead to congenital Zika syndrome which is characterized by microcephaly. Other malformations include limb contractures, high muscle tone, eye abnormalities, and hearing loss. Congenital malformations can follow both symptomatic and asymptomatic infections.

RT-PCR is the standard test for the diagnosis of Zika virus infection. In India, NCDC Delhi and the National Institute of Virology Pune, are the only institutes that can provide the diagnosis in an acute febrile stage.

There is no treatment available for Zika virus infection(options C & D). Plenty of rest and fluids along with antipyretics and/or analgesics are indicated for symptom relief. Medical attention should be sought if symptoms worsen. There is no vaccine available for the prevention of Zika virus infection(option B). The key measure for prevention is protection against mosquito bites. WHO also recommends contraceptive counselling for sexually active men and women, especially in regions with active Zika virus transmission.

The image below depicts the transplacental transmission of Zika virus infection.
questions.learning: Sexual abstinence, using condoms, and delaying pregnancy helps control the disease Sexual abstinence, using condoms, and delaying pregnancy help control Zika virus infections.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Peutz–Jeghers syndrome are true 1. Heterogeneous loss of function of the STK11 gene 2. Presents as multiple hamartomatous polyps in the GIT 3. Histology shows arborising smooth muscle bundles 4. It is an autosomal recessive condition 5. Extra-intestinal manifestations of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome include hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 3

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is due to loss-of-function mutation of the STK11 tumor suppressor gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It presents with multiple hamartomatous GI polyps showing classic arborizing smooth muscle bundles on histology. Retinal pigment hypertrophy is seen in familial adenomatous polyposis, not Peutz–Jeghers.

| Feature | Peutz–Jeghers | FAP

| ------- | ------------- | ---

| Gene | STK11 | APC

| Inheritance | AD | AD

| Polyp type | Hamartomatous | Adenomatous

| Histology | Arborizing smooth muscle | Dysplastic epithelium

| Cancer risk | Moderate–high (extraintestinal) | Very high (colon)

| Extra features | Mucocutaneous pigmentation | CHRPE (retinal lesions)
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 3 Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is due to loss-of-function mutation of the STK11 tumor suppressor gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements about working of septic tanks: 1. They are recommended for large communities, rather than small communities. 2. There should be no air space between the level of liquid in the tank and the undersurface of the cover. 3. Liquid effluent from the outlet pipe is free from all pathogens. How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. None of the statements

A septic tank is an on-site sewage disposal system used for individual houses and small communities where a centralized sewerage system is not available. It works by anaerobic digestion, where solids settle and decompose, while the liquid effluent is discharged for further treatment in a soak pit or dispersion trenches.

• 1. They are recommended for large communities\, rather than small communities. ✗

• Septic tanks are designed for individual households and small communities, not large populations.

• 2. There should be no air space between the level of liquid in the tank and the undersurface of the cover. ✗

• A septic tank should have an air space (about 30 cm) between the liquid level and the cover to allow gas accumulation and proper functioning.

• 3. Liquid effluent from the outlet pipe is free from all pathogens. ✗

• The effluent still contains pathogenic microorganisms and requires further disposal/treatment through a soak pit, leach field, or other methods.
questions.learning: None of the statements — A septic tank is an on-site sewage disposal system used for individual houses and small communities where a centralized sewerage system is not available.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presents to the emergency with pain, swelling and redness over the left foot following a trivial trauma 3 days back. On examination, the swelling over the left foot is poorly localised; local tenderness and erythema are present and crepitus is absent; distal pulsations are palpable. The most likely clinical diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cellulitis

This patient has the classical features of cellulitis, an acute bacterial infection involving the skin and subcutaneous tissue.

• Trivial trauma preceding infection
• Pain, swelling, and redness for 3 days
• Poorly localized swelling (diffuse inflammation)
• Local tenderness and erythema
• No crepitus (argues against necrotizing fasciitis)
• Distal pulses palpable (rules out vascular compromise and makes compartment syndrome less likely)

Why not the other options?

• A. Compartment syndrome ❌

• Presents with severe pain out of proportion to examination, pain on passive stretch, tense compartment, paresthesia, and later absent pulses.
• Redness and diffuse erythema are not typical early features.

• C. Abscess ❌

• Usually presents as a localized, fluctuant, tender swelling with a well-defined collection of pus.
• The swelling here is poorly localized.

• D. Fasciitis (Necrotizing fasciitis) ❌

• Rapidly progressive infection with severe pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, skin discoloration, bullae, and often crepitus (if gas-forming organisms are present).
• This patient has no crepitus or signs of severe systemic illness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What percentage of increase in FEV1/FVC ratio represents the minimum change required to demonstrate the reversibility of obstruction after administration of bronchodilators in bronchial asthma? FEV1 - Forced expiratory volume in the first minute FVC - Forced vital capacity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. > 12%

Reversibility of obstruction in asthma has to be demonstrated by a minimum of 12% increase in FEV1/FVC ratio in response to inhalation of short-acting beta-agonist (SABA).

In asthma, there is reversible bronchoconstriction leading to wheezing, breathlessness, and cough. Thus, on administering a SABA, there is bronchial relaxation and relief of symptoms.

Asthma is generally diagnosed clinically based on symptoms alone. However, there are a number of other conditions that can be misdiagnosed as asthma such as causes of wheeze (bronchogenic carcinoma, foreign body aspiration), cough (gastroesophageal reflux, chronic bronchitis, rhinitis), and dyspnea (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary edema, or obesity). Misdiagnosis would lead to a delay in management. Thus, it is ideal that the clinical diagnosis of asthma is confirmed by pulmonary function tests.

* Spirometry: It is a non-invasive investigation that can be used to approximate lung volumes. This shows an obstructive pattern

* Decreased FEV1

* Decreased or normal FVC

* Decreased FEV1/FVC

* Bronchodilator reversibility: Spirometry is performed both before and after inhalation of a short-acting bronchodilator (400 mcg of β2 agonist or 160 mcg of anticholinergic). A 12% and 200 mL increase in FEV1 compared to pre-bronchodilator value is diagnostic of asthma in adults.

* Bronchial provocation test: Provocative stimulus (histamine, methacholine, inhaled mannitol, exercise, eucapnic hyperventilation with dry or cold air) is used to test the presence of airway hyperresponsiveness.  A fall of ≥20% in FEV1 from baseline, with a standard dose of methacholine (methacholine challenge test), is diagnostic of asthma.

* Peak expiratory flow (PEF): PEF readings are taken twice daily for over 2 weeks. The average daily diurnal PEF variability of >10% is diagnostic of asthma in adults.

• Normal or increased in asthma
• Decreased in emphysema

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presenting with 36 weeks of gestation, underwent a C-Section for placenta accreta spectrum. During the procedure, there was profuse bleeding and she was transfused blood according to the massive blood transfusion protocol. Which of the following is not seen after a massive blood transfusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypokalemia

Hyperkalemia is seen after a massive blood transfusion.

Massive transfusion is defined as the transfusion of 50% of the patient’s total blood volume over 3 hours or >5–10 units of RBCs.

Complications are:

1. Citrate toxicity
2. Hypothermia (Rapid transfusion of blood components at 4°C )
3. Hypocalcemia that presents as circumoral paresthesia.
4. Hyperkalemia(RBC leakage during longer storage, and irradiation increases the concentration of potassium in the unit)
5. Dilutional coagulopathy

Prevention includes the usage of washed or plasma-reduced RBC components or a storage age of <7–10 days and the avoidance of RBC components stored for >24 h after irradiation. Treatment includes administration of insulin, glucose, calcium gluconate, and furosemide.

Note: As the question was a part of the INI-CET May 2023 exam, the best possible answer has been marked.
questions.learning: Hypokalemia Hyperkalemia is seen after a massive blood transfusion. Massive transfusion is defined as the transfusion of 50% of the patient’s total blood volume over 3 hours or >5–10 units of RBCs.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a complaint of epistaxis. Considering the patient’s age and the common causes of nosebleeds in children, bleeding is most often due to involvement of a specific artery within the nasal cavity. Which artery is most commonly affected in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Epistaxis (nosebleed) is extremely common in children and is typically divided into anterior and posterior sources. The sphenopalatine artery is often considered the most important artery for clinically significant epistaxis, as it is the "artery of epistaxis" supplying the posterior part of the nasal cavity. However, in children, the most frequent site of bleeding is Kiesselbach’s plexus (Little's area) in the anterior septum, where branches of the sphenopalatine, greater palatine (Option D), superior labial, and anterior ethmoidal (Option C) arteries anastomose. Posterior ethmoidal (Option A) is a rare source. While Little's area is the most common site, the sphenopalatine artery is the primary distal branch of the maxillary artery providing the most extensive blood supply to the nasal mucosa. Most childhood nosebleeds are anterior and result from local trauma (nose picking) or dry air; they can usually be managed with simple compression of the alae

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Infection with Clonorchis sinensis is associated with an increased risk of ___________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cholangiocarcinoma

Clonorchis sinensis or Chinese liver fluke causes clonorchiasis. It is also associated with an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

Clonorchis sinensis infection is endemic in south China, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan due to a long tradition of consuming raw freshwater fish or shellfish. Humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked fish containing encysted larvae (metacercariae).

The immature flukes after excystation in the duodenum enter the biliary ducts and differentiate into adults.

The hermaphroditic adults produce eggs that are excreted in the feces. Upon reaching freshwater the eggs are ingested by snails, which are the first intermediate hosts. The eggs hatch within the gut and differentiate first into larvae (rediae) and then into many free-swimming cercariae. Cercariae encyst to form metacercariae under the scales of certain freshwater fish (second intermediate host) which are then ingested by humans.

In humans, it infects the common bile duct and gallbladder. Liver imaging shows a dilated biliary tract. It is a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.

The life cycle of Clonorchis sinensis is given below:

Other options:

Option A: Cervical cancer - Human papilloma virus (HPV) infection, particularly with high-risk strains like HPV-16 and 18, is the main risk factor for cervical cancer. Clonorchis sinensis is not associated with cervical cancer.

Option C: Gastric carcinoma - Helicobacter pylori infection is a major risk factor for the development of gastric carcinoma. Clonorchis sinensis is not linked to gastric carcinoma.

Option D: Bladder carcinoma - The vesical blood fluke Schistosoma haematobium primarily infects the urinary bladder and increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Clonorchis sinensis is not associated with bladder carcinoma.
questions.learning: Cholangiocarcinoma Clonorchis sinensis or Chinese liver fluke causes clonorchiasis. It is also associated with an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient with a history of head trauma presents with blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg, bradycardia, and elevated intracranial pressure. Which reflex best explains this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cushing's reflex

Cushing reflex (Cushing triad) is a physiological response to markedly increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Rising ICP reduces cerebral perfusion pressure, triggering sympathetic activation to increase systemic blood pressure and maintain cerebral blood flow. The resulting hypertension activates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia, while brainstem compression leads to irregular respirations.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bainbridge reflex: Reflex tachycardia in response to increased venous return and right atrial stretch.
• C. Bezold–Jarisch reflex: Causes hypotension, bradycardia, and vasodilation due to ventricular mechanoreceptor activation, commonly during inferior wall MI or spinal anesthesia.
• D. Baroreflex: Regulates short-term blood pressure but does not explain the characteristic triad associated with raised ICP.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is undergoing pubertal changes. Her tanner stage is stage 4 for breast development and pubic hair scale. Which of the following pubertal changes is not due to estrogen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pubic and axillary hair growth

Pubarche or development of axillary and pubic hair is not due to estrogen. It is due to testosterone (in both the sexes).

Puberty in females :

* Involves the beginning of menstrual cycles (menarche), breast development (thelarche), and an increase in adrenal androgen secretion (adrenarche).

* Estradiol induces the development of secondary sex characteristics, including the breasts and reproductive tract, and increased fat in the hips.

* Estrogens also regulate the growth spurt at puberty, vaginal cornification and cervical mucus production, induce closure of the epiphyses, have a positive effect in maintaining bone formation, and can antagonize the degrading actions of parathyroid hormone on bone.

In young girls before puberty the vaginal epithelium is thin and comprised of only basal and parabasal layers. During the reproductive years, the vaginal epithelium thickens and develops a distinct cornified layer due to the influence of estrogen. Cervical mucous production and menstruation are also changes occuring under the influence of estrogen and also progesterone.
questions.learning: Pubic and axillary hair growth Pubarche or development of axillary and pubic hair is not due to estrogen. It is due to testosterone (in both the sexes).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The instrument given in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Jackson-Pratt drain

The given image is of a Jackson-Pratt drain.

Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely drain the air or fluids that may accumulate. They promote wound healing by preventing the formation of unnecessary cavities. Drains can be:

• Open : They are based on the principle of gravity
• Semi-open : Their action is based on capillary effect
• Closed : They carry out their actions through suction

Jackson-pratt drain is a closed, air-tight drainage system that operates by self-suction. The drain is sutured in place on the skin at the site of insertion to promote stability. There are two main parts to a JP drain:

1. Hollow tube
2. Collection bulb

The drain should be emptied as often as possible to allow the bulb to be compressed fully in order to maintain suction. This is usually done every 4-6 hours the first few days.

Other options:

Option A: Hemovac is also a closed type of suction drain which can typically handle larger amounts of fluid than the JP drain.

Option C: Minivac is a closed wound drainage system under negative pressure used in minor surgeries.

Option D: Corrugated drain is an open drainage system to remove excess fluid from the operated site.
questions.learning: Jackson-Pratt drain — The given image is of a Jackson-Pratt drain. Drains are placed at surgical sites to freely drain the air or fluids that may accumulate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which statement about Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in children is accurate?
options: Second most common cause of Nephrotic Syndrome in children
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Second most common cause of Nephrotic Syndrome in children

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is the second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, after Minimal Change Disease (MCD). It is also one of the most important causes of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) in childhood.

Pathological Features:

• Light microscopy: Focal and segmental sclerosis of glomeruli.
• Electron microscopy: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes.
• Immunofluorescence: Usually negative, though IgM and C3 trapping may be seen.

Minimal Change Disease is the most common cause, while FSGS ranks second and accounts for a significant proportion of children who do not respond to steroid therapy.

Why are the Other Options Incorrect?

B. Good response to steroids

• FSGS characteristically shows a poor response to corticosteroids.
• Many patients are steroid-resistant.

C. Relapses are rare

• Relapses are common, and the disease often follows a chronic course.

D. Renal biopsy is not required

• Renal biopsy is essential for diagnosis, especially in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.
• Biopsy shows sclerosis involving some (focal) glomeruli and only part (segmental) of the affected glomerulus.
questions.learning: Second most common cause of Nephrotic Syndrome in children Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is the second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, after Minimal Change Disease (MCD).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presenting with signs of meningeal irritation undergoes cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, which reveals lymphocytic predominance with normal glucose levels and elevated protein. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Differentiating meningitis types through CSF analysis is a core clinical skill. Viral (aseptic) meningitis characteristically shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis (lymphocytosis) with normal glucose (sugar) and only mildly elevated protein. Pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis (Option A) shows a neutrophilic predominance and very low glucose. Tubercular (Option C) and Fungal (Option D) meningitis both show lymphocytosis and elevated protein, but they are classically associated with very low glucose. Therefore, the "normal sugar" is the critical differentiator that points toward a viral etiology. Common viral causes include enteroviruses and herpes simplex virus. Patients typically present with fever, headache, and photophobia but are usually less critically ill than those with bacterial meningitis. While viral meningitis is often self-limiting, the normal CSF glucose is the laboratory anchor that prevents unnecessary prolonged antibiotic therapy once bacterial cultures remain negative
questions.learning: Differentiating meningitis types through CSF analysis is a core clinical skill. Viral (aseptic) meningitis characteristically shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis (lymphocytosis) with normal glucose (sugar) and only mildly elevated protein.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats is suspected to have tuberculosis. A sputum sample is cultured on Löwenstein–Jensen (LJ) medium. If the organism grows, what staining property would it characteristically exhibit?
questions.explanation: The patient's clinical symptoms (chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats) are highly suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. M. tuberculosis is characterized by its unique waxy cell wall containing high concentrations of mycolic acids. This structure makes the organism resistant to traditional Gram staining (Options A and B). Instead, it is identified using Acid-Fast staining (such as the Ziehl-Neelsen stain), where the bacteria retain the primary carbol fuchsin dye even after washing with acid-alcohol. Growth on Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium, which shows rough, tough, and buff-colored colonies, confirms the diagnosis. Therefore, "acid fast" is the definitive staining characteristic for these mycobacteria. This property is essential for the rapid identification of TB in sputum samples
questions.learning: The patient's clinical symptoms (chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats) are highly suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a patient with suspected gastrointestinal infection, which culture medium is commonly used in the laboratory to differentiate lactose- fermenting bacteria from non-lactose fermenters?
questions.explanation: MacConkey agar is a specialized differential and selective culture medium widely used in microbiology. It contains bile salts and crystal violet, which inhibit the growth of gram-positive bacteria, making it selective for gram-negative organisms (like Enterobacteriaceae). Crucially, it contains the sugar lactose and a neutral red pH indicator. Bacteria that are lactose fermenters (e.g., E. coli) produce acid, which turns the colonies pink. Non-lactose fermenters (e.g., Salmonella or Shigella) do not produce acid and appear as pale or colorless colonies. Bile salt agar (Option A) is used for isolating Vibrio cholerae. Thayer-Martin agar (Option B) is selective for Neisseria species. Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (Option D) is used for the growth of fungi. Identifying the lactose fermentation pattern on MacConkey agar is the foundational first step in the laboratory identification of aerobic gram-negative bacilli, helping clinicians narrow down the etiological agent of a gastrointestinal or urinary tract infection

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The “DASH diet” is a lifestyle modification for management of which of these conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypertension

DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is a dietary pattern specifically designed to prevent and treat hypertension. It has been shown to significantly reduce blood pressure and also lowers the risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, and chronic kidney disease.

• A. Cancer ✗: Although a healthy diet may reduce cancer risk, the DASH diet was not specifically developed for cancer management.
• B. Diabetes ✗: DASH can improve metabolic health, but its primary indication is hypertension.
• C. Anaemia ✗: DASH is not designed for the treatment of anemia.
• D. Hypertension ✓: DASH is the recommended dietary intervention for patients with hypertension and prehypertension.
questions.learning: Hypertension DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is a dietary pattern specifically designed to prevent and treat hypertension. It has been shown to significantly reduce blood pressure and also lowers the risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke,…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A female with abdominal pain and bleeding per vagina with 3 months of amenorrhea. On examination her BP was 90/60mmHg. Which of the following statements is/are true about ectopic pregnancy?

1. Abdominal pain is the most common presenting symptom of ectopic pregnancy and maybe present in at least 90% of the patients.
2. PID and sexually transmitted infections are a major risk factor.
3. Low values of progesterone are usually diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy, however there's no specific value to completely rule out or exclude ectopic pregnancy.
4. Oral methotrexate is a viable medical alternative to surgery in ectopic pregnancy patients presenting with shock or renal failure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2,3

An ectopic pregnancy is one in which the fertilized ovum is implanted and develops outside the normal endometrial cavity.

Clinical features :

The classic triad of symptoms is - abdominal pain (100%), preceded by amenorrhea of 6-8 weeks(75%), and lastly, the appearance of vaginal bleeding (70%).
Abdominal pain is the most constant feature. (Statement 1) Pain is located in the lower abdomen. Shoulder tip pain (25%) (referred pain due to diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum) may be present.
Pelvic examination - Vaginal mucosa is blanched white; uterus seems normal in size or slightly bulky; extreme tenderness on fornix palpation(75%).

Risk factors of ectopic pregnancy:

• Previous ectopic pregnancy
• Tubal corrective surgery, tubectomy
• Assisted reproductive technology
• Documented tubal pathology
• Pelvic inflammatory disease (Chlamydia infection and salpingitis isthmica nodosa), Genital tuberculosis, sexually transmitted diseases (Statement 2)
• Endometriosis, Pelvic adhesions
• Prior abortion, Prior Caesarean delivery
• Multiple sexual partners
• Progesterone-only pills (POPs)

Diagnosis:

• Serum рrοgеѕtеrone – concentrations are higher in viable IUPs than in ectopic pregnancies and IUPs that are destined to abort, and measurement of serum рrοgеѕtеrоne may be useful in a patient with abdominal pain and bleeding who has a serum hCG level below that expected for the gestational age. However, the definition of low рrοgеѕterοոе is unclear as there is no specific value to diagnose ectopic pregnancy. (Statement 3)
• ß-hCG - lower concentration of hCG and doubling in plasma failing to occur in 2 days.
• Transvaginal sonography (TVS) features are absence of intrauterine pregnancy with a positive pregnancy test.
• Color Doppler sonography can identify the placental shape (ring-of-fire pattern).

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

1. Medical management is preferred in the following cases:

• Low initial serum beta-hCG level (Less than 5,000 IU/L)
• Small ectopic pregnancy size (Less than 3.5 cm)
• Absent fetal cardiac activity
• Hemodynamically stable

2. Expectant management: A low initial serum hCG concentration, a considerable reduction in levels over 48 hours, and a sonographic inhomogeneous mass instead of a tubal halo or other gestational features are predictive variables for success.

3. Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

• Gestational sac >3.5 cm
• Fetal cardiac activity present
• Beta-hCG >5000 mIU/mL
• Significant pain and hemoperitoneum

Oral methotrexate is not the preferred route for treating ectopic pregnancy, as it may lead to variable absorption and unreliable dosing. Intramuscular injection is the preferred route of administration for methotrexate in the management of ectopic pregnancy. (Statement 4)
questions.learning: 1,2,3 An ectopic pregnancy is one in which the fertilized ovum is implanted and develops outside the normal endometrial cavity. Clinical features : The classic triad of symptoms is - abdominal pain (100%), preceded by amenorrhea of 6-8 weeks(75%), and…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The graph shown below is the titration curve of a biochemical compound. Which of the following statement is true?
options: The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B
The points A and B represent the range of maximum ionization of the amine and carboxyl group
The compound has three ionisable side chains
The compound has one ionisable group
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B

The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B, which corresponds to the pK1 and pK2 of the compound.

Other options:

• The points A and B represent the pKa of carboxyl and amino groups respectively.
• The amino acid has no ionizable side chains as the graph shows only two pKas.
• The amino acid has two ionizable groups: an amino group and a carboxyl group.

The above graph resembles the titration curve of the amino acid glycine.

Titration curve of Glycine:

The titration is completed at a pH of 12, where the glycine predominantly exists in the form of H2N - CH2 - COO-.

pK1 and pK2 correspond to the point where the buffering capacity is maximum.

Characteristics of the titration curve:

• Buffering capacity is referred to as the ability of the aminoacid to resist the change in pH due to the addition of acid (H+) or base (OH- equivalents), by accepting or losing the protons respectively.
• An ionizable group refers to the group which can either lose or accept a proton and becomes negatively charged or positively charged ion respectively.
• During the titration, the buffering capacity of the compound reaches its maximum, at points where the pKa of the ionizable groups is reached.
• Each of these pKa are labeled as pK1, pK2, pK3, etc.
• The presence of two pKas indicates that the compound has two ionizable groups. Ex. Glycine.
• The presence of three or more pKas indicates the presence of side chains on the amino acid, with additional ionizable groups.
• Ex. histidine has three ionizable groups, an amino group, an imidazole group (on the side chain), and a carboxyl group. The pKas of these groups respectively correspond to the pK1, pK2, pK3 of the titration curve of histidine.
questions.learning: The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B The maximum buffering capacity of the compound is represented by points A and B, which corresponds to the pK1 and pK2 of the compound.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct definition of postpartum pyrexia?
questions.explanation: Postpartum pyrexia, or puerperal pyrexia, is traditionally defined as a temperature rise to ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, occurring on any two of the first ten days following delivery, excluding the initial 24 hours. The first 24 hours are typically excluded because a mild temperature elevation during this period is often due to dehydration or the physiological stress of labor. Option B, C, and D are incorrect because they specify timeframes within the first 24 hours, which do not meet the standard diagnostic criteria for morbid pyrexia. The most common cause of pyrexia during the puerperium is genital tract infection (puerperal sepsis), but clinicians must also consider urinary tract infections, mastitis, and deep vein thrombosis. Accurate diagnosis requires a thorough physical examination and relevant cultures. Prompt treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics is vital to prevent severe maternal morbidity or mortality associated with sepsis
questions.learning: Postpartum pyrexia, or puerperal pyrexia, is traditionally defined as a temperature rise to ≥ 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, occurring on any two of the first ten days following delivery, excluding the initial 24 hours.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 14-month-old child with Hb 6.3 was undergoing repeated blood transfusions. The last transfusion was given in the 9th month. Which of the following investigation is used for a definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Globin gene sequencing

The given clinical scenario of repeated transfusion, low hemoglobin level, and target cells in the smear are suggestive of thalassemia. Globin gene sequencing is used for its definitive diagnosis.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is used as a screening test for thalassemia (option A).

Thalassemia is a hemoglobinopathy that arises due to deficient synthesis of the globin chains. Depending on the chain affected, it is classified into α-thalassemia and β-thalassemia.

β-thalassemia is caused by point mutations of the β-thalassemia gene on chromosome 11, which diminish the synthesis of β-globin chains. Splicing mutations are the most common cause of (β+) thalassemia.

There is a deficit in the synthesis of HbA with an elevation of HbA2 and HbF levels in β-thalassemia. Children with severe thalassemia present with distinctive facial features such as maxilla hyperplasia, a flat nasal bridge, and frontal bossing. Other manifestations include pathologic bone fractures, significant hepatosplenomegaly, and cachexia.

Blood smears show marked anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and microcytic hypochromic anemia. Target cells, basophilic stippling, and fragmented red cells also are common. A radiographic image of the skull shows the classic 'crew cut' appearance.

Hb Electrophoresis and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) are used as screening tests for thalassemia. DNA diagnosis to detect β-thalassemia mutations is used for definitive diagnosis. The Mentzer index is the ratio of MCV to RBC count. It is used to differentiate between iron-deficiency anemia and β-thalassemia trait. The Mentzer index is <13 in thalassemia minor syndrome.

Transfusions are administered every 3-4 weeks to maintain a pretransfusion hemoglobin level of 9.5-10.5 g/dL. Transfusion-induced hemosiderosis is a significant complication in transfusion-dependent thalassemia. Iron deposition occurs in the liver, endocrine organs, and heart, resulting in complications including hypothyroidism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, diabetes mellitus, heart failure, and arrhythmias.

questions.learning: Globin gene sequencing — The given clinical scenario of repeated transfusion, low hemoglobin level, and target cells in the smear are suggestive of thalassemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 34-year-old woman was brought to the AIIMS emergency following a road traffic accident. She was hemodynamically stable and her GCS score was 3. She was intubated and sent for non-contrast CT which was found to be normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

GCS- Glasgow coma scale
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diffuse axonal injury

The clinical scenario of a patient with a poor GCS score and a normal NCCT brain scan following a road traffic accident is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

Diffuse axonal injury (white matter shearing) results from shearing forces, typically from a rotational acceleration of the brain within the rigid cranium. This causes damage to microvasculature and disruption of axons in the subcortical parasagittal white matter, cerebellum, fornix, and internal and external capsule.

Most commonly it occurs in automobile accidents. Patients are usually unconscious from the moment of impact and remain the same until death.

Diffuse axonal injury is characterized by multiple focal lesions with a characteristic distribution:

• CT may be normal.
• MRI is the modality of choice for assessing suspected diffuse axonal injury, even in patients with entirely normal CT of the brain. MRI, especially SWI (susceptibility-weighted imaging) demonstrates small regions of susceptibility artifact or hemorrhage.

Other options:

Option A: Subdural hemorrhage is often due to the rupture of veins that cross the subdural space. In subdural hemorrhage, the CT shows concavo-convex opacity.

Option B: Extradural hemorrhage is mostly due to the rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Since the dura matter tends to adhere to the skull the hemorrhage is seen in CT as a biconvex dense area. They usually do not cross cranial sutures.

Option D: Cerebral contusion occurs due to traumatic brain injury, at the sites that come in direct contact with the skull. Imaging may show microhemorrhages and edema. Usually, no treatment is required.
questions.learning: Diffuse axonal injury — The clinical scenario of a patient with a poor GCS score and a normal NCCT brain scan following a road traffic accident is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent discomfort, pain, and a feeling of pressure behind her left eye. She has intermittent, reducible proptosis, with symptoms worsening when bending forward. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The hallmark of orbital varices is intermittent, transient proptosis (eyeball protrusion) that is triggered by maneuvers that increase venous pressure in the head and neck. Specifically, the symptoms characteristically intensify when the patient bends forward, strains (Valsalva maneuver), or coughs. Varices are low-flow venous malformations that expand under high pressure. Orbital hemangioma (Option A) is a more common orbital tumor, but it causes constant and slowly progressive proptosis rather than the posture-dependent intermittent type. Orbital metastasis (Option C) typically presents in older patients with rapid, painful proptosis and a known primary cancer. An Orbital dermoid cyst (Option D) is a slow-growing, firm, painless mass usually found at the orbital margins from birth. Diagnosis of orbital varices is confirmed by imaging, such as CT or MRI, performed while the patient is performing a Valsalva maneuver to visualize the venous dilation. Management is usually conservative unless the varices cause severe pain, vision loss from nerve compression, or significant cosmetic disfigurement
questions.learning: The hallmark of orbital varices is intermittent, transient proptosis (eyeball protrusion) that is triggered by maneuvers that increase venous pressure in the head and neck.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A woman presents with multiple small, pink- colored papules on the face, each showing central umbilication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of multiple small, pink, umbilicated papules (dome-shaped with a central dimple) is the classic clinical presentation of molluscum contagiosum. This is a viral infection caused by a poxvirus and is highly common in children. Herpes simplex (Option B) presents as grouped vesicles on an erythematous base rather than umbilicated papules. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) (Option C) causes warts, which are typically hyperkeratotic and rough, lacking central umbilication. Acne vulgaris (Option D) is characterized by comedones, inflammatory papules, or pustules, but not umbilicated papules. Therefore, the characteristic "dimple" or central umbilication described in the scenario is pathognomonic for molluscum contagiosum
questions.learning: The presence of multiple small, pink, umbilicated papules (dome-shaped with a central dimple) is the classic clinical presentation of molluscum contagiosum.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the most reliable indicator of recent malaria transmission?
questions.explanation: In community health and malariology, the infant parasite rate (IPR) is considered the most sensitive and reliable indicator of recent malaria transmission in a specific locality. Since infants (children under 1 year of age) are usually kept indoors and have had a limited window of exposure to mosquito bites, finding parasites in their blood indicates that they were infected very recently within that area. If the IPR is zero, it suggests that transmission has been effectively interrupted. Spleen rate (Option A) measures the prevalence of enlarged spleens in children and is used to determine the endemicity of malaria but represents long-term rather than acute transmission. Parasite density index (Option C) measures the severity of infection in individuals. Slide positivity rate (Option D) indicates the percentage of fever cases that are actually malaria but can be influenced by many external factors. Therefore, IPR is the primary surveillance tool for assessing the immediate success of malaria control programs
questions.learning: In community health and malariology, the infant parasite rate (IPR) is considered the most sensitive and reliable indicator of recent malaria transmission in a specific locality.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Peritoneal dialysis is associated with all of the following complications except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight loss

Peritoneal dialysis (PD) complications include:

• Peritonitis → most common and serious complication
• Poor filtration / inadequate clearance → especially in large or long-term patients
• Hyperglycemia → due to absorption of glucose-containing dialysate
• Weight loss is NOT typical

PD commonly causes weight gain, not loss, due to:

• Glucose absorption
• Increased caloric load
• Fluid retention

| Feature | PD | HD

| ------- | --- | ---

| Access | Peritoneal catheter | AV fistula/graft

| Frequency | Daily (continuous) | 3×/week

| Hemodynamic stability | ✅ Better | ❌ More fluctuation

| Residual renal function | ✅ Better preserved | ❌ Faster loss

| Peritonitis risk | ✅ Higher | Lower

| Weight change | ↑ Weight GAIN | Variable

| Protein loss | ✅ Higher | Lower

| Preferred in | Diabetics, children, remote areas | High-clearance needs

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Considering that the stone visible in the image measures 2 mm, what is the most appropriate management or treatment option?
questions.explanation: The size of a urinary stone is the most important factor in determining the likelihood of spontaneous passage. Small stones measuring less than 4–5 mm have a very high probability (up to 80% or higher) of passing through the urinary tract on their own with adequate hydration and pain management. Therefore, for a 2 mm stone, the most appropriate and standard initial management is "watchful waiting" or medical expulsive therapy. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (Option A) is reserved for large stones ( cm). Ureteroscopy (Option B) and Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL) (Option C) are interventions used for larger stones (typically mm) or for smaller stones that fail to pass after an observation period or cause significant complications. For a simple 2 mm stone, invasive or costly interventions are unnecessary and carry more risk than benefit. Thus, observation is the correct therapeutic choice
questions.learning: The size of a urinary stone is the most important factor in determining the likelihood of spontaneous passage. Small stones measuring less than 4–5 mm have a very high probability (up to 80% or higher) of passing through the urinary tract on their own with…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about cancer treatment according to the Colombo plan?
options: Help with PET scan units for diagnosis of cancer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Setting up cobalt therapy units

Aid to set up cobalt therapy units for cancer treatment at medical institutions in India was a part of the Colombo plan.

The Colombo Plan is a regional organization that upholds the concept of a collective intergovernmental effort to strengthen the economic and social development of member countries in the Asia-Pacific region.

It was formed at a meeting of the commonwealth foreign ministers with the headquarters at Colombo in January 1950. It comprises 20 developing countries within the region and 6 non-regional members - Australia, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, the UK, and USA. It involves foreign aid and technical assistance for the economic and social development of the region.

The contribution of Canada in supplying cobalt therapy units to medical institutions in India was an important item of aid under the Colombo plan. AIIMS New Delhi was established with financial assistance from New Zealand under the Colombo plan. Cobalt therapy is a form of radiotherapy that uses cobalt-60, a radioactive isotope, to generate high-energy gamma rays for treating cancer. Cobalt therapy units were an important tool for cancer treatment in the mid-20th century, and their provision under the Colombo plan significantly improved cancer treatment capabilities in India.
The Colombo Plan has evolved over the years and now focuses on a broader range of development goals, including education, public administration, agriculture, and industry. This reflects the changing needs of the Asia-Pacific region and the importance of a comprehensive approach to development.

Other Options:

Option A (Help with PET scan units for diagnosis of cancer): While PET scan units are important for cancer diagnosis, they were not part of the Colombo plan's cancer treatment initiatives in India.

Option B (Human resource strengthening): Although the Colombo plan aims to improve the economic and social development of member countries, human resource strengthening in the context of cancer treatment is not explicitly mentioned as part of the plan.

Option C (Setting up chemotherapy units): The Colombo plan's focus in cancer treatment was on providing aid for cobalt therapy units, not chemotherapy units.
questions.learning: Setting up cobalt therapy units Aid to set up cobalt therapy units for cancer treatment at medical institutions in India was a part of the Colombo plan.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old man reports progressive low back pain and morning stiffness for the past six months, with relief on physical activity. He also has a known history of ulcerative colitis. Based on the X-ray of the lumbar spine shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of chronic inflammatory back pain (worse in the morning, improves with exercise) and a history of inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) is highly suggestive of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. The provided X-ray provides the definitive diagnosis, showing vertical syndesmophytes fusing the vertebral bodies, creating the classic "bamboo spine" appearance of Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option C). Pott’s spine (Option A) is spinal tuberculosis, which causes vertebral destruction and angulation (gibbus) rather than smooth fusion. Psoriatic arthritis (Option B) can cause sacroiliitis but usually presents with asymmetric large syndesmophytes. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) primarily affects the small joints of the hands and the cervical spine, not the lumbar spine in this manner. Therefore, the pathognomonic "bamboo spine" in the context of IBD confirms Ankylosing Spondylitis
questions.learning: The combination of chronic inflammatory back pain (worse in the morning, improves with exercise) and a history of inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) is highly suggestive of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is the test for immediate memory?
options: Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed
Serial (100-7) subtraction test up to 5 steps
Digit span backwards up to 5 digits with 2 skips allowed
Serial (20-1) subtraction test up to 5 steps
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed

Forward digit span test is the best test among the given options.

Memory is of 3 types:

• Immediate
• Recent
• Remote

Immediate memory is attention dependent. Tests of attention and memory include

• Digit span test: Most important and best test for immediate memory
• Serial (100-7) subtraction test is the best for concentration
• Days of the week backwards
• Spell WORLD backwards
• (20–3) test

Digit span test

The examiner recites numbers randomly without any sequence and asks the patient to repeat the same. The examiner starts with a 2-number sequence and the digit span increases from 2 numbers to 3 numbers and so on. The patient is asked to repeat until he/she fails to repeat all numbers correctly.

Digit forward

• Normally a person can repeat up to 7 digits (+/- 2)
• E.g., Examiner says 2 - 4 –8 –1 –5 –7 - 9. The person has to repeat in the same order 2 – 4 – 8 –1 –5 –7 –9.

Digit backward

• Reproduction of longer digits in backward direction.
• Normally a person can repeat up to 5 digits (+/- 1) in backward direction (making option C wrong)
• Eg : Examiner says 2 - 4 –8 –1 –5 –7 - 9. The person has to repeat it backwards. 9 -7 -5 -1 -8- 4- 2.

Serial (100-7) subtraction test

• 5 scores / steps are taken in to account

• 1st score – When the patient tells 93 (100 - 7 = 93)
• 2nd score - When the patient tells 86 (93 – 7 = 86)
• And so on . . 100 , 93 , 86 , 79 , 72 , 65

Hence among the given options :

Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed would be the answer of choice as it is the best test for immediate memory
questions.learning: Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed Forward digit span test is the best test among the given options. Memory is of 3 types: • Immediate • Recent • Remote Immediate memory is attention dependent.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Based on the given clinical details, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of inspiratory stridor in infants. It is a congenital condition in which the supraglottic laryngeal structures are soft and floppy, causing them to collapse inward during inspiration and partially obstruct the airway. The characteristic clinical features include loud, high-pitched inspiratory stridor that typically worsens when the infant is crying, feeding, or lying supine and improves when the infant is prone. On laryngoscopic examination, classical findings include an omega-shaped epiglottis, shortened aryepiglottic folds, and redundant arytenoid mucosa. Why the other options are incorrect: 1. Vocal cord paralysis usually presents with a weak or hoarse cry and may be associated with aspiration. 2. Subglottic stenosis causes biphasic stridor and is often linked to a history of prolonged intubation. 3. Laryngeal papilloma presents with progressive hoarseness due to wart-like lesions on the vocal cords. 4. Most cases of laryngomalacia are benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously by 18–24 months as the laryngeal cartilages mature
questions.learning: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of inspiratory stridor in infants. It is a congenital condition in which the supraglottic laryngeal structures are soft and floppy, causing them to collapse inward during inspiration and partially obstruct the airway.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A case of a road traffic accident which occurred 20 mins ago was brought for autopsy. Postmortem examination reveals stiff neck, upper limbs, and lower limbs and primary relaxation is absent. What is this suggestive of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cadaveric spasm

Since the voluntary muscles are involved with no primary relaxation this is suggestive of cadaveric spasm.

Cadaveric spasm doesn’t indicate time since death. It only indicates the manner of death.

Cadaveric spasm/Instantaneous rigor/cataleptic rigidity/death clutch:

* It is a phenomenon where a group of muscles that are in a state of contraction at the time of death remains contracted after death till molecular death occurs.

* It occurs immediately after death. There is no stage of primary relaxation.

* It is seen in cases of deaths coupled with emotional disturbances like in case of excitement, fear, severe pain, exhaustion at the time of death, cerebral hemorrhage, injury to the nervous system, drowning, strychnine poisoning.

* It is an ante mortem phenomenon and it indicates the manner of death and not the time since death.

Examples:

* In case of drowning, weeds and grass caught in hand during struggle remain firmly grasped even after death. This indicates that the person was alive when entering the water.

* In case of suicides, weapons remain firmly grasped in the hand.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As a Medical Officer at a Primary Health Center planning a focus group discussion with antenatal mothers, what is the ideal number of participants to ensure effective interaction and meaningful engagement?
questions.explanation: A Focus Group Discussion (FGD) is a qualitative research and educational tool used to explore the attitudes and behaviors of a specific group. For an FGD to be effective, the group must be large enough to generate diverse viewpoints but small enough to allow every participant to speak and for the moderator to maintain control. The internationally recognized "ideal" number of participants for an FGD is 6 to 12 people. Option A (4-6) and Option B (3-5) are often too small, potentially leading to a lack of group dynamic or the conversation being dominated by a single individual. Option D (12-15) is typically too large, making it difficult for quieter members to participate and for the moderator to follow deep thematic threads. A group of 8 to 10 is often considered the "sweet spot" within the broader 6-12 range. This size fosters a comfortable, interactive environment where rich, qualitative data about health beliefs can be collected effectively

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which medication should be given to a 45-year- old woman with lung adenocarcinoma to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, considering she experienced these symptoms during prior treatment cycles?
questions.explanation: Palonosetron is a highly effective, second-generation 5-HT3 receptor antagonist specifically utilized for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV). It has a significantly longer half-life (approximately 40 hours) compared to first-generation agents like ondansetron, making it particularly useful for both acute and delayed vomiting phases. Metoclopramide (Option A) and Domperidone (Option C) are dopamine antagonists with prokinetic properties; while they can treat general nausea, they are less effective than 5-HT3 antagonists for the highly emetogenic stimulus of chemotherapy. Ropinirole (Option B) is a dopamine agonist used for Parkinson's disease and has no role in managing CINV. Therefore, because Palonosetron is part of the gold-standard antiemetic protocols for cancer patients, it is the most appropriate medication for this woman. Prevention is prioritized by administering these agents before chemotherapy begins. Consequently, palonosetron is the definitive pharmacological choice in this scenario
questions.learning: Palonosetron is a highly effective, second-generation 5-HT3 receptor antagonist specifically utilized for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which secondary ossification center of the femur is the first to fuse with the shaft?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lesser trochanter

The lesser trochanter is the first secondary ossification center of the femur to fuse with the shaft, typically fusing around 16–17 years of age. Knowledge of the appearance and fusion of femoral ossification centers is important in pediatric radiology, forensic age estimation, and orthopedics.

Order of Fusion of Femoral Secondary Ossification Centers

1. Lesser trochanter → first to fuse
2. Greater trochanter
3. Femoral head
4. Distal femoral epiphysis → last to fuse

Why Not the Other Options?

• Greater trochanter: Fuses later than the lesser trochanter.
• Femoral head: Fusion occurs after the trochanters.
• Distal end of femur: Although it is the first ossification center to appear (near birth), it is among the last epiphyses to fuse with the shaft.
questions.learning: Lesser trochanter — The lesser trochanter is the first secondary ossification center of the femur to fuse with the shaft, typically fusing around 16–17 years of age.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Revised A patient comes with a history of category 3 dog bites. He received prophylaxis for a monkey bite 6 months back. What is the next step in management? RIG- Rabies immunoglobulin
options: Wound cleaning+ rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wound cleaning+ rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3

This patient should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

In India, monkeys are known to transmit rabies. Hence the national rabies control program advises a full course of PEP for monkey bites. This patient who was bitten by a monkey 6 months back would have received PEP for rabies.

Management of a new dog bite in a previously immunized individual with either pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is as follows:

* Category I: Wound treatment only

* Category II/ III:

* Wound treatment with soap and running water for 15 min and apply antiseptic

* Receive Anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) 2 doses ID (0.1 ml, 1 site)/ 2 doses IM (1 VIAL, 1 site) on days 0 and 3.

Rabies immunoglobulin is not given for any category in case they have completed a full course of PEP.

*Note: In developing countries like India, the vaccination status of animals alone, doesn't play a significant role in determining the initiation of prophylaxis in humans.

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment
questions.learning: Wound cleaning+ rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3 — This patient should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man who regularly wears contact lenses presents with eye pain, redness, and purulent discharge from the right eye. Examination reveals a characteristic greyish- white, serpiginous ulcer on the lower cornea, along with a 4 mm hypopyon and moderate anterior chamber flare. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation is highly characteristic of an acute bacterial corneal ulcer, likely caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is a common and aggressive pathogen associated with contact lens wear. The "snake-shaped" (serpiginous) greyish-white ulcer is a classic clinical description for certain bacterial keratitis. The presence of a significant hypopyon (a collection of white blood cells in the anterior chamber) and anterior chamber flare further indicates a severe infectious process. Viral ulcers (Option A) usually present with a dendritic appearance and less prominent discharge. Fungal ulcers (Option C) typically have "feathery" edges and satellite lesions following vegetative trauma. Parasitic ulcers (Option D), such as Acanthamoeba, cause disproportionate pain and a ring-shaped infiltrate. Bacterial ulcers are a medical emergency requiring intensive topical fortified antibiotics to prevent corneal perforation. Therefore, given the acute purulent presentation and contact lens history, a bacterial etiology is the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation is highly characteristic of an acute bacterial corneal ulcer, likely caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is a common and aggressive pathogen associated with contact lens wear.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complaints of greenish-black material in the nasal cavity accompanied by a foul (fetid) smell. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s description of greenish-black crusts and a "merciful" foul smell (ozena) is pathognomonic for Atrophic Rhinitis. The term "merciful" refers to the fact that while the smell is offensive to others, the patient is unaware of it due to concurrent atrophy of the olfactory nerves (anosmia). This condition involves chronic atrophy of the nasal mucosa and underlying turbinate bones. Allergic rhinitis (Option A) presents with clear watery discharge, sneezing, and itching, not crusting. Rhinitis caseosa (Option C) features "cheese-like" foul material and is typically associated with extensive nasal polyps or infection. Rhinitis sicca (Option D) involves simple dryness of the mucosa, often in hot environments, but lacks the characteristic greenish crusts and ozena. Management includes regular nasal douching with alkaline solutions to clear the crusts and prevent secondary infections like Klebsiella ozaenae

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent chest infections and abdominal pain. There is a history of 1 blood transfusion in the past. On examination, he had icterus and mild splenomegaly. Electrophoresis shows increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sickle cell disease

The given scenario with electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike is suggestive of sickle cell disease.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis.

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

• Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
• Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.
• Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.
• Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.
• Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.
• Spleen

• In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.
• Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.
• Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

• Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled red cells on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased levels of HbA2, HbF, and S spike. The changes in the skull resemble a crewcut in radiographic studies as a result of compensatory erythroid hyperplasia.

The image given below shows the sickling of RBCs in sickle cell disease.

The image given below shows Howell-Jolly bodies seen in asplenia.

Note: The sickle cell trait protects against falciparum malaria in certain African populations.

Other options:

Option A: Beta-thalassemia is an autosomal codominant disorder, caused by mutations in alpha or beta globin that reduce hemoglobin synthesis. Peripheral smear shows microcytic, hypochromic cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, target cells, and basophilic stippling. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbF and HbA2.

Option B: HbC disease is caused by mutation in the beta-globin chain in which glutamate is replaced by lysine in the sixth position of the beta-globin chain. Patients usually present with very mild anemia and microcytosis. Peripheral smear shows hexagonal HbC crystals. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbC levels.

Option D: Acute coronary syndrome is very rare in children and may be associated with Kawasaki disease. Children with Kawasaki disease present with fever, conjunctival ingestion, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and hand and foot changes. They are treated with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a direct hernia is posted for Lichtenstein repair. Which of the following is used in the mesh?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Polypropylene

A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used.

Polypropylene is a monofilament, non-absorbable suture material. It is a propylene polymer. It is used in plastic surgery, cardiovascular surgery, hernia repair, ophthalmic surgery, and general surgical subcuticular skin closure. Polypropylene mesh is used for hernia repair.

A Lichtenstein mesh repair is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. It is an anterior tension-free mesh repair that reduces the chances of recurrence of a hernia. A piece of prosthetic nonabsorbable mesh is used to fit the canal to bridge the defect in this repair.

Other surgical methods used for the repair of a hernia are:

* Bassini repair - It is done for the reconstruction of the inguinal floor in adults. In this method, a mesh is not used. It is associated with a high recurrence and is not used frequently now. It is used only in cases of hernial strangulation and peritonitis where the use of a mesh is not preferred. It is performed by suturing the transversus abdominis and internal oblique musculoaponeurotic arches/conjoined tendon to the inguinal ligament.

* Shouldice repair - It is a multilayered repair, where the posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strengthened by continuous sutures. It involves double-breasting of the transversalis fascia. It is associated with a very low recurrence rate.

* Gilbert repair (plug and patch repair) - It is an extension of Lichtenstein’s original mesh repair and has now become the most commonly performed primary anterior inguinal hernia repair. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used. It is deployed like an upside-down umbrella when inserted into the internal inguinal ring to occlude the hernia

* McVay repair (Cooper's ligament repair) is used for the correction of direct inguinal hernia, large indirect hernia, recurrent hernia, femoral hernias (particularly suited for strangulated femoral hernias). In this method, the transversus abdominis aponeurosis is approximated to Cooper's ligament.

* Stoppa-Rives repair - It is used for the repair of large, recurrent, or bilateral hernias. In this method, a sub-umbilical midline incision is given to place a large mesh into the preperitoneal space.

* Herniotomy - It is used to treat inguinal hernia in a child which occurs due to the presence of a patent processus vaginalis. Therefore in herniotomy, the repair of the inguinal ring is not done

Other options:

* Polyglactin (Vicryl)- This is an absorbable suture material and is commonly used in gut anastomoses, biliary anastomoses, and kidney and ureter surgeries.

* Polyglycolic acid- Used for other absorbable sutures, in particular where slightly longer wound support is required.
questions.learning: Polypropylene — A Lichtenstein mesh repair is currently one of the most frequently used methods for treating an inguinal hernia. In this technique, a cone-shaped plug of polypropylene mesh is used.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
Oculocephalic reflex assesses the integrity of which of the following cranial nerves?

A. III
B. IV
C. VI
D. VIII
E. VII
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A, C, and D

The oculocephalic reflex or doll's eye reflex is used to assess the integrity of the cranial nerves III, VI, and VIII.

It is a brainstem reflex examined by observing the the motion of eyes during the sudden rotation of the head of the patient by the examiner. It is done in both directions laterally, followed by flexion and extension. In a normal positive reflex, the eyes move conjugately in the opposite direction of the movement of the head to maintain their position in space.

The reflex has afferents in the vestibular nerve (VIII) that relay to the brainstem nuclei and bring about conjugate eye movements through the oculomotor nerve (III) and abducens nerve (VI).

A negative reflex occurs in any of the above cranial nerve palsies or brainstem injuries, where the eyes show no movement or movement in the same direction as head movement. This is used to assess brainstem reflexes in a comatose patient as a criterion of brain death.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which metallic poisoning causes proximal convoluted tubule damage with proteinuria and muscle pain ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arsenic

Arsenic poisoning causes PCT damage with proteinuria and muscle pain.

Nephropathy is caused by most of the heavy metals. However, muscle pain is seen with arsenic poisoning.

Salient features of Arsenic poisoning:

Acute poisoning: Resembles cholera; garlicky odor

Chronic poisoning: Following features are seen:

• Raindrop pigmentation seen on temples, eyelids and neck
• Aldrich-Mee’s lines (transverse white striae on the fingernails)
• Hyperkeratosis of palms and soles
• Painful paraesthesia of hands and feet
• Red velvety appearance of stomach
• Blackfoot disease - a gangrenous condition affecting the extremities

Tests to detect Arsenic poisoning:

• Marsh test and Reinsch test

Treatment:

Freshly prepared hydrated ferric oxide.

BAL(British Anti Lewisite)

Penicillamine(If BAL not available)

Note: Mercury does not cause muscle pain though it commonly causes PCT damage.

Mee’s lines- Transverse white striae of the fingernails

Hyperkeratosis of palms and soles

Rain drop pigmentation
questions.learning: Arsenic Arsenic poisoning causes PCT damage with proteinuria and muscle pain. Nephropathy is caused by most of the heavy metals.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Calculate the percentage of burns in a preschool child shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 25-30%

From the given image, the percentage of burns in the child is 25-30% calculated based on Lund and Browder chart.

In the given image, the right arm, chest, abdomen, and both thighs are involved in burns. According to Lund and Browder chart, 2% is for the right arm, 13% for chest and abdomen involvement, and 4% for each thigh. Hence, the total involvement is 2+13+4+4 = 23%. The closest value to 23% among the given options is 25-30% (option B).

Lund and Browder chart is an accurate method to measure burns if it is used correctly. In this, different proportions of body surface areas in children are taken into consideration. This chart compensates for the changes in the shape of the body with age and can accurately assess the burns area in children.

The below image shows the Lund and Browder chart.

Note: Wallace's rule of nines is used in estimating medium to large burns in adults. It helps in the quick estimation of the burns. In this, the total burn is calculated by dividing the body into areas of 9%. It is not accurate in children.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with thiamine deficiency develops lactic acidosis. Which of the following enzymes is affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pyruvate dehydrogenase

Pyruvate dehydrogenase is the enzyme affected in a patient with thiamine deficiency who develops lactic acidosis.

Pyruvate is transported from the cytosol into the mitochondria, where undergoes oxidative decarboxylation to form acetyl CoA in the presence of the multi-enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC) in the mitochondrial matrix.

The PDHC primarily consists of three enzymes: Pyruvate decarboxylase (also called Pyruvate dehydrogenase), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase. It also requires the following co-enzymes:

1. Thiamine pyrophosphate, essential for pyruvate decarboxylase and is tightly bound to it
2. Lipoic acid and coenzyme A, essential for dihydrolipoyl transacetylase
3. FAD and NAD+, essential for dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase.

In a patient with thiamine deficiency, due to the inactive thiamine pyrophosphate, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is unable to act on pyruvate, which begins to accumulate on the body and is then shunted towards lactic acid formation by the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase.

This results in lactic acid accumulation and subsequent lactic acidosis in the patient.

Wernicke–Korsakoff, an encephalopathy-psychosis syndrome due to thiamine deficiency, may be seen in chronic alcoholics. It occurs due to insufficient production of ATP by the brain cells via the citric acid cycle as the PDHC is inactive.

Other options:

Option A: Pyruvate carboxylase facilitates the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate by carboxylation.

Option C: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase is involved in the decarboxylation and phosphorylation of oxaloacetate to form phosphoenolpyruvate seen in gluconeogenesis.

Option D: Transketolase with coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate is an enzyme involved in the non-oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway.
