questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A patient who is a known case of alcohol dependence syndrome presents with sudden and unintentional weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?

• ALP - 240 IU/L
• S. Direct bilirubin - 1 mg/dL
• AST/ALT - 0.5
• Alpha fetoprotein- 600 ng/mL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hepatocellular carcinoma

The most likely diagnosis in this patient with a history of alcohol dependence, sudden unintentional weight loss, and raised AFP is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

HCC is the most common cause of primary liver cancer. It is more commonly seen in males, and the peak age group is between 65-70 years. The main risk factor for HCC is cirrhosis and associated chronic liver damage due to chronic infection by hepatitis B or C virus (HBV or HCV), alcohol abuse, metabolic syndrome, or hemochromatosis. The incidence of HCC is increasing worldwide. This is contributed by the increase in HCV and HBV infections, along with lifestyle disorders like obesity. Obesity is associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This progresses on to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) causing cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Thus, NASH and NAFLD are risk factors for HCC.

Regular surveillance, including liver imaging and monitoring of alpha-fetoprotein levels, is recommended for high-risk populations, such as those with liver cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B or C infection, or significant alcohol consumption. Early detection of HCC can improve treatment outcomes and overall prognosis.

Very early HCC is treated by ablation. Early HCC with a single nodule is resected, but when there are multiple nodules over 3 cm, ablation or transplantation are considered. Intermediate-stage HCC is treated by chemoembolization. Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) is used for multinodular lesions.

Other Options:

Option A: Hepatic adenomas are benign liver tumors that are often associated with oral contraceptive use and anabolic steroid use. The patient's history of alcohol dependence and high alpha-fetoprotein levels are not consistent with hepatic adenoma. Additionally, hepatic adenomas are usually asymptomatic and do not present with sudden unintentional weight loss.

Option B: Cholangiocarcinoma is a cancer that arises from the bile ducts within the liver. While patients with alcohol dependence may have an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma, the elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels are not typical for this type of cancer. Cholangiocarcinomas usually present with jaundice, pruritus, and abdominal pain, but sudden weight loss is less characteristic.

Option D: Alcoholic hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver caused by excessive alcohol consumption. It usually presents with jaundice, fever, and abdominal pain. While the patient's history of alcohol dependence might suggest alcoholic hepatitis, elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels and unintentional weight loss are not typical for this condition. Moreover, the AST/ALT ratio is usually greater than 2 in alcoholic hepatitis, but it is 0.5 in this case.
questions.learning: Hepatocellular carcinoma — The most likely diagnosis in this patient with a history of alcohol dependence, sudden unintentional weight loss, and raised AFP is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient, chronic smoker presented with cough and skin hyperpigmentation. During further evaluation, he is found to have high ACTH levels that remained high even after administration of high-dose dexamethasone. What is the underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor

Elevated ACTH levels that do not get suppressed by a high-dose dexamethasone test are suggestive of Cushing’s syndrome secondary to an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor. Considering the patient's smoking status and cough it is likely to be a lung tumor.

Dynamic testing for Cushing’s syndrome

High dose dexamethasone suppression test
CRH stimulation test

Pituitary adenoma
Positive (suppressed cortisol)
Positive (increase in ACTH and cortisol)

Ectopic ACTH
Negative
Negative

Iatrogenic: Suppressed ACTH levels that are not affected by dynamic testing

Adrenal mass or hyperplasia:  Suppressed ACTH levels that are not affected by dynamic testing

Ectopic sources of ACTH include small cell lung cancers and pulmonary carcinoid tumors. The most effective treatment strategy is the management of the underlying SCLC or carcinoid.

Option A: Exogenous steroid administration presents with suppressed ACTH levels.

Option B: Pituitary adenoma presents with elevated ACTH but a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is positive (suppressed).

Option C: Adrenal adenoma presents with suppressed ACTH levels.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient came to the emergency room with severe pain in the abdomen. Serum triglyceride level was 1500 mg/dL. Identify the defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Apo CII

Very high triglycerides (>1000 mg/dL) with acute abdominal pain suggests hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis, classically seen in familial chylomicronemia (Type I hyperlipoproteinemia).

• Deficiency of Apolipoprotein C-II (Apo C-II)
• Apo C-II is a cofactor for lipoprotein lipase (LPL)

Pathophysiology:

• Without Apo C-II → LPL cannot be activated
• Impaired breakdown of chylomicrons → massive accumulation of triglycerides
• Leads to pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis

Why other options are incorrect:

• Apo B-48: Needed for chylomicron formation (defect → abetalipoproteinemia)
• Apo B-100: Required for LDL/VLDL metabolism (familial hypercholesterolemia-like states)
• LDL receptor: Causes ↑ LDL (Type IIa), not severe triglyceridemia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the refractive error.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myopia

In the above image, parallel rays are focused in front of the retina and hence the refractive error shown is Myopia.

Myopia, also known as short sightedness, is that dioptric condition of the eye in which, with the accommodation at rest, incident parallel rays come to a focus anterior to the light-sensitive layer of the retina. In myopia the defect in vision is more for objects present at a distance.

American Optometric Association (AOA) Grading of Myopia:

• Low myopia, when the error is ≤ –3D.
• Moderate myopia, when the error is between -3D to -6D.
• High myopia, when the error is ≥ –6D.

Option B: Presbyopia is used to define physiological insufficiency of accommodation that causes progressive loss of near vision. It is commonly seen in elderly due to age-related decline in ciliary muscle power. Bifocals spectacles are prescribed in presbyopia.

Option C: In hypermetropia, parallel rays of light are focussed behind the retina causing defective vision which is more for near objects.

Option D: In astigmatism, the rays of light entering the eye fail to converge at a point focus but they form focal lines. Strum’s connoid of astigmatism represents the configuration of a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic(toric) surface and helps in understanding the optics of regular astigmatism.

questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 51-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to chest tightness that started 30 minutes prior to arrival. He has 2 histories of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Initial ECG Shows ST elevation in leads I and aVL. Cardiac enzymes are elevated. Emergent cardiac catheterization in this patient will most likely show occlusion of which of the following arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left circumflex artery

ST elevation in leads I and aVL localizes to the high lateral wall of the left ventricle. High-lateral STEMI is most commonly due to occlusion of the left circumflex (LCX) (or a diagonal branch), and among the given options LCX best fits.

A. Distal LAD – Usually causes anterior/apical changes (V3–V6), not isolated I/aVL.

C. Left main coronary artery – Produces widespread ST changes with severe instability, not isolated high-lateral.

D. Right coronary artery – Inferior MI (II, III, aVF) ± RV involvement

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the current scenario treatment for urea cycle disorder is available. Administration of amino acid phenylbutyrate can decrease ammonia formation. Which amino acid provides phenylbutyrate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamate

The amino acid that provides phenylbutyrate in the treatment of urea cycle disorders is glutamate.

Ammonia to Urea cycle: Ammonia gets converted to glutamate (non toxic form) through transamination.  Glutamate is transported to the liver as glutamine (by glutamine synthase). In the liver, ammonia is released from glutamine, converting it to alpha keto glutatamte. The released ammonia enters the urea cycle.

In acetylation therapy, Phenylbutyrate (a prodrug) which is metabolized to phenylacetate. Phenylacetate combines with glutamine (a nitrogen-rich amino acid) to form phenylacetylglutamine. Phenylacetylglutamine is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine. This process helps trap excess nitrogen, bypassing the urea cycle.

Other drugs that can be used to achieve the same outcome (ammonia scavengers) include:

• Phenylacetate
• Benzoate

Other Options:

Option A and C: Arginine and Aspartate do not play a role in this specific reaction.

Option D: Glycine: The combination of benzoate and glycine forms hippuric acid, a non-toxic compound. When Benzoate is administered to the body, it acts as a nitrogen-scavenging agent. Hippuric acid is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine, effectively removing one nitrogen molecule from the body per molecule of hippuric acid formed. This mechanism is similar to how phenylacetate acts as a scavenger for glutamate.
questions.learning: Glutamate — The amino acid that provides phenylbutyrate in the treatment of urea cycle disorders is glutamate. Ammonia to Urea cycle: Ammonia gets converted to glutamate (non toxic form) through transamination.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with confusion, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and is diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis. What is the primary treatment to control her elevated blood glucose levels?
questions.explanation: In the acute management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), the primary goal of insulin therapy is to stop ketogenesis and gradually normalize blood sugar. Regular (Short-acting) insulin is the only correct choice for initial management in an emergency setting. It is typically administered as a continuous intravenous drip because of its rapid onset and short half-life, allowing for precise titration based on hourly glucose monitoring. Lente insulin (Option B) is an intermediate-acting insulin used for chronic basal control, not for emergencies. Glyburide (Option C) is an oral sulfonylurea that is ineffective in Type 1 diabetes (where there is absolute insulin deficiency) and never used for DKA. insulin (Option D) is a pre-mixed combination used for daily maintenance. Therefore, regular insulin remains the global standard of care for stabilizing patients with DKA to effectively resolve acidosis and hyperglycemia
questions.learning: In the acute management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), the primary goal of insulin therapy is to stop ketogenesis and gradually normalize blood sugar.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following steps in the metabolism of Vitamin D requires sunlight?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol

In the metabolism of vitamin D, the conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol requires sunlight.

Vitamin D metabolism occurs in 3 steps:

Step 1- Skin: 7-dehydrocholesterol (an intermediate in cholesterol synthesis that accumulates in the skin) undergoes a nonenzymic reaction on exposure to ultraviolet light, yielding cholecalciferol, which is absorbed into the bloodstream.

Step 2- Liver:  Cholecalciferol is hydroxylated to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol. This is released into the circulation bound to a vitamin D–binding globulin, which is the main storage form of the vitamin.

Step 3- Kidney: 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol, the biologically active form by the enzyme 1α-hydroxylase.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Gastric lavage is contraindicated in which of the following poisonings?
questions.explanation: Gastric lavage ("pumping the stomach") is a common decontamination procedure, but it is strictly contraindicated in hydrocarbon poisoning (e.g., kerosene, gasoline, or thinner). These substances have low viscosity and high volatility. During the process of lavage or vomiting, they can easily be aspirated into the lungs, where even a tiny amount can cause a severe, life-threatening chemical pneumonitis. Lavage is also contraindicated in corrosive (acid/alkali) poisoning due to the risk of esophageal perforation. Strychnine (Option A) and Paraldehyde (Option B) poisonings can be managed with lavage if done early. For iron tablet poisoning (Option D), whole bowel irrigation is often preferred over simple lavage because the tablets are large and heavy and difficult to remove through a tube. In hydrocarbon cases, management is purely supportive, and inducing vomiting must be avoided at all costs to protect the patient's airway
questions.learning: Gastric lavage ("pumping the stomach") is a common decontamination procedure, but it is strictly contraindicated in hydrocarbon poisoning (e.g., kerosene, gasoline, or thinner).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which artery is the most common source of Cirsoid Aneurysms of the scalp? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superficial temporal artery

Cirsoid aneurysm is an arteriovenous malformation that most commonly affects the superficial temporal vessels on the forehead and scalp. These lesions present as pulsatile masses and represent abnormal communications between arteries and veins without an intervening capillary network. The superficial temporal artery is the primary arterial feeder in these malformations, making it the most common source of cirsoid aneurysms of the scalp.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A male infant was brought to the emergency pediatric unit with abdominal distention. There was a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. On examination, he was found to have urinary retention. Imaging showed bilateral hydronephrosis. What could be the probable diagnosis of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior urethral valves

The given clinical scenario with USG finding of bilateral hydronephrosis is suggestive of posterior urethral valve.

Posterior urethral valve:

* The valves are membranes that have a small posterior slit within them, which typically lie just distal to the verumontanum

* They function as flap valves and are obstructive to antegrade urinary flow. A urethral catheter can be passed retrogradely.

* Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound, which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis above a distended bladder

* If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary infection in the neonatal period or with uraemia and renal failure

* The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography

* Definitive treatment is by urethroscopic destruction of the valves with continuing lifelong supportive treatment of the dilated urinary tract, the recurrent urinary infections and the uraemia.

Vesicoureteric reflux would present with unilateral hydronephrosis, on the affected side.

Pearl PF1540: Causes of Hydronephrosis

Unilateral hydronephrosis

Extramural obstruction

* Tumor from adjacent structures, e.g., cervix, prostate, rectum, colon, or cecum

* Retrocaval ureter

Intramural obstruction

* Congenital stenosis

* Ureterocele

* PUJ obstruction

* Congenital small ureteric orifice

* Inflammatory stricture following removal of ureteric calculus, repair of a damaged ureter, or tuberculous infection

* Neoplasm of the ureter or bladder cancer involving the ureteric orifice

Intraluminal obstruction

* Calculus in the pelvis or ureter

* Sloughed papilla in papillary necrosis (especially, in patients with diabetes, analgesic abuse, or sickle cell disease)

Bilateral hydronephrosis

Congenital:

* Posterior urethral valves (associated with pulmonary hypoplasia)

* Urethral atresia

* PUJ obstruction

Acquired:

* Benign prostatic hypertrophy or carcinoma of the prostate

* Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond's disease)

* Postoperative bladder neck scarring

* Urethral stricture

* Phimosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 23-year-old female visited the clinician with a solitary thyroid nodule and was advised for thyroid function tests where TSH level is 27.3 mU/L, T3 is 1.24 ng/ml, and T4 is 4.87 microgram/ml. Which of the following manifestations is true regarding the condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s laboratory results show a significantly elevated TSH (27.3 mU/L) with normal to low-normal T3 and T4 levels, which is characteristic of primary hypothyroidism. Weight gain is a classic manifestation of hypothyroidism due to a decreased basal metabolic rate. Other typical symptoms include cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, and dry skin. In contrast, heat intolerance (Option A), tachycardia (Option B), and diarrhea (Option C) are hallmark symptoms of hyperthyroidism, where metabolic processes are accelerated. The most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in developed regions is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, while iodine deficiency remains a major cause globally. Given the high TSH, the body is attempting to stimulate a failing thyroid gland. Weight gain, puffiness, and lethargy are the most consistent clinical findings in this metabolic state
questions.learning: The patient’s laboratory results show a significantly elevated TSH (27.3 mU/L) with normal to low-normal T3 and T4 levels, which is characteristic of primary hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A male patient with a history of HIV infection was initiated on Anti Retroviral Therapy consisting of Tenofovir 150mg, Lamivudine 300mg, and Dolutegravir 50mg once daily at night, and now he is subsequently diagnosed with TB and started on antitubercular therapy. What is the required dose adjustment in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Add Dolutegravir 50 mg in morning

In this scenario where a patient on ART (under TLD regimen) is newly diagnosed with TB, the dosage of Dolutegravir is adjusted by adding 50mg in the morning. The dose modification is due to the drug Rifampicin(ATT regimen), which is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 activity. Dolutegravir is susceptible to this effect and its plasma concentration is affected which makes us increase the dose requirement.

Meanwhile, the other drugs in the regimen, Lamivudine and Tenofovir are unaffected by the CYP3A4 activity of Rifampicin and do not require any dose modification.

Dolutegravir is an integrase inhibitor, used in HIV-1 and HIV-2, preventing the integration of viral DNA into the host chromosome.

In a patient with coexistent tuberculosis and HIV, the preferred first-line ART regimen for all with age >10 years and weight >30kg is Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir as FDC in a single pill once a day.

In a patient with HIV-TB co-infection, it is ideal to start the Tuberculosis treatment before initiating ART (as soon as possible after 2 weeks and before 2 months).

Pearl PF1757: NACO ART Guidelines- 2021

ART regimen

First-line for:

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir

• All PLHIV who are age >10 years and body weight >30 kg with HIV-1, HIV-2, HIV 1&2 co-infection who have not received any ART
• Those with HIV-TB and HIV hepatitis co-infections
• Pregnant women, pregnant women presenting in active labour and breastfeeding women

Abacavir + Lamivudine + Efavirenz

• All PLHIV with abnormal serum creatinine values
• All PLHIV with bodyweight less <30 kg

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Efavirenz /Lopinavir /Ritonavir

• Women of childbearing age group who do not wish to take Dolutegravir

* All PLHIV who were on the previous recommended regime (Tenofovir+Lamivudine+Efavirenz) to be counselled to switch to new regime. Continue older regime if response is good

* Women in child-bearing age group to be counselled about Dolutegravir with opt-out option before switching to new regime

*PLHIV: People living with HIV

Pearl PF1966: Opportunistic Infections/HIV related conditions and ART initiation

Clinical scenario
Action

Any undiagnosed active infection with fever
Diagnose and treat first; start Anti-Retroviral Therapy (ART) when stable

Tuberculosis (TB)
Start TB treatment first; start ART as soon as possible after 2 weeks and before 2 months. For those with CD4 less than 50/cmm, start ART within 2 weeks Caution is needed for PLHIV with TB meningitis, since immediate ART is associated with more severe adverse events than initiating ART 2 months after the start of TB treatment

Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)

Treat PCP first; start ART when PCP treatment is completed

Invasive fungal diseases: Oesophageal candidiasis, penicilliosis, histoplasmosis
Start treatment for oesophageal candidiasis first; start ART as soon as the patient can swallow comfortably. Treat penicilliosis, and histoplasmosis first; start ART when the patient is stabilized or opportunistic infection treatment is completed.

Cryptococcal meningitis
Treat cryptococcal meningitis. ART initiation should be deferred until there is evidence of sustained clinical response to anti-fungal therapy and after 4 weeks of induction and consolidation treatment with amphotericin B containing regimen.

Bacterial pneumonia
Treat pneumonia first; start ART when treatment is completed

Malaria
Treat malaria first; start ART when treatment is completed

Acute diarrhoea which may reduce absorption of ART
Diagnose the cause and treat diarrhoea first; start ART when diarrhoea is stabilized or controlled

Non-severe anaemia (Hb< 9 g/dl)
Start ART if no other causes for anaemia are found (HIV is often the cause of anaemia)

Skin conditions such as PPE and seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, HIV-related exfoliative dermatitis
Start ART (ART may resolve these problems)

Suspected Mycobacterium Avium Complex (MAC), Cryptosporidiosis and Microsporidiosis
Start ART (ART may resolve these problems)

Cytomegalovirus retinitis
Start treatment for CMV urgently and start ART after 2 weeks of CMV treatment

Toxoplasmosis
Treat toxoplasmosis; start ART after 6 weeks of treatment and when the patient is stabilized

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Infertility in Kartagener’s syndrome is due to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asthenospermia

Kartagener’s syndrome is a type of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the classical triad of

• Situs inversus
• Chronic sinusitis
• Bronchiectasis

Infertility in Kartagener’s syndrome is due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function), not azoospermia (complete absence of spermatozoa in ejaculate).

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility. It occurs due to ultrastructural defects in the dynein arm of cilia. This causes the retention of secretions due to a failed mucociliary clearance mechanism. Clinically, this manifests as chronic sinusitis and recurrent infections that ultimately lead to bronchiectasis. As ciliary function is necessary to ensure proper rotation of the developing organs in the chest and abdomen, its absence will lead to situs inversus or a partial lateralizing abnormality. Approximately half of the patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia have Kartagener syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which feature is most useful in differentiating a true bruise from an artificially produced (fabricated) bruise?
options: Progression of the color of bruise over time
questions.explanation: A bruise (contusion) is an injury where blood escapes from ruptured vessels into the surrounding tissues. A hallmark of a genuine bruise is the systematic progression of color changes over several days as hemoglobin is broken down (from dark purple to blue, then green, yellow, and finally brown). This chronological color change cannot be accurately mimicked in a fabricated bruise. Fabricated bruises, often created using dyes or chemicals, typically have regular and well-defined margins (Option C), whereas genuine bruises usually have blurred, irregular edges due to the diffusion of blood. Positive chemical tests (Option A) might confirm the presence of a dye but not the biological nature of a genuine injury. The presence of vesicles (Option D) is characteristic of a burn or scald, not a contusion. Therefore, the physiological degradation of hemoglobin over time is the most reliable forensic indicator of a true bruise

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with long-standing diabetes presents with severe persistent otalgia and purulent otorrhea despite receiving appropriate antibiotics. Examination reveals granulation tissue in the external auditory canal. Imaging demonstrates erosion of the adjacent temporal bone, and the patient has developed facial nerve palsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malignant otitis externa

The clinical picture is characteristic of malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa, an aggressive infection of the external auditory canal that can progress to skull-base osteomyelitis.

It occurs classically in elderly patients with diabetes and immunocompromised individuals. The most common causative organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Important clinical clues include:

• Elderly patient with diabetes
• Severe, persistent otalgia, often disproportionate to examination findings
• Persistent otorrhea
• Granulation tissue in the external auditory canal, classically near the bony-cartilaginous junction
• Failure to respond to routine treatment for otitis externa
• Bony erosion/skull-base osteomyelitis
• Cranial nerve involvement, with facial nerve (CN VII) palsy being an important complication

Why not the other options?

• B. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: Commonly presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, nasal symptoms, and unilateral middle-ear effusion due to Eustachian tube obstruction rather than painful external auditory canal granulation.
• C. Chronic suppurative otitis media: Characterized by chronic middle-ear infection with tympanic membrane perforation and persistent/recurrent otorrhea. Severe disproportionate pain in an elderly diabetic with EAC granulation strongly favors malignant otitis externa.
• D. Acute suppurative otitis media: An acute middle-ear infection typically presenting with fever, otalgia, and a bulging tympanic membrane. Skull-base erosion and persistent EAC granulation are not typical features.
questions.learning: Malignant otitis externa — The clinical picture is characteristic of malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa, an aggressive infection of the external auditory canal that can progress to skull-base osteomyelitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with pain during defecation and a progressively enlarging mass at the anal verge over the past few months. Clinical evaluation and biopsy confirm squamous cell carcinoma of the anus. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: The primary treatment for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the anal canal is combined chemoradiotherapy, known as the Nigro protocol. Unlike many other GI cancers, SCC of the anus is highly sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy (typically using 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin C or cisplatin). This approach is preferred because it achieves high cure rates while preserving the anal sphincter and avoiding a permanent colostomy. Abdominoperineal resection (Option B), which involves removing the rectum and anus and creating a permanent stoma, is now reserved for patients who fail primary chemoradiation or have recurrent disease. Chemotherapy alone (Option A) is not curative for localized disease. Wide local excision (Option D) might be considered for very small, well-differentiated tumors of the anal "margin" (the skin outside), but not for carcinomas of the anal canal itself. Therefore, the sphincter-sparing combined chemoradiation remains the standard of care for anal SCC

questions.text: A 30-year-old man weighing 70 kg had a sodium level of 120 mEq/L. Calculate the sodium deficit.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 840 mEq

The sodium deficit in the given scenario is 840 mEq.

Sodium deficit is calculated as 0.6 x body weight x (target plasma sodium concentration - starting plasma sodium concentration).

Substituting the given values in the formula :

Sodium deficit = 0.6 x 70 x (140 - 120) = 840 mEq.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: This is the radiograph of a child with a foreign body in the oesophagus. What is the sign seen in this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Double ring sign

The presence of a halo sign or double ring sign is indicative of the foreign body being a button battery.

Button batteries and sharp objects in the oesophagus and foreign bodies associated with respiratory symptoms all mandate urgent endoscopic removal.

Button batteries, in particular, are very dangerous foreign bodies, which must be expediently removed because they can cause:

• Mucosal injury in 1-hour contact time
• Involve all layers of the oesophagus in 4 hours

Injury is thought to be secondary to electrochemical burns from electrical discharge. Chemical burns from electrolyte alkali leakage and pressure necrosis also may contribute to mucosal injury.

Asymptomatic blunt objects and coins lodged in the oesophagus can be observed for up to 24 hr in anticipation of passage into the stomach.

Another AP and lateral X-ray demonstrating the presence of a button battery in the oesophagus is as shown below.

Other options

Option A: Thumb sign is seen in acute epiglottitis.

Option B: A steeple sign is seen in croup or laryngotracheobronchitis.

Option D: String sign on the barium enema is in ileocecal tuberculosis.

The image below shows the string sign of Kantor associated with Crohn's disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following nerve is least injured during thyroid surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marginal mandibular nerve

The marginal mandibular nerve is least likely to be injured during thyroid surgery as it is high up (mandibular margin) than the dissection plane of the approach to thyroid surgery.

Other nerves that might be at risk of injury include:

• Recurrent laryngeal nerve may be injured if dissection is done below the cricoid cartilage or near the tracheoesophageal groove (option A).
• Ansa cervicalis may be injured if strap muscles are not cut high enough. (option B)
• External laryngeal nerve may be injured during ligation of superior thyroid vessels as it lies very close to the superior thyroid artery (option C).

Complications of thyroidectomy:

• Hemorrhage - most common complication overall; due to slipping of ligature
• Nerve injury

• External laryngeal nerve - hoarseness (more common)
• Recurrent laryngeal nerve - hoarseness if unilateral, life-threatening aspiration and aphonia if bilateral

• Respiratory obstruction

• Laryngeal edema - the most common cause of respiratory obstruction
• Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
• Laryngomalacia
• Tension hematoma

• Hypoparathyroidism - infarction of parathyroids
• Thyroid storm - inadequately prepared for surgery
• Hypothyroidism
• Recurrent thyrotoxicosis
• Wound infection, stitch granuloma, keloid.
questions.learning: Marginal mandibular nerve — The marginal mandibular nerve is least likely to be injured during thyroid surgery as it is high up (mandibular margin) than the dissection plane of the approach to thyroid surgery.

questions.text: Which of the following veins drain into brachiocephalic vein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left superior intercostal vein

The left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein.

Tributaries of the brachiocephalic vein:

• Left and right internal thoracic veins
• Left and right inferior thyroid veins
• Left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein.

The right superior intercostal vein drains into the azygos vein.

Option A - Hemiazygous vein drains into the azygous vein.

Option B - Superior thyroid veins drain directly into internal jugular veins.

Option C - Right superior intercostal vein drains into the azygous vein.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 33-year-old male met with a road traffic accident. There is persistent watery discharge mixed with blood from his nose for 3 days which cannot be sniffed back. Which of the following should not be done in this condition?
options: Plan surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery
Bed rest and avoiding strenuous activity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plan surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery

In the given scenario of a male presenting with watery nasal discharge mixed with blood that cannot be sniffed back following a road traffic accident is suggestive of CSF rhinorrhea. Surgical treatment with functional endoscopic sinus surgery should not be done in this patient.

CSF rhinorrhea refers to the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid into the nose. It can occur as clear fluid or be mixed with blood, particularly in cases of acute head injuries. Fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid is the most common cause of this. Other causes include accidental or surgical trauma, infection and inflammation of the sinuses, neoplasms, and congenital lesions associated with skull base defects or may occur spontaneously.

When CSF rhinorrhea occurs after head trauma, it often contains a mixture of blood, leading to a characteristic appearance known as the double-target sign when collected on a piece of filter paper. This sign presents as a central red spot (indicating blood) surrounded by a lighter peripheral halo.

CSF fluid gushes down on straining and bending forward. It cannot be sniffed back. CSF doesn’t stiffen a handkerchief, but nasal secretions do because of their mucus content.

High-resolution computerized tomography (HRCT) is the investigation of choice for localizing the site of the leak.(Option A)

Beta-2 transferrin protein detection by electrophoresis is a sensitive and specific test for detecting CSF rhinorrhea. Beta trace protein is another protein that is secreted by meninges and choroid plexus and is specific to CSF.

Treatment of CSF rhinorrhea:

* Bed rest with head elevation.

* Avoid blowing the nose, sneezing, and straining. (Option C)

* Prophylactic antibiotics can be administered to prevent meningitis. (Option D)

* Early cases of post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhea are managed conservatively by placing the patient in a semi-sitting position.

* Persistent cases may be treated surgically by intracranial or nasal endoscopic approach.(option B)

Feature

Nasal secretion

History

Nasal or sinus surgery, Sneezing, nasal stuffiness, head injury, or intracranial tumor

Sneezing, nasal stuffiness, head injury, or itching in the nose, or lacrimation

Flow of discharge

A few drops or a stream of fluid gushes down when bending forward or straining and cannot be sniffed back

Continuous. No effect on bending forward or straining. Can be sniffed back

Character of discharge

Thin, watery, and clear

Slimy (mucous) or clear (tears)

Sugar content

More than 30 mg/dl

Less than 10 mg/dl

The presence of beta-2 transferrin and beta-trace proteins

Always present. It is specific to CSF

Always absent

Pearl PF1951: Features of CSF rhinorrhea

* Reservoir sign - In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose.

* Double ring sign or halo sign or target sign - CSF is mixed with blood and collected on a piece of filter paper. It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo.

The image below shows the double ring sign in CSF rhinorrhoea:

* CSF can’t be sniffed back.

* CSF doesn’t stiffen the handkerchief.

Note: The repeated reappearance of pus immediately after cleaning, in the external auditory canal of patients with acute mastoiditis/coalescent mastoiditis is also referred to as Reservoir sign.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which term is used to describe the practice of disseminating a particular belief system with the aim of influencing public opinion and behavior?
questions.explanation: Health propaganda is defined as the communication of information or a particular belief system with the specific intent to influence public opinion and behavior, often using emotional appeals rather than objective facts. It is typically one-way and aims for immediate persuasion or "indoctrination". In contrast, health education (Option C) is a two-way process designed to empower individuals with knowledge, allowing them to make their own informed health decisions based on scientific evidence. Health information (Option D) refers to the dissemination of raw, objective health facts without a specific behavioral agenda. A health doctrine (Option A) is a formal set of principles or beliefs held by an organization. The key differentiator for propaganda is its manipulative nature and focus on behavioral control rather than autonomous learning. Understanding this distinction is vital for public health practitioners to ensure their community outreach remains ethical, empowering, and grounded in the principles of authentic education rather than mere influence
questions.learning: Health propaganda is defined as the communication of information or a particular belief system with the specific intent to influence public opinion and behavior, often using emotional appeals rather than objective facts.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female went on vacation and fell asleep while sitting on a beach. After some time she woke with sunburn. Later when she went back home, she experienced pain while taking a warm bath (40°C). Which of the following receptors is responsible for the pain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Innocuos thermal receptor - allodynia

The receptors responsible for this are innocuous thermal receptors which have perceived ordinarily non-noxious stimulus (i.e., warm bath) as severe pain also known as allodynia.

In this case, the warm bath at 40°C (typically not painful) causes pain due to sunburn, which sensitizes the skin. After sunburn, the skin becomes more sensitive, and thermal receptors that usually detect warmth now trigger pain signals in response to non-painful thermal stimuli, leading to allodynia.

Innocuous thermoreceptors, which detect non-harmful temperature changes(cold and warm), are specialized nerve endings found on the skin. Cold receptors are located on the dendritic endings of Aδ and C fibers, while warm receptors are situated on C fibers. The specific thermosensitive molecular channels mediating innocuous heat stimuli is transient receptor potential (TRP) cation channel TRPV1 and TRPM8 cation channel for innocuous cold stimuli.

Thermal hyperalgesia(increased response to noxious stimulation) is mediated by activation of NMDA receptors.  After tissue or nerve injury, C-fibers discharges release glutamate and neurokinins from primary afferent terminals, leading to the release of peptides (e.g., substance P; calcitonin gene-related peptide, CGRP). As a result, a voltage-dependent magnesium block on NMDA receptors is removed allowing for an influx of calcium that triggers a cascade of intracellular events leading to the development and maintenance of hyperalgesia.(Option D)
questions.learning: Innocuos thermal receptor - allodynia — The receptors responsible for this are innocuous thermal receptors which have perceived ordinarily non-noxious stimulus (i.e., warm bath) as severe pain also known as allodynia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Plummer-Vinson syndrome: I. Findings include cervical oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia. II. It is a rare disease, mainly affecting middle-aged women. III. There is predisposition to postcricoid, cervical oesophageal cancer. IV. Treatment is usually surgical. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

Plummer–Vinson syndrome (Paterson–Brown–Kelly syndrome) is a rare disorder characterized by the triad of:

• Iron deficiency anemia
• Upper (postcricoid/cervical) esophageal web
• Progressive dysphagia

It predominantly affects middle-aged women and is considered a premalignant condition, with an increased risk of postcricoid and upper esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

The following statements are true:

• I. Findings include cervical oesophageal web, iron deficiency anaemia and dysphagia: This is the classic triad of Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
• II. It is a rare disease, mainly affecting middle-aged women: Most commonly affects women between 40–70 years of age.
• III. There is predisposition to postcricoid, cervical oesophageal cancer: Patients have an increased risk of postcricoid and upper esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, necessitating long-term follow-up.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Treatment is usually surgical: Treatment is primarily conservative:

• Iron supplementation often improves dysphagia.
• Persistent esophageal webs are treated with endoscopic dilatation, not surgery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman presents with fatigue, easy bruising, and recent onset of hematochezia. Over the past month, she has noted progressive weakness and decreased energy. On examination, she is pale with multiple ecchymoses over the trunk. There is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings: • Hemoglobin: 7.2 g/dL • MCV: 90 fL • Platelets: 10,000/mm³ • Leukocytes: 1,050/mm³ (Neutrophils 5%, Lymphocytes 95%) Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient’s condition?
options: Autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells
Bone marrow infiltration by malignant proliferating cells
Splenic sequestration due to reticuloendothelial hyperactivity
Immune-mediated platelet destruction via anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells

A plastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow due to immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells, most commonly by cytotoxic T cells. It presents with anemia, infections (neutropenia), and bleeding (thrombocytopenia) in the absence of organomegaly.

• Pancytopenia (↓ RBC, ↓ WBC, ↓ platelets)
• Normocytic anemia (MCV normal)
• No hepatosplenomegaly
• Bleeding + infections

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

B. Leukemia → usually organomegaly + blasts

C. Hypersplenism → splenomegaly present

D. ITP → isolated thrombocytopenia
questions.learning: Autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells — A plastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow due to immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells, most commonly by cytotoxic T cells.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which vaccines are typically administered to newborns?
questions.explanation: The "birth dose" regimen in India’s National Immunization Schedule consists of exactly three vaccines administered immediately after birth. These are BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) to protect against severe forms of tuberculosis, OPV (zero dose of Oral Polio Vaccine), and Hepatitis B (birth dose). Pentavalent and Hib (Option A) are initiated at 6 weeks. MR (measles-rubella, Options A and B) is given at 9 months. IPV (inactivated polio vaccine, Option D) is administered at 6 and 14 weeks. This combination of three vaccines at birth provides foundational immunity against TB, Polio, and Hepatitis B before the infant leaves the hospital. Therefore, Option C represents the complete and accurate standard of care for neonatal immunization

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure(s) in the following histological image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glomerulus

The above histology image shows the glomerulus.

Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium. Blood enters the tuft through an afferent arteriole and leaves it through an efferent arteriole. It is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.

Option A: Leydig cells, also known as interstitial cells of Leydig, are present in the interstitial connective between seminiferous tubules.

The testis contains numerous seminiferous tubules separated by connective tissue in between. Seminiferous tubules are lined by several spermatogonia cells, which produce spermatozoa, and Sertoli (sustentacular) cells, which have a supportive function.

The connective tissue in between the tubules is made up of Leydig cells, collagen fibers, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, blood vessels, and lymphatics. Leydig cells are large, round, or polyhedral cells with eccentric nuclei. They are lightly stained and often have a foamy appearance. They secrete testosterone upon stimulation by luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary.

The image below shows seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells.

Option B: Islets of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers and contain numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. The islet cells are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The islet of Langerhans is mainly composed of three types of cells:

• α or A cells - located peripherally and secrete glucagon
• β or B cells - located centrally and produce insulin
• δ or D cells - scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

The image given below shows the islets of Langerhans.

Option C: Hassall's corpuscles are small rounded structures present in the medulla of the thymus. Each corpuscle has a central core of degenerated epithelial cells and macrophages surrounded by concentrically arranged epithelial cells. The degenerated cells ultimately give pink staining hyaline mass. The function of the corpuscles of Hassall is still not known.

The image given below shows Hassall's corpuscle.
questions.learning: Glomerulus — The above histology image shows the glomerulus. Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Zika virus is transmitted by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aedes aegypti

Zika virus may be transmitted by the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus.

The symptoms of Zika virus disease include fever, rash, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, malaise, or headache. These symptoms are mild and usually last for 2-7 days.

It can spread via:

* Mosquito bites

* Bloodstream

* Unsafe sexual practices

* Vertical transmission

Zika virus infection during pregnancy may lead to microcephaly or congenital Zika syndrome.

The complications include:

* Guillain-Barré syndrome

* Encephalitis

* Meningitis

* Myelitis

Pearl PF0821: The Mosquito

* Mosquitoes are global in distribution.

* The main species of mosquitoes include the Anopheles, Culex, Aedes and Mansonia.

* Flight range varies up to 11 kms, except Aedes for which it is 100 metres.

* Life span of mosquitoes is around 8 to 34 days.

* Their morphology consists of a head with a proboscis, a pair of palpi and a pair of antennae; a thorax and an abdomen.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to law, an act is not considered an offense if it is committed by a person of unsound mind who is incapable of understanding the nature of the act or that it is wrong. Which legal rule of insanity applies in this situation?
questions.explanation: The legal principle described is the Mc Naughton's (M'Naghten) rule, which serves as the foundational standard for the insanity defense in many jurisdictions, including India (Section 84 of the IPC). It states that a person is not criminally responsible if, at the time of the act, they suffered from a "defect of reason" from a disease of the mind such that they were unaware of the nature and quality of the act, or that the act was wrong or contrary to the law. Durham's rule (Option A) is a broader standard stating an act is not an offense if it was the "product" of a mental disease. Curren's rule (Option C) relates to the substantial capacity to conform conduct to the law. The Irresistible impulse rule (Option D) focuses on a person's inability to control their actions even if they knew they were wrong. Mc Naughton's remains the most widely used legal test for criminal responsibility in forensic psychiatry
questions.learning: The legal principle described is the Mc Naughton's (M'Naghten) rule, which serves as the foundational standard for the insanity defense in many jurisdictions, including India (Section 84 of the IPC).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with acute epigastric pain and fever. He has a past history of cholelithiasis. On examination, abdominal guarding and rigidity present. His serum amylase, lipase are raised and patient has leucocytosis. What is true regarding his condition?
options: Serum amylase remains elevated even after 30 days of resolution of acute pancreatitis
Serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase
Increase in the level of serum lipase is directly proportional to the severity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase

The patient presents with features suggestive of acute pancreatitis (epigastric pain, fever, history of cholelithiasis, guarding/rigidity, raised serum amylase and lipase, and leukocytosis). For acute pancreatitis, serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase.

Lipase has a higher specificity for diagnosing acute pancreatitis, as elevated amylase can occur in other conditions such as salivary gland disorders, intestinal obstruction, or renal failure. Lipase also remains elevated longer than amylase.

The diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis require at least two of the following three features:

1. Characteristic Abdominal Pain:
Acute onset of severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back.
Pain may worsen after eating and is associated with nausea and vomiting.
2. Serum Lipase and/or Amylase Elevation:
At least 3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN).
Lipase is preferred due to its higher specificity and longer half-life.
3. Imaging Findings:
Characteristic findings of pancreatitis on imaging (CT scan, MRI, or ultrasound), such as:
Pancreatic enlargement
Peripancreatic fluid collections
Inflammatory changes in and around the pancreas

Other Options:

Option A: Amylase levels normalize within 3-5 days after an episode of acute pancreatitis.

Option C: Hypocalcemia is more commonly observed, due to fat saponification in severe cases.

Option D: The degree of elevation of serum lipase does not correlate with the severity of acute pancreatitis. Severity is assessed using clinical scores like Ranson's criteria, APACHE II, or CT severity index.
questions.learning: Serum lipase is more specific than serum amylase — The patient presents with features suggestive of acute pancreatitis (epigastric pain, fever, history of cholelithiasis, guarding/rigidity, raised serum amylase and lipase, and leukocytosis).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 40-year-old man reports excessive, uncontrollable worry about everyday activities, financial matters, and his health for the past two years, accompanied by restlessness, fatigue, and disturbed sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) (Option D): excessive and uncontrollable worry about a variety of topics (finances, health, daily life) occurring more days than not for at least six months. He also exhibits the required physical symptoms, including restlessness, fatigue, and disturbed sleep. Depression (Option A) primarily involves a low mood and loss of interest rather than pervasive worry. Illness anxiety disorder (Option B) is limited to worries about having a serious illness. Somatoform disorder (Option C) involves multiple unexplained physical complaints. GAD is a chronic condition that significantly impairs daily functioning. It is often treated with a combination of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and medications like SSRIs or SNRIs . Because the man's anxiety is broad, persistent, and accompanied by physiological tension, GAD is the definitive clinical diagnosis for his presentation
questions.learning: The patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) (Option D): excessive and uncontrollable worry about a variety of topics (finances, health, daily life) occurring more days than not for at least six months.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient got pricked by a rose thorn and presents with multiple vesicles on hand and multiple eruptions along the lymphatics. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sporothrix Schenckii

Presence of multiple vesicles on hand and multiple eruptions along lymphatics in a patient pricked by a thorn suggests infection with Sporothrix schenckii.

Sporothrix schenckii causes sporotrichosis, a chronic granulomatous disease, by traumatic inoculation into the skin. This is usually followed by spread along the draining lymphatics and lymph nodes.

It is a thermally dimorphic fungus. It is in the yeast phase in tissues and in cultures at 37°C, and in the mycelia phase in nature and cultures at 25°C. When it is cultured, the colonies are blackish-brown and fuzzy. The organism produces branching, septate hyphae, and microconidia clustered at the ends of conidiophores. It exists as cigar-shaped yeast cells. Stains used for identifying yeast forms:

* Gomori methenamine silver-cell wall appears black

* Periodic acid-Schiff stain - cell wall appears red

* Fluorescent antibody staining

The image given below shows, (A)- (i) culture at 37°C (ii) culture at 25°C. (B) fungi with clustered microconidia with conidiophore.  (C) Magnified image showing branching and septate hyphae.

Clinical features: The initial infection develops as a nodule, which may break down to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. Untreated, the disease progresses and new nodules develop along the lymphatics leading to a chain of nodules. Less commonly it may also cause systemic infection following inhalation, which causes local pulmonary disease or may lead to widely disseminated lesions in joints, meninges, and skin.

Direct microscopic examination of necrotic material in KOH mount or histopathological examination of tissue sections stained by methenamine silver stain shows the asteroid body. Asteroid body is a rounded or oval, basophilic, yeast-like body 3-5 μmin diameter, with rays of an eosinophilic substance radiating from the yeast cell.

Treatment:

* Cutaneous infection – Potassium iodide-250mg thrice daily for 2-4 months

* Lymphocutaneous infection - Itraconazole, fluconazole(400mg/day), terbinafine(250mg/day) and cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen

* Disseminated infection - Amphotericin B

Other options:

Option A: Blastomycosis is an infection caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. It causes a chronic infection with granulomatous and suppurative lesions, which starts in the lungs but may disseminate to other organs. Symptoms of an acute lower respiratory tract infection with pulmonary infiltrates are the most common clinical presentations. Histopathological staining shows thick-walled yeast, with single broad-based budding (figure 8 appearance).

The image given below is that of Blastomyces which is a thick-walled yeast, with single broad-based budding (figure 8 appearance).

Option B: Coccidiomycosis is caused by Coccidioides immitis which is a thermally dimorphic fungus. It occurs as a spherule in tissues and culture at 37°C and as the mycelial form in soil and culture at room temperature. They are endemic to the arid desert regions of the southwestern USA and California. Infection is acquired by inhaling dust containing arthrospores of the fungus.

Option D: Candida species are yeast-like fungi, which normally inhabit the skin and mucosa. Candida albicans is an ovoid or spherical budding cell, which produces pseudohyphae both in tissues and in culture. Candidiasis is an opportunistic endogenous infection.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy presents with tremors, difficulty in speech, and behavioral changes. On examination, he has hepatomegaly and a golden-brown ring at the limbus of the cornea (Kayser–Fleischer ring). Wilson’s disease is suspected. Which of the following is the best investigation to support the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver biopsy for copper estimation

Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by defective copper transport and impaired biliary excretion. This results in excess copper accumulation in the liver, brain (basal ganglia), and cornea, producing features such as hepatomegaly, neurological symptoms, behavioral changes, and Kayser–Fleischer rings.

The most definitive investigation to support the diagnosis is liver biopsy for quantitative copper estimation, which directly measures hepatic copper concentration. Markedly increased hepatic copper confirms abnormal copper accumulation.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Serum ceruloplasmin: Often decreased in Wilson disease but can be normal in some cases, so it is not definitive.
• Serum copper: Usually low due to reduced ceruloplasmin-bound copper and is not reliable for diagnosis.
• Urinary copper excretion: Increased in Wilson disease and useful for screening/monitoring but less definitive than hepatic copper estimation.
questions.learning: Liver biopsy for copper estimation Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by defective copper transport and impaired biliary excretion.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For a newborn born to an HIV-positive mother who did not receive antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy, what is the recommended initial post-exposure prophylaxis regimen to reduce the risk of mother-to-child HIV transmission?
questions.explanation: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) is critical for HIV management. When a newborn is delivered by a high-risk woman (e.g., one who was not on treatment or has a high viral load), dual post-exposure prophylaxis is required. The current recommendation is a combination of Nevirapine and Zidovudine for 6 weeks. This intensified regimen is more effective than monotherapy in preventing vertical transmission in high-risk scenarios. Nevirapine monotherapy for 6 weeks (Option D) is the standard for low-risk infants whose mothers were stable on ART. Options A (6 months) and B (Zidovudine only) are not the standard protocols for this specific situation. Alongside prophylaxis, these infants require early infant diagnosis via HIV-DNA PCR testing at 6 weeks. Breastfeeding recommendations vary; in India, exclusive breast feeding is encouraged for 6 months if the mother is on ART. Early identification of maternal status and rapid neonatal intervention significantly reduce the rate of pediatric HIV
questions.learning: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) is critical for HIV management. When a newborn is delivered by a high-risk woman (e.g., one who was not on treatment or has a high viral load), dual post-exposure prophylaxis is required.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy was brought to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints of intense itching, photopobia and ropy discharge from his eyes. Moreover, on examination the following finding is present. What is the most probable diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis

The above image depicts cobblestone appearance, which is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, and also the presence of ropy discharge points towards the diagnosis of vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) or spring catarrh .

* It is also called as warm weather conjunctivitis

* It primarily affects boys, and the onset is generally from the age of 5 years.

* It is primarily a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction that is IgE mediated. It also involves type 4 hypersensitivity reaction.

Classical features of conjunctiva in VKC:

Palpebral VKC

* Cobblestone papillae: upper tarsal conjunctiva

* Associated with ropy discharge

* Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

Limbal VKC: Horner–Trantas spots are white dots consisting of eosinophils and epithelial debris in the limbal area.

Corneal signs in VKC:

* Shield ulcers

* Vernal plaques

* Subepithelial scarring

* Pseudo-gerontoxon resembles arcus senilus; it has a cupid's bow outline

Image: Horner Trantas spots

Below image- Bitot spots

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the drug of choice for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Voriconazole

Voriconazole is the drug of choice in the treatment of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

Voriconazole can also be used against Candida species (including glabrata and krusei), Scedosporium and Fusarium. The other options - itraconazole, posaconazole, lyophylised Amphotericin B - can be used as alternatives for the treatment of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis if voriconazole is unavailable.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct statement regarding Huntington's chorea?
options: It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder
There is loss of function type of mutation
There are abnormal repeats of CUG
Abnormality is seen due to mutation in chromosome 6
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder

Huntington's chorea is a trinucleotide repeat disorder.

It is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder. It is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeats (>40). It occurs due to a gain-of-function (expansion) mutation in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4p.

The disease shows genetic anticipation and has an early-onset (2-3 decades) if inherited from the father.

Cognitive impairment is an early feature. Pathologically, atrophy of caudate and putamen with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly is seen. Decreased acetylcholine leads to dementia and decreased GABA and increased dopamine lead to chorea.

Treatment consists of haloperidol and tetrabenazine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the most effective indicator for assessing the overall disease burden?
questions.explanation: The Disability Adjusted Life Year (DALY) is a composite time-based measure that combines years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLL) and years lived with a disability (YLD). It is widely considered the most effective indicator for assessing the global burden of disease because it quantifies the "gap" between current health status and an ideal health situation where the entire population lives to an advanced age, free of disease and disability. Quality-adjusted life years (QALY, Option A) are primarily used in cost-utility analysis to measure the quality and quantity of life gained from an intervention. Health adjusted life expectancy (HALE, Option B) estimates the number of years a person can expect to live in "full health". Disability-free life expectancy (DFLE, Option D) measures the remaining years of life spent without any functional limitations. DALY stands out because it captures both fatal and non-fatal health outcomes in a single metric, allowing for a comprehensive comparison across different diseases and populations
questions.learning: The Disability Adjusted Life Year (DALY) is a composite time-based measure that combines years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLL) and years lived with a disability (YLD).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Although many animals are implicated in the spread of rabies, dogs are the most common ones. Also, it usually affects children in developing countries. Knowing this, what is the most cost-effective and logical way to reduce the incidence of rabies?
options: Testing all the dogs for rabies
Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs
Increase capacity of healthcare workers for surveillance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs

Reducing the stray dog population and vaccinating all dogs is the most cost-effective and logical way to reduce the incidence of rabies. The Animal Birth Control initiative from the Government of India is directed towards this goal.

Rabies is a highly fatal viral disease caused by Lyssavirus type 1, affecting the central nervous system. Dogs are considered the major source of rabies infection. Thus immunization of dogs at the age of 3-4 months and booster doses at regular intervals is recommended to control rabies. The type of vaccines used are:

• BPL inactivated nervous tissue vaccine - it is a single-dose vaccine. Booster is advised after 6 months and subsequently every year.
• Modified live virus vaccine - it is also a single-dose vaccine and a booster is given every 3 years.

Other methods to control rabies include:

• Registration and licensing of all domestic dogs
• The immediate killing of dogs and cats bitten by rabid animals
• 6 months quarantine for imported dogs
• Educating people regarding dog care and prevention of rabies.

Note: Strengthening laboratory facilities and surveillance are also the methods used to reduce the incidence according to the National Rabies Control Program (NRCP)

Humans get infected after a deep bite or scratch by an infected animal. The transmission also occurs when the saliva of the infected dog comes into direct contact with human mucosa or fresh skin wounds.

Rabies in man is also known as hydrophobia. The clinical features usually begin as prodromal symptoms like headache, and fever followed by neurological symptoms. The patients usually present with confusion, hallucination, irritability, hydrophobia, aerophobia, and muscle spasms. They also present with symptoms of autonomic dysfunction such as hypersalivation, lacrimation, cardiac arrhythmias, etc.

Laboratory tests for rabies include:

• Fluorescent antibody test is a highly reliable and best test for rapid detection of rabies antigen in the infected specimens
• Microscopic examination of the brain tissue to demonstrate Negri bodies.
questions.learning: Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs Reducing the stray dog population and vaccinating all dogs is the most cost-effective and logical way to reduce the incidence of rabies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones primarily acts on the post-ovulatory endometrium?
questions.explanation: Following ovulation, the ruptured follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, which secretes high levels of Progesterone. Progesterone is the primary hormone that acts on the post-ovulatory endometrium, transforming it into a secretory state that is receptive to embryo implantation. While Estrogen (Option D) is present throughout the cycle and helps maintain the lining, it is the dominant hormone of the pre-ovulatory (proliferative) phase. Luteinizing hormone (Option A) and Follicular stimulating hormone (Option B) are pituitary gonadotropins that stimulate the ovaries but do not directly act on the endometrial tissue to induce secretory changes. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses, leading to a sharp drop in progesterone, which triggers the shedding of the endometrium during menstruation. Understanding this hormonal sequence is fundamental for evaluating menstrual irregularities and infertility. The secretory transformation of the endometrium is the defining biological event of the luteal phase

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Histopathological examination reveals follicular cells with abundant pink, eosinophilic cytoplasm. This finding is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid often features cells with abundant, granular, pink eosinophilic cytoplasm. These are known as Hürthle cells (oncocytes), and they are highly characteristic of certain variants of follicular neoplasms. The eosinophilic appearance is due to the dense accumulation of mitochondria within the cytoplasm. Regarding the distractors, Papillary CA (Option A) is identified by "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies, but not typically by Hürthle cell changes. Medullary CA (Option C) arises from parafollicular C-cells and is distinguished by amyloid stroma and polygonal cells. Anaplastic CA (Option D) is highly undifferentiated with pleomorphic giant cells and lacks the follicular architecture seen in this description. While Hürthle cells can appear in benign conditions like Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, their presence in a thyroid malignancy strongly points toward a follicular origin
